102zhmb09yv: There are five gas parameters. SOURCE_ACCOUNT_ACCESS_COST is COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS if source is cold and WARM_ACCESS if it is warm. SETCODEFROM_SOURCE_GAS is SOURCE_ACCOUNT_ACCESS_COST + WARM_ACCESS, SETCODEFROM_CURRENT_ACCESS_GAS is WARM_ACCESS, SETCODEFROM_WRITE_GAS is ACCOUNT_WRITE, and SETCODEFROM_STATE_GAS is 0. Each execution attempt first charges SETCODEFROM_SOURCE_GAS. It is the sum of loading the source account leaf (SOURCE_ACCOUNT_ACCESS_COST) and verifying the source code (WARM_ACCESS, a fixed cost covering the code storage access needed to inspect the bytecode). Once this charge is made, source is added to EIP-2929's accessed_addresses regardless of validity. Verification reads only source's own code and does not follow EIP-7702 delegation, so the delegation target is not accessed, charged, or warmed. If source is valid, SETCODEFROM_CURRENT_ACCESS_GAS is charged, the two code hashes are compared, and if they differ SETCODEFROM_WRITE_GAS is charged and the update is made. The write cost follows ACCOUNT_WRITE from EIP-8038. Based on the current EIP-8038 values (ACCOUNT_WRITE 9000, COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS 3000, WARM_ACCESS 100), an invalid source costs 3100 when cold and 200 when warm, a valid source with the same hash costs 3200 and 300, and an actual update costs 12200 and 9300. Because there is no code storage work, the cost is independent of the source code size, and it is the same when executed inside initcode. The state gas for adding an account leaf at creation itself may be incurred separately.

Solidity has had overflow checks turned on by default for all arithmetic operations since 0.8, and before that OpenZeppelin's SafeMath library served the same role. 10nsq6n9yzv: The EL learns several minutes in advance when its own validator will propose. An EL run by the same operator would learn this a few seconds in advance anyway through the payload attributes, but a remote or shared EL, or anyone reading engine API traffic that is authenticated with JWT but not encrypted, can also learn it. Since the proposal duty itself is public, what this exposes is which node runs that validator, and that becomes a lead for targeted attacks. Preparation that peers can observe, such as collecting the full blob set or a change in gossip behavior, carries the same risk, so the specification requires randomized start timing and that the information not be exposed through public RPC, metrics, or logs. For DoS, only an authenticated CL can call it, requests are capped at 256, and the only damage a misbehaving CL can cause is wasting preparation resources that the EL itself bounds. For correctness, the call cannot change what the block is built on, and prepared results are only used when what they depended on still holds for the actual parent and payload attributes, a check that is the EL's responsibility.

10r7pbg8nck: 0x00 is the withdrawal credential format from Ethereum's launch. Withdrawals are controlled by a BLS key and there is no execution-layer address. After the Capella upgrade opened a one-way transition to 0x01, the roughly 600,000 0x00 validators that existed then have fallen to about 9,200 (as of mainnet in August 2026), but the decline has stalled. The number of migrations has dropped to double digits per month, and among the still-active 0x00 validators, several hundred appear to have lost their keys, having not attested in over six months. Yet no one can exit a 0x00 validator that has lost its key. Voluntary exit requires a signing key, and EIP-7002, which triggers exits from the execution layer, requires an execution address that 0x00 does not have. Natural attrition through penalties alone, at the measured penalty rate (about 0.55 ETH per year), would take roughly 28 years. In the meantime every fork must keep maintaining 0x00-related code, and when the transition to an era where BLS signatures are broken by quantum computers arrives, these validators, which cannot act, become a burden on the whole design.

10rgzh6zk5d: Chunks have no individual signatures. Authenticity comes entirely from the bid signature through payload_chunks_root. The root carried in a chunk is not authenticated by itself, but a chunk is accepted only if a bid that passed signature verification committed to that root. A chunk that points to an unknown root is not forwarded, so unsigned chunk spam is filtered out at the first hop. slot and beacon_block_root are included in neither the bid signature nor the inclusion proof, so they are restricted to lookup use only. A chunk resent with a changed slot fails the (slot, payload_chunks_root) membership check, and a chunk with a changed beacon_block_root is rejected once the block containing the bid is known. Chunk bytes are bound to the proof, so a message that differs only in the hint fields cannot alter the reassembled envelope. For two different chunks at the same (payload_chunks_root, index) to both verify, a Merkle tree collision would be required, so per-index chunk equivocation is impossible. The upper bound on chunk.index is a key safeguard. is_valid_merkle_branch reads only the low CHUNK_INCLUSION_PROOF_DEPTH bits, so without the bound the same chunk could be spread again as index + k * TOTAL_EXECUTION_PAYLOAD_CHUNKS. Buffering before the block is also bounded. A node stores at most TOTAL_EXECUTION_PAYLOAD_CHUNKS chunks per payload_chunks_roots entry, and the size of that set is limited by bid gossip validation (the builder signature and the slot window). A chunk passing gossip validation does not make the reassembled envelope valid, and full envelope validation takes place after reassembly, as in EIP-7732.

10ypefci94v: Currently the SELFDESTRUCT instruction deletes the code and storage of a contract account entirely and sends the remaining ether to a specified address. This is an operation that changes account state significantly. Ethereum plans to hold state in a new data structure called a Verkle tree. In a Verkle tree, one account's data is stored scattered across multiple keys, and it is not visible from the outside which account those keys belong to. As a result, deleting an entire account becomes practically impossible. The source document explains that removing this instruction is a necessary condition for statelessness, where nodes do not need to hold the full state. On the other hand, there is no strong reason to need SELFDESTRUCT as it stands today, and apps that use it only to recover funds keep working after the change. So the proposal is to replace the instruction with a simple behavior that only sends ether, instead of removing it.

11c4irwj6v: Deploying the same code to many addresses is very common onchain, and smart account wallets are the prime example. To reduce deployment cost, ERC-1167 clones or upgradeable proxies are used. Clones are lightweight but their implementation address cannot be changed, while proxies can be changed but pay the cost of reading the implementation address from storage on every call. Both need EVM code that copies the received calldata into memory and performs a delegate call. According to a Geth team survey (EthCC[9] "Not all state is equal"), 97.1% of about 50 million deployed contracts are code that has already been deployed before, and 28.6% of unique bytecode is small code under 1 KiB. Clones and proxies likely make up a large share of that, so a way is needed to handle this role at the protocol level more compactly and cheaply.

11cwa1u5ohh: You can create an account whose ECDSA private key no one has ever held. It works on the same principle as Nick's method (ERC-2470), which is used for keyless contract deployment. The creator generates an ML-DSA-44 key pair and computes the authorization message for nonce 0, then picks the x-coordinate of a secp256k1 curve point whose discrete log is unknown as r, picks an arbitrary nonzero value as s, and recovers the address via ecrecover(msg_hash, y_parity, r, s). Fund that address with ETH and submit the tuple as a type 0x06 transaction, and the conversion is complete. Recovering the ECDSA private key would require solving the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem, which proves there is no backdoor key. The recommended construction derives r from r_seed = keccak256("nkd-v1" || chain_id || pk) and sets s = 1, so third parties can reproduce it and confirm there is no trapdoor. Because the address is deterministic, funds can be deposited before the conversion transaction is sent. Note, however, that a tuple with chain_id = 0 is valid on every chain, so anyone can replay a published tuple on a different chain to install the same account there.

11qhj9ybx8r: Today on Ethereum, the penalty a validator receives for missing an attestation (a vote on a block) does not depend on how other validators behaved. A validator that misses alone and one that misses together with 30% of the network pay exactly the same penalty each epoch. As a result there is almost no economic reason to diversify across nodes, regions, clients, internet providers and cloud vendors, because the only benefit is lowering the probability that all validators stop at once. Historical attestation data shows that validators under the same operator miss together far more often than chance, while solo stakers behave almost independently. Penalizing correlated failure can reduce the economies of scale of large, homogeneous staking operations without having to identify the operating entity. The protocol already prices correlated failure, but only when a third or more of the stake stops and the inactivity leak turns on. In the range below that, from 1% to 33%, correlated failure is effectively free. This EIP smoothly attaches a cost proportional to the size of the event in that range.

11vhzctf934: TXTRACE gives only the topics and the data length of an event, and the variable-length data itself cannot be returned as a single stack word. EVENTDATACOPY copies that data into memory. The stack, from the top, is event_index, memOffset, dataOffset, length, and there is no output. It copies length bytes of the event's non-indexed data, starting at dataOffset, to memOffset, and the copy and memory expansion are the same as CALLDATACOPY. Gas is also the same as CALLDATACOPY: a fixed 3 plus memory expansion and copy costs. However, the source range check is stricter. If event_index is greater than or equal to events_count, execution aborts with an exception, and if dataOffset + length exceeds the event data length, execution aborts with an exception even when length is 0. The difference is that CALLDATACOPY does not abort because of the source range. The addition is computed without 256-bit wrapping.

With this structure, it is not possible to efficiently prove a specific part of a receipt, such as a single log. As a result, smart contracts that handle L2 fraud proofs or apps that verify log data must fetch the entire receipt, which is a significant burden. Missing information is also a problem. When a receipt is queried via JSON-RPC, it returns the from, gasUsed, and contractAddress values, but the receipt as actually recorded on chain contains no information to verify these values. This EIP solves both problems together by converting receipts into an SSZ (Simple Serialize) format that is hashed as a Merkle tree, and by embedding the missing information directly into the receipt.

Also, if a contract using a currently undefined opcode is already deployed, that contract's behavior could break later when a new instruction is assigned to that opcode. The execution layer uses EIP-7928-style keccak256(RLP(CAL)) in the chunk header, while the consensus layer uses SSZ hash_tree_root for inclusion proofs; both point to the same RLP-encoded CAL data. 12spzoen52x: Following FIPS 204, the precompile computes ML-DSA.Verify(pubkey, message, signature) over the raw message. It also performs the matrix expansion Â = ExpandA(ρ) and the internal hash μ = H(BytesToBits(tr) ‖ M') itself, and returns success only when verification passes. Malformed encodings, such as coefficients out of range, a non-canonical hint h, or a ‖z‖ bound violation, MUST return failure rather than revert. This is so that callers can treat 'invalid signature' as a boolean. The output is always exactly 32 bytes. 0x00..01 is a valid signature, and 0x00..00 is an invalid or malformed signature, or an input shorter than PK_LEN + SIG_LEN. Because it does not revert except on gas exhaustion, the call success flag carries no signature information, and calling code must check the returned word with ISZERO along with the success flag. The fixed-length return is a deliberate difference from ECRECOVER and the EIP-7951 secp256r1 verification, which return an empty byte string on failure. A call to an address with no code also succeeds and returns an empty value, so with the empty-value approach 'invalid signature' and 'fork not activated or address not assigned on this chain' are byte-for-byte identical. This is the repeated complaint about P256VERIFY. In this proposal, a return length other than 32 means the precompile is absent, and 32 zero bytes means the signature failed. The cost is one word of memory and the accidental fail-closed behavior that Solidity gained when decoding an empty return value, and nothing more.

1332utwehbi: Regular accounts on Ethereum today use a signature scheme called ECDSA. This scheme can be broken once a sufficiently powerful quantum computer appears. The quantum-resistant signature algorithms meant to replace it (FALCON, DILITHIUM, etc.) rely on polynomial multiplication as their core operation, but implementing this directly in the EVM today is prohibitively expensive in gas. By the source text's measurement, a single FALCON signature verification costs about 1.8 million gas, which can only be experimented with on low-fee L2s and is impractical to use on L1. This EIP lowers that cost substantially by providing the NTT transform, a common building block of polynomial multiplication, as a precompile (a fast operation built into the client in advance). Because it embeds a general-purpose operation rather than one specific algorithm, it can be used to implement either DILITHIUM or FALCON at low cost, and the same operation also accelerates STARK verifiers, helping both scalability and preparedness against the quantum threat.

Every client team must implement and maintain them on its own, so there is an ongoing maintenance cost, and if implementations diverge, it can lead to consensus bugs. The burden is greater for zkEVMs, which verify EVM execution with zero-knowledge proofs, because each precompile needs a separate optimized non-EVM implementation. Yet these three precompiles are hardly used in practice. RIPEMD-160 has very little onchain usage. 99.99% of MODEXP usage is 256-bit moduli for SNARK verification, and BLAKE2f is in practice used by a single contract. This EIP replaces the three precompiles, which are little used or can be replaced at low cost, with ordinary EVM code, reducing the number of special implementations every client must maintain and simplifying the protocol.

Row subnets must use cell-level deltas (EIP-8136) without eager push, and the GroupID is the block root, as with column subnets. The function that assigns blobs to subnets, get_blob_row_subnet(blob_index, slot), is a per-slot pseudorandom permutation that applies compute_shuffled_index seeded with hash(b"ROW_SUBNET" + uint_to_bytes(uint64(slot))). If the blob count is at most ROW_SUBNET_COUNT, the blobs in a slot receive different subnets. If it is larger, blobs whose remainder after division by ROW_SUBNET_COUNT is the same share a subnet, so each subnet carries at most ceil(blob_count / ROW_SUBNET_COUNT) rows. Because the seed depends only on the slot, it can be computed without chain state. A node's designated row subnet is determined by get_row_subnet(node_id), which is the remainder after dividing bytes [8:16] of hash(uint_to_bytes(uint256(node_id))) by ROW_SUBNET_COUNT. Custody group derivation uses bytes [0:8] of the same hash, so the two assignments are independent of each other at no extra hashing cost. A row reconstructor must subscribe to its designated row subnet (MUST), and other nodes are recommended to subscribe when they support cell-level deltas (SHOULD). Subscribing carries no obligation to retain data.

13e2oj4ut6g: Ethereum's state (the full data of accounts and storage) grows larger over time, and the cost of maintaining that larger state grows along with it. However, the gas cost charged for creating a new storage slot for the first time is fixed at the amount originally set, so it no longer matches the actual cost. As a result, the real cost of transactions that create new storage ends up being subsidized by all other users who perform other operations. This price distortion is also one reason raising the gas limit is something people are reluctant to do. This proposal is a stopgap measure that brings the price of state growth closer to its actual cost, so that storage creation is no longer subsidized by other users.

13ezc7qt9oe: The gas cost of an operation that touches state is seen as the sum of up to three independent components. The first is Access, the cost of reading an account or storage slot from the database. COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS, COLD_STORAGE_ACCESS and WARM_ACCESS belong here, and they are renamed EIP-2929 parameters. This EIP raises only COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS and leaves the other two and the cold and warm determination rules unchanged. The second is Write, the cost of writing a leaf when a value changes. Storage slots pay STORAGE_WRITE, and the nonce, balance and code hash of an account pay ACCOUNT_WRITE, and both are constants newly created by this EIP. In the existing scheme, this share was dissolved inside composite constants such as GAS_STORAGE_UPDATE, CALL_VALUE and GAS_CREATE. STORAGE_WRITE is netted per transaction. The SSTORE that moves a slot away from its value at the start of the transaction pays it, and the SSTORE that later reverts it is refunded. ACCOUNT_WRITE is paid per operation. Making a value-bearing CALL to the same recipient twice pays it twice. The rule of paying only once per authority when processing EIP-7702 authorizations exists only in EIP-2780. The third is State creation, which is GAS_STORAGE_SET for a new slot and GAS_NEW_ACCOUNT for a new account. This EIP does not change these values, and EIP-8037 reprices them in the state gas dimension.

The target flag has the widest inclusion window, the whole next epoch, so it reflects whether a validator is alive regardless of block space or timing luck. Source timeliness fails after five slots without a block, so builder, relay or proposer failures can cause source misses for healthy validators. The two-flag condition excludes view disagreements. A validator that missed only the target, because the epoch boundary block was late, a proposer split the view, or a correct minority client saw things differently from a buggy majority, pays only today's penalty. In historical replay, 91 to 97% of baseline stake that was alive but had the wrong target sits in epoch slot 0, and under this condition none of it is weighted or counted in the offline balance. EIP-8333 pins the checkpoint to the last block before the epoch and removes this phenomenon at the root. This EIP is compatible with it but does not depend on it. The option of using the source vote as the basis was rejected. At the peak of the May 2023 incident, 5.3% of stake had a target but no source, versus 0.11% for the opposite case. 13sq3q23msz: The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) operates on 256-bit values by default. EIP-7937 already proposes an EVM64 instruction set that uses only 64-bit operations, but it does so by prefixing existing opcodes, which gives it the best compatibility with the existing EVM at the cost of longer, multi-byte instructions. This EIP takes a different approach. It marks a code section in the new EOF (EVM Object Format) container contract format as an 'EVM64 type', so that the moment execution enters that section the interpreter switches entirely into 64-bit mode. Since no prefix is needed, code size shrinks, and within the section the interpreter has room to optimize execution with a 64-bit stack. The tradeoff is that it only works in EOF contracts, and interacting with system calls that read block information, balances, or storage becomes harder.

13ylidwq97o: Today, Ethereum charges the most expensive cold fee every time a transaction reads an account or storage slot for the first time. In practice, however, because clients (node software) keep recently used data cached in memory for a short time, the actual cost of rereading data that was just used is much lower. In other words, the gas fee schedule is set for the worst case, and it diverges from the actual cost of the common case. This gap also makes it hard to raise the block gas limit, because nodes must provision for the worst case rather than the average case. This proposal discounts the first-access fee for items accessed within the last 32 blocks based on recency, bringing the gas price closer to the actual processing cost and allowing more execution to fit within the same gas limit. The original text explains that most actively used contracts are accessed repeatedly within a few blocks, and in that case total gas usage per block can drop by several percent.

13zzlmh7xnd: Safety depends on the invariant MAX_EXPIRY_SECS x peak_tps <= RING_CAPACITY. With MAX_EXPIRY_SECS = 60 (5 Ethereum slots) and RING_CAPACITY = 2**18, expiring transactions sustained at up to about 4369 TPS will not cause a still-live deadline to be evicted. If deadlines had no upper bound, an attacker could pin a single slot far into the future, and once the ring wrapped past that point a live entry could be evicted, opening a replay window. The replay window is bounded by the deadline d. Resubmission after d is rejected by the expiry_verify frame, and resubmission before d is rejected by the seen check.

147kkygi75h: The index tables are maintained at five levels. The table at each level holds TABLE_SIZES = [1, 4, 16, 64, 256] blocks, first_block is always a multiple of table_size, and TABLE_SIZES[i] is a multiple of TABLE_SIZES[i-1]. So one higher-level table can be built by merging the 4 tables (a fixed number) of the level directly below. The level 0 single-block table is recorded immediately after all transactions in that block are processed, and higher-level tables are recorded after a delay of TABLE_SIZES[i] // 4 blocks. This delay lets merging proceed asynchronously from block processing, so block processing latency does not increase. The root hash of each level is stored in a ring buffer of length TABLES_PER_LEVEL = 1024. A common ratio of 4 is a compromise. A smaller ratio increases the number of levels and so adds tree hashing, and a larger one increases the number of small tables needed for a proof, which makes the proof bigger.

Phase 1 is variable slot time infrastructure: removing the 12-second assumption and replacing functions such as compute_time_at_slot and the fork transition logic with a schedule-based design. Phase 2 is CL performance characterization, using devnets and benchmarks to measure consensus layer bottlenecks (blob propagation, proof aggregation, local block production time). CREATE in a TCREATE account yields the same address sequence in each transaction in which it is created. These addresses are bound to the TCREATE initcode but not to the initcode passed to CREATE. A contract that runs TCREATE for arbitrary callers should put the caller address in the salt, as today's CREATE3 factories do, and the TCREATE account should accept CREATE requests only from the account that deployed it. Otherwise anyone could deploy arbitrary code at an address another user expects. The end-of-transaction finalization does not clear state that other accounts hold about a TCREATE address, such as owners, allowances, and allowlists. The deploying account can later recreate the account with the same salt and initcode and reuse those permissions, and the initcode may return different runtime code each time. Therefore persistent permissions must not be granted to a TCREATE address, and contracts created by that account must receive the privileged address explicitly as an initcode argument. Setting an EIP-7702 delegation to a TCREATE address has the same problem. Between transactions, that address has no code, so a call succeeds with empty code, and the code can be used only after the deploying account creates the account in the same transaction. An account must not delegate to a TCREATE address.

14k1g6kvrcq: The concept of call and return originates with Turing's 1946 ACE design and has proven its value for 80 years. Forth and ACE use a separate return stack isolated from data, and the EVM proposals covered in this document follow the same design. The JVM, CLR, and Wasm all prevent bytecode from touching return addresses and share three common properties: directly interpretable portable bytecode, static control flow verified before execution, and linear-time runtime compilation to machine code. Most of the smart contract world also has native calls. NEAR, Polkadot, Cosmos, and Stellar run Wasm, Solana runs an eBPF-family VM, Aptos and Sui run Move, Starknet runs Cairo, and the latest zkVMs run RISC-V. Algorand's TEAL and eBPF started out with jumps alone but added subroutines once verifiers and analyzers hit their limits. Today, only the EVM, as deployed, remains stuck with unverified code, synthesized calls, and dynamic jumps.

14kra0swddm: Consensus liveness: the builder for slot N+1 cannot build a canonical block before it receives the lists gossiped in slot N. Builders (including proposers who build blocks themselves) therefore need good connectivity to committee members, and there must be enough time between the view freeze (t=9s of slot N) and block propagation to collect the lists and update the payload. Equivocation: a P2P rule propagates at most two lists per member. If two different lists from the same member are seen, all of that member's lists are ignored. In the worst case, gossip subnet bandwidth can double. Payload construction: a naive approach that checks the lists' missing transactions against the post-state, appends a valid one to the end, and then restarts the check from the beginning can require n + (n-1) + (n-2) + ... checks for n transactions, that is, O(n^2) checks. One example is when only the nth transaction is valid, and its execution sends balance to the sender of the (n-1)th transaction, making each one valid in turn. Instead, before building the payload, the builder can store the nonce and balance of every EOA involved in the list transactions and update them only when a nonce rises or a balance changes without a nonce change (for example, when an account abstraction transaction interacted with that EOA), which lets it judge validity in real time.

14qk2kjsxy: This EIP specifies only the interface and the properties it depends on, not a particular construction. leanXMSS is a stateful signature scheme with a 32-byte public key and a 2404-byte signature; unforgeability holds only if each leaf index is used to sign at most once. Signing the same message twice from the same leaf also counts as reuse, and any leaf index in [0, 2**32) can be used. The first 4 bytes of the signature carry the leaf index in little-endian form. The VRF tree is a hash tree whose leaves commit to secret values; once the root and index are fixed, the output is pinned to a single value absent a hash collision, and nobody can predict it before it is opened. Selection proofs normally use the hash of a unique BLS signature, but since leanXMSS signatures are not unique and can be ground, a VRF root registered before the input is known pins a single output per index. The root is not checked at registration time, so the validator client checks the tree itself before registering. 14t03dp5ei5: Non-negative least squares (NNLS) linear regression is used to estimate the time of a single operation out of the block's total execution time. All coefficients are forced to be non-negative so execution time cannot come out negative. Simple operations are estimated as runtime = intercept + slope x operation_count, while operations with a parameter add a param_coef x operation_count x param term to this. The intercept represents baseline overhead including test setup and teardown, and the slope is the per-operation execution time. Models are built independently per client and operation, and only well-fitted models with R² > 0.5 and p-value < 0.05 are used in the conclusions. Gas conversion uses the formula gas = (anchor_rate x runtime_ms) / 1000, with anchor_rate set to 100 Mgas/s. A model-fit report and the core output CSV are attached to the EIP.

This is a problem when timing matters. This proposal presents a way for a contract to reserve a function call to be executed in the next block, offering ETH in exchange. If a function schedules itself repeatedly, it behaves like a bot that runs every block without any human intervention. 15q1uiu0f3c: Censorship resistance is a core property of a decentralized blockchain. EIP-7805 (FOCIL) has a role called the includer propagate inclusion lists (ILs) and has witnesses check via fork choice whether the transactions in that list made it into the block, so that a builder constructing the block cannot leave out specific transactions. However, FOCIL has no mechanism for ranking transactions within an IL, so once a block is full, censorship resistance cannot be upheld. A builder can fill the block with fake transactions and ignore the IL. This problem is even bigger in multidimensional fee markets that price each resource separately, since filling just one resource is enough to make the block count as full, and the cost of doing so can be very low. For time-sensitive transactions that must land within a few blocks, even a few blocks of delay can be fatal. This EIP adds an auction that ranks transactions by how much they are willing to pay above the base fee, ensuring that a higher-bidding IL transaction must be included even when the block is full.

Verifying these signatures on Ethereum is currently prohibitively expensive or practically impossible. 16nwfkxtuz0: Every reconstruction duty arises only when the node holds at least 64 distinct verified cells of that row. Subscribing alone does not count as holding. Nodes that are not row reconstructors are also recommended to collect at least 64 cells for each row of their designated row subnet and announce this by bitmap (SHOULD). The row subnet pools the custody cells of its members, so the cells need not be in the node's own custody. Phase 1: a row reconstructor must recover the rows assigned to its designated row subnet that have enough cells (MUST) and update its bitmap. This is possible with its own column subscriptions alone, and a short random delay (recommended range TBD) avoids simultaneous execution across nodes. Phase 2: after collecting cells from getBlobs, columns and rows during a somewhat longer random delay (TBD), a supernode should recover all missing rows (SHOULD), and other row reconstructors may do so (MAY). This is because only a supernode subscribed to all column subnets can see rows being completed elsewhere and cancel duplicate work. Phase 3: after a delay longer than in phase 2 (TBD), any node that has joined a row subnet should recover rows that are still incomplete (SHOULD). It runs only when earlier phases fail, so the expected CPU cost is close to zero. All delays are measured from the moment the node first obtains a valid block root for that slot, and the duty attaches to only one block root per slot (the current head branch, or the first valid block root seen). Other block roots in the same slot are OPTIONAL, so double proposals cannot inflate the work. A row completed first through another path must cancel any pending reconstruction (MUST), and delays have a maximum value (TBD) so that recovery is not postponed indefinitely.

17eh3xmfntu: This addresses, with five layers of defense, 'probabilistic front-running,' where an attacker pre-commits several options, watches others reveal their keys, and only reveals its own key when advantageous. The plaintext, call data, and actual signer are hidden until commitment (the plaintext signer may differ from the ticket signer), no ciphertext substitution, reordering, or new insertion is possible after commitment, and execution is based on the block header at the time of commitment. Commitments are ordered by ToB fee, so merely holding a slot repeatedly costs tob_fee / TOB_FEE_FRACTION each time, and failing to reveal the key forfeits the entire tob_fee. Also, if the sender limits via max_preceding_commitments the number m of commitments that can precede it, then even if an attacker buys all m slots at a higher fee, at most 2^(m-1) execution patterns remain selectable. Bundles sum the ToB fees of the STs they contain, making the economics of such attacks even worse.

17m33kce0eh: The calldata of the verification operation is n * RECENT_ROOT_TUPLE_BYTES (72) bytes, with 1 <= n <= MAX_RECENT_ROOT_REFERENCES (16). Empty calldata, a length that is not a multiple of 72, and more than 16 tuples all revert, and none overlaps with the 64-byte write encoding. For each tuple it checks slot < current_slot, current_slot - slot <= RECENT_ROOT_USABLE_WINDOW (8191), and storage[storage_key] == entry_hash, and if any one fails the whole call reverts. Duplicate tuples are each checked separately, and if all pass, it succeeds with no return value, logs, or state changes. The current slot is read with SLOTNUM, no other account is called, and only storage keys derived from calldata are read. The recent root verifier frame that carries this operation has mode == VERIFY, target == RECENT_ROOT_ADDRESS, flags == 0, value == 0, limits.state == 0, and a data length that is a multiple of 72 between 72 and 16 * 72 inclusive. In public mempool classification it is called recent_root_verify. It executes with EIP-8141 STATICCALL semantics, and if the contract reverts or the frame halts exceptionally, the transaction becomes invalid. Gas is ordinary EVM gas, target access and storage reads follow the usual warm and cold rules, and data follows the EIP-8141 transaction data fee. By using a standard frame instead of an envelope field, EIP-8141's encoding, signature hash, execution, gas, and frame lookup are reused as they are, and the transaction payload and signature hash do not change either.

17mofj27qvx: Ethereum has multiple clients, such as Go-Ethereum, Besu, and Nethermind, and all of them must execute smart contracts under the same rules. To inspect the execution process, each client has already implemented a trace feature that records every instruction, but because the common format was never rigorously defined, outputs differed slightly between implementations. When formats differ, it becomes hard to build tools that automatically compare execution results across clients, which greatly reduces the usefulness of traces. This EIP moves the format to a prominent, official specification and rigorously defines corner cases that earlier versions did not address. Once all major clients implement it, differential fuzzing infrastructure can be built to compare EVM implementations across mainnet and upcoming hard forks, making it possible to find bugs hidden in clients or quickly pinpoint execution differences when a chain split occurs.

Before allocating buffers or starting hashing, implementations must validate the descriptor, including the balance condition, confirm that the number of supplied nodes equals the 1-bit count, and impose a context-appropriate limit on descriptor length. Chain-shaped descriptors can push a naive recursive implementation to depth N, so this should be avoided by using iterative traversal or by capping recursion depth to the maximum tree depth possible in that context. Also, the descriptor does not prove the tree structure itself. A single bit does not say whether a node is a leaf or the root of an unexplored subtree. A 32-byte value alone cannot tell whether it is a piece of data or the hash of two children, so for fixed-shape SSZ types the index is statically determined, but for SSZ lists or progressive trees with varying depth, the shape of the structure must first be validated, for example through a length mix-in, before it can be interpreted as a specific leaf.

Adjacent slots fall into the same group, so access to slots that sit together, such as mappings and arrays, shares a path. ML-DSA-44 has PK_LEN 1312 and SIG_LEN 2420, so the minimum input is 3732 bytes. ML-DSA-65 has 1952 and 3309, giving 5261 bytes. ML-DSA-87 has 2592 and 4627, giving 7219 bytes. There are three reasons for splitting addresses instead of using a single precompile that separates the three levels with a selector byte. Each address has a fixed input shape and gas, so no branch byte needs to be parsed. There is no room to confuse the selector with the first byte of the public key. And a chain can enable each level and set its gas price separately.

19fa388es10: On Ethereum, validators that have been penalized (slashed) for breaking the rules have their blocks rejected by the network even if they produce them. Yet currently such validators can still be selected as block proposers. When selected, the block is invalidated, so that slot simply ends up empty. Normally slashing is rare, so this is not a big problem, but it becomes a different story when an incident causes many validators to be slashed at once. Empty slots repeat for the long period until all slashed validators have fully exited, degrading chain performance. If mass slashing coincides with a network failure, the empty slots could make recovery work considerably harder. This EIP reduces this disruption by filtering out slashed validators at the proposer selection stage.

19lvc0k56x: On Ethereum, a log is an event record that a smart contract emits, and it can be written at a much lower gas cost than writing to state. However, the protocol does not provide an efficient way to look these logs up. The bloom filter in each block was reasonably useful early on, but it is now saturated and practically useless. As a result, most users depend on remote providers (RPC services), which cannot prove that their query results are correct. If a contract sits on a trustless distributed ledger but its output has to be taken on trust, the original purpose is defeated. As Ethereum's throughput grows, this information asymmetry gets worse. This EIP proposes an index structure that can be updated far more cheaply than the state trie while still allowing lookup results to be verified with moderately sized proofs. The goal is to increase the usefulness of logs while keeping their low gas cost.

19vka499qsz: The current SSZ list type, List[type, N], requires a maximum capacity N to be fixed in advance. In practice, however, actual data is usually far shorter than the cap, so empty slots are padded with zeros and hashed anyway, which is wasteful. When lists are nested inside lists, as with transaction lists, the waste grows even larger. Also, N values such as MAX_BYTES_PER_TRANSACTION are arbitrarily large numbers chosen with future design headroom in mind, so their justification is weak. If N is changed at a fork, the position each element occupies in the tree (gindex, the generalized index) changes, breaking external verification code that validated proofs using that position. This EIP discards the notion of a capacity cap and introduces a Merkle tree shape that grows progressively to match the actual number of elements, addressing all three problems together.

However, the emergence of dedicated mining hardware (ASICs) tailored to this algorithm made them far more efficient than ordinary graphics card (GPU) miners. The author believes that because ASIC devices cost thousands of dollars and their production is monopolized by a small number of companies, the entire Ethash mining network risks becoming dependent on a handful of firms. 1al96a0tfbn: ETH issued as validator rewards is proportional to the square root of total stake, parameterized by BASE_REWARD_FACTOR 2**6 (64). This was chosen as a more stable and sustainable curve than the two alternatives, fixed total issuance and a fixed interest rate per ETH. The base reward takes the form k * D_i / sqrt(sum(D_j)): a fixed interest rate increases uncertainty in both total issuance and total stake, while fixed total reward is vulnerable to the discouragement attack, so this sits between the two. 1ao20f8dkta: Ethereum's signatures currently rely on the secp256k1 elliptic curve cryptography. This scheme rests on the assumption that the elliptic curve discrete logarithm problem (ECDLP) is hard, and once quantum computers become practical, this assumption breaks down, putting on-chain assets and core infrastructure at risk. The source says preparation must happen before quantum attacks become real, because existing apps take years to adopt a new signature scheme. Falcon, a lattice-based signature standardized by NIST, has a relatively small signature size of 666 bytes (Falcon-512) and fast verification, making it well suited to blockchains where gas cost matters. However, the SHAKE256 hash used by the NIST standard has no dedicated EVM opcode, making it expensive to compute. So this proposal splits verification into a hashing step and a core computation step, allowing the hashing step to be replaced with Keccak256, which the EVM already has.

Once zkEVM is introduced, however, validators only need to receive and check a proof and a header instead of the payload. The problem is that the implicit requirement to download the data disappears. A malicious or selfish block producer could publish only a valid proof and withhold the transaction data itself. Then only that producer could build the next block. RPC providers and indexers, which cannot operate on proofs alone and must re-execute the data, would halt. This proposal forces the execution payload data to be placed in blobs and carried in the same beacon block, so the data is always published even in the proof era.

For example, the eth_feeHistory RPC, which reports fee history, returns a blob gas usage ratio (blobGasUsedRatio), and computing this value requires knowing the maximum blob count. 1aqv6ep22wo: Today the default block gas limit is tied to client releases. A new default turns on not at a time set by the network but at the moment an operator updates the node. This creates trouble when trying to raise the limit substantially. If a release with the new default ships before the activation time, nodes that update early start voting to raise the limit right away, before the network has agreed it is safe. Conversely, shipping a release right after activation and asking all operators to update quickly is cumbersome and slow. Creating a temporary flag for every increase shifts the coordination burden onto individual operators. On top of that, there is no single place that states the gas limit the network should run, so raising the limit today requires months of social coordination, with every client team shipping a new default or many operators changing their settings. EIP-7935 showed that coordinating default recommendations at a set epoch in Fusaka works, and this EIP generalizes that into a reusable schedule.

1bn6z4qjzbx: The source points out that Ethereum has many precompiles and that nearly half of them have no clear use. Unused precompiles still create ongoing maintenance costs, raise the risk of consensus bugs, and increase the development burden when implementing new clients in languages suited to ZK-EVM or formal verification. This proposal therefore presents a procedure for gradually retiring little-used precompiles, and picks the simplest one, the identity precompile, as the first target. The identity precompile was introduced at a time when memory copying was a common operation but no instruction existed to do it directly. Later, the criteria for which functions to accept as instructions changed, and the MCOPY instruction was introduced by EIP-5656. The source notes that the same technique could later be applied to more complex precompiles, such as rarely used hash functions and MODEXP.

1bwlvqh5g9r: Three opcodes are added: DUPN (0xe6), SWAPN (0xe7), and EXCHANGE (0xe8). Each instruction is followed immediately by a 1-byte immediate operand, and using 1-indexed counting, DUPN n duplicates the nth stack item to the top, SWAPN n swaps the (n + 1)th item with the top item, and EXCHANGE n m swaps the (n + 1)th item with the (m + 1)th item. During execution, 3 gas is deducted, then the immediate is read and checked against the forbidden range, and if the decoded depth exceeds the current stack depth, execution halts with an exception. On success, pc is incremented by 2. If the immediate byte goes past the end of the code, it is evaluated as 0, just like PUSH.

1c39gpdessi: Copying memory is a very basic operation in smart contracts, but until now the EVM had no dedicated instruction for it. Developers therefore used workarounds. The other is to move 32 bytes at a time by hand with the MLOAD and MSTORE instructions, which costs at least 12 gas per word and, when the length is not an exact multiple of 32 bytes, needs extra work to read the last piece, mask it and store it back. For example, copying 256 bytes costs at least 157 gas with the identity precompile (after EIP-2929) and at least 96 gas with unrolled MLOAD/MSTORE, but only 27 gas with MCOPY. An analysis of real blocks (blocks 10537502 to 10538702) also showed that about 10.5% of memory copies would have performed better had MCOPY existed. Languages such as Solidity and Vyper use memory copies heavily, so a dedicated instruction has a large effect.

1cemwuzknn1: As in EIP-2200, the original value is the slot's value at the start of the transaction, and the current value is the value just before the SSTORE. The cost is the sum of three components. The access component is COLD_STORAGE_ACCESS if the slot is cold and WARM_ACCESS if it is warm. The write component STORAGE_WRITE is charged only when the new value differs from the current value and the current value equals the original value, that is, only when the slot is first moved away from its value at the start of the transaction. The state creation component GAS_STORAGE_SET is charged as state gas under EIP-8037 when the original and current values are 0 and the new value is nonzero. Refund rules are evaluated on every SSTORE. First, if the original and current values are nonzero and the new value is 0, STORAGE_CLEAR_REFUND is added. Second, if the original value is nonzero, the current value is 0 and the new value is nonzero, STORAGE_CLEAR_REFUND is subtracted. This reverses the first rule so that clearing and then refilling a slot in the same transaction does not yield a gain. Third, if the new value equals the original value and differs from the current value, STORAGE_WRITE is refunded. Without this reversal, a round trip from x to 0 and back to x would leave a net refund even though the slot is unchanged. Across the whole transaction, a slot that ends with a changed value pays the write and creation components exactly once, and a slot that ends at its original value pays only the access cost. Refunds accumulate in the transaction refund counter and are applied only up to 20% of total gas used. The refill rules for state gas are in EIP-8037.

1cf9p4jjtgr: The subnet count is not tied to the maximum blob count in order to avoid every node's subnet assignment changing at each Blob Parameter Only fork, which would make the row meshes collapse all at once and be rebuilt. With a fixed constant, the assignment of nodes to subnets stays stable across forks, and the blob count affects only the per-slot blob mapping. The value 128 was chosen to keep the expected number of nodes per subnet in a healthy range. As of August 2026, mainnet has about 12K nodes, of which about 2K are supernodes and about 500 hold 64 to 127 columns, so there are about 2.5K row reconstructors. With ROW_SUBNET_COUNT = 128, full participation gives about 94 nodes and about 20 row reconstructors per subnet. This value is larger than the currently planned maximum blob count, so in practice each subnet carries one row per slot, and even with more blobs the per-node load is bounded by ceil(blob_count / ROW_SUBNET_COUNT). The reason for using a per-slot pseudorandom permutation instead of a simple rotation ((blob_index + slot) % ROW_SUBNET_COUNT) is that a rotation keeps one subnet busy for blob_count consecutive slots and then idle for a long stretch, so the load bunches up. With a permutation, two blobs in one slot never land on the same subnet, and compute_shuffled_index is a function that clients have already implemented. Even if the mapping is public, the block builder decides the blob indexes, so hiding it gains almost nothing, and the column topics continue to provide the guarantee against targeted suppression. The original proposal states firmly that this EIP is not FullDAS and does not include cell-level sublinear sampling, column-direction encoding, or retrieval of individual L2 blobs.

1cgyk272c1a: Ethereum nodes operate by requesting data such as block headers, block bodies, and receipts from other nodes (peers) and receiving responses. However, the existing eth protocol had no number pairing requests with responses. If a node sent several requests to the same peer at once, there was no guarantee responses would come back in the order sent, so the node had to guess which request a given response belonged to by examining its contents against every pending request one by one. Responses that cannot be distinguished by content alone, such as empty responses, were especially hard to match. This approach forced unnecessarily complex code on every Ethereum client and also hurt communication efficiency. This EIP attaches a number when sending a request and has the response echo back the same number, allowing responses to be matched directly to requests.

1cq86w4x4c: Today, for a smart contract to send ether to another address, it must call that address. A call hands the execution flow to the other party, so even if you only want to send money, the recipient's code runs too. This causes several problems. Reentrancy attacks are possible, where the recipient calls the sender back. Denial of service attacks are also possible, where the recipient uses up all the gas or reverts execution to block the transfer itself. The 2300 gas that comes with every call by default cannot modify regular storage, but it can modify transient storage (EIP-1153), which leaves room for unintended state changes. Running code also costs gas, so you pay more even if you only want to send funds. Future call-family instructions may have no way to limit the amount of gas passed on. Also, since EIP-7702 lets a regular account (EOA) delegate to code, even a transfer to an ordinary wallet address now executes code and uses gas. A dedicated instruction that only sends ether avoids all of these problems at once.

1czm35vrzcy: In the EVM today, pure computation (compute) opcodes such as addition are significantly underpriced relative to state operations that read and write storage. This is because client optimization and hardware advances have made computation faster, while the growing size of Ethereum's state has made state operations slower. This has led to proposals that lower compute costs and raise state costs, but there is a dilemma here. Lowering compute cost causes any operation that should cost less than 1 gas to be rounded up to 1 gas, reducing the number of operations that fit in a block. According to the source's analysis, the average rounding error reaches 59.3% against a 50Mgas/s anchor. Conversely, pegging the fastest opcode at 1 gas and repricing everything else upward would inflate gas costs and limits roughly a hundredfold, forcing users to relearn the concept of gas itself. This proposal avoids both problems by splitting only the internal EVM computation into thousandths.

1d7uf0i28zf: The builder specifies marginal_ranking_fee_per_gas in the block body, and every transaction pays an inclusion_fee_per_gas of base_fee_per_gas + marginal_ranking_fee_per_gas before its priority fee. So during execution, each transaction is charged based on max_fee_per_gas rather than effective_gas_price, unused gas is refunded, and the priority fee is not yet paid to the block author. After all execution finishes, priority_fee_per_gas is computed as min(max_priority_fee_per_gas, max_fee_per_gas - inclusion_fee_per_gas), the difference is refunded to the signer, and only the priority fee is paid to block.author. 1dbg68yaif: While the transaction gas limit field allows an arbitrarily long integer by specification, the clients that actually process it each impose their own internal limits. For example, implementations like geth handle gas values as 64-bit integers. When such practical limits are not explicitly fixed in Ethereum's consensus rules, different clients may handle things slightly differently. This is a potential risk to consensus safety, where the entire network must agree on the same result. This proposal pins the gas limit's upper bound at 2^63-1, bringing this implicit discrepancy into the consensus rules.

1dcvoa0dazo: Three kinds of index entries, log, transaction, and block, are laid out in order in the global linear index space. Each entry produces one or more map values: a log entry produces 1 address value and 0 to 4 topic values, and a transaction entry and a block entry produce 1 each. Map value hashes are computed as sha2(address), sha2(topic), sha2(tx_hash + b"\x01"), and sha2(block_hash + b"\x02"). For each transaction, the transaction entry is added first, followed by its log entries in EVM execution order. The block entry for block N can be inserted only after the block hash is final, so it appears as the first entry in the index state of block N+1. Each entry carries LogMeta, TransactionMeta, or BlockMeta metadata, which makes it possible to prove receipt and block hash lookups as well.

1dd21a9onek: Ethereum is preparing a major shift of its state storage structure to the Verkle tree. In this structure, block validation requires generating a witness, the bundle of data needed for validation, but current gas costs do not reflect the cost of producing that witness. This EIP therefore reprices gas costs in the fork immediately preceding the Verkle tree fork. The goal is to give dapp developers enough time to adapt their contracts to the new storage model and to push client developers to migrate their database formats before the Verkle fork. At the same time, this change makes reading and writing multiple values within the same branch cheaper, and if clients leave their current database structure unchanged, this could open a denial-of-service (DoS) attack vector. The proposal therefore also requires restructuring the database alongside the gas changes.

1disfswbj4l: TXTRACE and EVENTDATACOPY are lookup capabilities strong enough to break code encapsulation. They are allowed only inside an ASSERT frame so that they are used only to judge the validity of the result and to revert the execution body. Because ASSERT must come at the very end, the difference TXTRACE sees is always the final result, and because a failure reverts the entire execution body, it cannot be partly avoided with an atomic batch or an earlier frame. Multiple ASSERT frames can be present, so different assertion providers can each check in their own frame without coordinating. If an ASSERT failure removed the transaction from the block and also reverted the gas payment, it would become a DoS path where an attacker spends up to the block gas limit and reverts for free, so the transaction is kept valid and the gas is still charged. No new gas constants were added. The slots and accounts in the difference were already written by the transaction and are therefore warm, and reading them with SLOAD or BALANCE costs WARM_STORAGE_READ_COST, so the same value is charged, and values such as counts or addresses were also priced uniformly. A client can build an index of the difference and logs once, when the ASSERT frame first reads, and reuse it, and that cost is covered by the access costs and LOG costs the transaction has already paid. The reason events are used as the transfer channel is that EIP-8141 discards transient storage between frames and does not provide the return data of earlier frames, so length-capable events are the only way to pass pre-execution values to the ASSERT frame. For state changes, a slot written many times through reentrant calls is still one entry, so execution order cannot give a deterministic order, and they are sorted by address and slot key, while events have a log index and use the order of occurrence.

1doklkfo89h: Today, for a call with value, a stipend of 2300 is added to the gas the caller provides. Under this EIP, if the gas limit after applying the 63/64 rule is at least CALL_STIPEND, execution proceeds as is, and if it is lower the callee's gas limit is raised to 2300. The gas raised this way was prepaid by the base charge and is not returned, and on success or revert the caller gets back only min(callee_gas_remaining, original gas limit). If the call fails before entering the sub-frame because of insufficient balance or the depth limit, the original gas limit is returned. This prevents the cost of repeated transfers from falling as low as 1700, which could happen if the additive approach were kept. As a compatibility impact, a call given an explicit gas limit receives up to 2300 less gas than before, so an execution that used to succeed may fail, and a contract that reads gasleft() before and after a value transfer may observe different values. The 2300 guarantee for patterns that pass no gas, such as Solidity's transfer and send, is preserved.

STARKs, the zero-knowledge proofs, are even worse: generating them quickly can grow them to up to 512 kB, with verification gas running into the millions. If this size and cost were carried as-is into the block for every transaction, privacy protocols using STARKs would be unusable in practice, and they also could not mesh with the inclusion-list enforcement feature FOCIL (EIP-7805) or frame transactions (EIP-8141). Distinguishing between the two can cause security problems such as phishing attacks, and its use has been discouraged since mid-2016. For example, if a contract that checks permissions with ORIGIN holds tokens or privileges, any transaction an ERC-4337 bundler (the entity that batches multiple user operations and submits them) processes in a bundle could hijack those privileges. 1e8mv1wjqop: last_written_block is set to the current block_number when state is modified, and writing again within the same block changes nothing because it already has the same value. There are four slot rules. When SSTORE changes a non-zero value to a different value, both the slot's field and the owning account's field are updated (because storageRoot is recomputed). When a slot is cleared to 0, the slot is removed from the trie and only the account field is updated. Writing the same value again changes nothing. A new slot is created holding the current block number. On the account side, a balance transfer of a non-zero amount updates both the sender and the recipient, and nonce increments and new account creation are also updates. SELFDESTRUCT follows the balance transfer rules of EIP-6780. A contract not created in the same transaction is not removed, so when its balance changes, it updates itself and the recipient account, and if the recipient is itself, the balance does not change and no update is made. A contract created and destroyed in the same transaction is removed from the trie and does not have this field.

1ecwhtawcl7: The classic way to prevent reentrancy attacks is a reentrancy guard, which writes to and reads from a single storage cell inside the contract to determine whether reentrancy is occurring. Because this approach reads and writes the same storage cell on every call, it conflicts with parallel execution designs that aim to run the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) across multiple threads simultaneously. The most successful parallelization approach so far detects conflicts at the storage-cell level, and the reentrancy guard's read-write pattern is exactly what blocks that parallel execution. Because it's difficult to automatically analyze and parallelize already-deployed contracts, there is a need for a way for future contracts to prevent reentrancy without touching storage.

1es3kyg4p10: The step in EIP-8141 where payment approval increments the sender nonce is replaced by consume_nonce_set(sender, nonce_keys, nonce_seq). If nonce_keys == [], increment_account_nonce(sender) raises the current account nonce by 1. It does not overwrite with tx.nonce_seq + 1, so EIP-8141 behavior is preserved even when an earlier frame has already changed the nonce through CREATE, CREATE2, or account deployment. If the incremented value exceeds MAX_NONCE_SEQ, execution aborts with an exception. If nonce_keys != [], MAX_NONCE_SEQ or nonce_seq + 1 is written for each key. This consumption happens once per transaction, at a payment-scope APPROVE (scope 0x1 or 0x3) that changes payer from None to resolved_target. The order is as follows. 1) Compute nonce_state_gas: for an empty key set, STATE_BYTES_PER_NEW_ACCOUNT * CPSB if the sender does not exist; for a key set, KEYED_NONCE_FIRST_USE_STATE_GAS * first_use_count. 2) Abort with an exception if state_gas_left is insufficient. 3) Charge the state gas. 4) Run consume_nonce_set. 5) Commit the remaining approval effects. Steps 3 to 5 are applied together as one transition, all or nothing. If the enclosing frame reverts, the transition is reverted too, but once that frame has succeeded, it is not reverted by a later frame failure or an atomic batch rollback. If the transaction itself is invalid, all effects are discarded.

1et1bi3yc0z: On send, a Snappy compression step is inserted immediately before the DEVp2p message is encrypted. A message consists of {Code, Size, Payload}; the original Payload is compressed with Snappy and stored in the same field, Size is updated to the compressed length, and the message is then encrypted and transmitted exactly as before. On receive, a symmetric decompression step is inserted immediately after decryption, restoring the Payload and resetting Size to the original length. Because the encryption and decryption logic remains entirely oblivious to whether compression occurred, changes to the existing transport code are minimized. Second, the starting multiplier is 1 + PENALTY_SLOPE * spike, which gives about 9x for a 1% simultaneous failure, about 39x for 5%, about 78x for 10%, and about 154x for 20%. But this warm status disappears once the transaction ends. Even if multiple transactions in the same block read the same slot, each one pays the cold cost again from scratch. However, modern node software caches storage access at the block level, so from the second access onward the actual computation cost is much cheaper. This means the gas fee charged and the actual cost are misaligned. This proposal aims to maintain the warm status until the block ends, reducing redundant warming costs, aligning gas fees with the actual computational burden, and increasing network throughput without compromising security. 1g8b3yx8qzn: Ethereum does not yet have a post-quantum signature verifier that contracts can call. ML-DSA is a signature scheme based on lattice mathematics, and it is the first lattice signature that the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published as a final standard (FIPS 204). Cloud key management services and hardware security modules already generate ML-DSA keys at three security levels and sign with them, and certificate and transport protocol specifications use the same FIPS 204 encoding. 1h003hpanox: Right now frame transactions (EIP-8141) only have two signature schemes that the protocol verifies directly: secp256k1 and P-256. To use any other authentication method, the proof must be carried as an ARBITRARY entry and verified by the account code directly inside the VERIFY frame. That mixes expensive, state-independent cryptographic computation into the same frame as cheap, state-dependent account authorization checks. Sequencers (the parties who order transactions) and block builders then have a hard time separating this expensive work from account state in order to pre-bound its cost or cache the result. This proposal moves only the expensive, state-independent part into protocol-level verification and attaches a fixed, protocol-defined gas budget so that the cost of every custom authentication signature is statically known. 1hjd9e46wmz: Without the limit, block construction is a one-dimensional problem of maximizing fees under the single constraint that total gas stay under the limit, and a greedy strategy based on fee per gas is close to optimal. Adding the limit turns it into a two-dimensional knapsack problem, where the sum of deposit counts must also stay at or below 8192, which is NP-hard in general. Builders are expected to use heuristics such as reserving a budget of deposit slots, which is not optimal and can be exploited. For example, a transaction that looks attractive by fee per gas but generates many deposits can be used to grief the builder by exhausting its budget early, crowding out more profitable deposit transactions. However, filling the limit requires at least 8192 x 1 ETH ~= 8192 ETH at the 1 ETH minimum deposit, which acts as a deterrent on cost. 1hp0ttnphh3: To verify a block, an Ethereum node must compute the post-execution state root, a value summarizing all account state, and compare it against the block header. So a partially stateful node cannot obtain the storage root of an account it does not hold when that account is modified, cannot build the state trie leaf, and therefore cannot verify the block's state root. This EIP closes that gap by including the post-execution storage root for each modified account in the BAL. Balance, nonce, and code information are already in the BAL, so once the storage root is added, any node can assemble the state trie leaves of all modified accounts, whatever part of the state it stores.

1hpgxb5bfa: A ZK prover works from an actual execution trace, so it does not search paths. The jump destination is already recorded by the time it is executed. So the benefit lies not in path search but in the efficiency of the code being proven and the tractability of surrounding analysis. First, today's zkVMs run an EVM interpreter compiled to RISC-V, but statically-controlled-flow code could be compiled to RISC-V once in linear time, eliminating per-step interpreter overhead. Second, stack discipline that removes static jumps, explicit subroutine calls, and SWAP/DUP workarounds produces smaller, simpler bytecode, reducing the number of instructions to be proven. Third, stack underflow, static stack depth, and reachability can all be verified once in linear time at deployment. These improvements follow through to faster proof generation and lower hardware requirements. For optimistic rollups, deployment-time verification also secures a safety property that dispute resolution can rely on, simplifying the implementation of bisection-style interactive verification games.

1hr8t9emn3z: Currently, when a transaction or a subcall within it reverts, all state changes made within it, such as storage changes, contract creation, and log emission, are cancelled. Yet the user still pays the original high gas cost as if these operations had actually taken effect. Since EIP-3298, the gas refund mechanism only works when storage is restored to its original value within the same transaction, and when a revert occurs, even the gas refunds accumulated up to that point are wiped out entirely. This creates the paradoxical situation where, instead of reverting a transaction, manually sending tokens back at the end to restore state by hand ends up being cheaper. Since reverted operations did incur real data access costs during execution but ultimately did not incur state-change costs, this proposal arose from the recognition that gas should be recalibrated to reflect only the cost actually incurred.

1ic9iac3171: EIP-8037 splits transaction gas into gas_left for execution and a reserve gas (state_gas_reservoir) dedicated to state creation. But the GAS opcode shows only gas_left, not the reserve gas. A bundler like the ERC-4337 EntryPoint, which measures a call's gas consumption by comparing two readings of gasleft(), misses costs covered instead by the reserve gas, such as creating a new storage slot, and measures 97,920 gas less than the actual amount. Nor does the caller have any way to notice if the callee has used up all of its own reserve gas. EIP-8141's TXPARAM (TXPARAM_STATE_GAS_LEFT) shows a similar value, but that instruction halts under the reserve-gas-model transaction, so library code that does not know which of the two transaction models it is running under cannot use it.

1igu7tihhri: Today, verifying a beacon block requires re-executing the execution payload inside it against the full execution layer (EL) state. This needs all account and storage data, and the cost of re-execution grows in proportion to the gas limit. As a result, the hardware a node needs is tied to the chain's throughput and state size. As the gas limit rises or the state grows, the hardware threshold for becoming a validator rises with it. This EIP separates nodes that produce proofs from nodes that check proofs. It opens a path for the checking side to confirm payload validity in constant time without EL state. However, because proof systems are still maturing, the EIP does not make them mandatory from the start. Instead, only nodes that want to turn them on do so, building operating experience and metrics on a real network. There is no reward for proof-generating nodes, so participation is considered voluntary.

1iqny70i1c3: The ticket contract is a system contract deployed at TICKET_CONTRACT_ADDRESS, the same approach used by EIP-4788 and EIP-7002, and it has three code paths. A call with value is a ticket purchase: it takes (blob_count, bls_pubkey), requires payment of at least blob_count * GAS_PER_BLOB * fee, and sends the payment to ZERO_ADDRESS to burn it. There are no refunds, which is the primary defense against capacity preemption attacks. A call with no value and no calldata returns the current fee, and at the end of the block SYSTEM_ADDRESS executes a system call. Tickets are stored in a ring buffer of per-slot buckets whose ring length equals TICKET_LOOKAHEAD. The total AOT reservation for a single slot cannot exceed MAX_AOT_BLOBS_PER_BLOCK (B2 - R). 1itcgmc3akn: Register machines such as x86, ARM and RISC-V keep the return address in a link register or in a single stack mixed with data. Stack machines such as Forth, the JVM, Wasm and the CLR, by contrast, effectively use separate data and return stacks. The EVM is a stack machine, so it adopts the same proven approach. Another reason is that data stack items are 32 bytes while a jump destination needs only a byte or two. Because the return address lives only on its own stack and cannot be read, modified or moved with ordinary stack operations, the class of vulnerabilities in which code corrupts its own control flow disappears entirely. The remaining risks are checked at execution time as defined by the instructions.

1ivstilus5p: There are now many EVM chains, and most developers want to deploy a contract at the same address on every chain. When addresses differ between chains, apps and wallets have to maintain separate per-chain address lists, and because smart contract accounts get deployed at different addresses on different chains, there have been real cases of lost funds. The CREATE2 opcode supports deployments with predetermined addresses, but the created address is computed from the address of the contract that executes the opcode, so a factory that exists at the same address on every chain is needed first. Until now, this factory has been deployed with a keyless transaction that anyone can broadcast as is, but that transaction has a fixed gas price and limit, so deployment was often impossible on chains with different gas rules. Gas schedule changes have started to cause the same problem on Ethereum itself and on devnets, so the proposal aims to guarantee the existence of the already widely used factory through the rules themselves.

1iybbhskfxb: EOF (EVM Object Format) is a new container format that splits contract code into multiple code sections. The current definition (EIP-3540) presumes that every code section is interpreted the same way by the EVM, so there is no way to mark what kind of code a given section is. As a result, there is no way to run only the compute-heavy parts on a faster alternative interpreter (such as EVM64), or to support other execution models like RISC-V on a per-section basis in the future. This EIP attaches a type value to each section so interpreters can interpret each code section differently. 1izeb3c8red: Any node, even a new node with no prior state, must be able to verify a snapshot without trusting its source. There are two checks. First, internal consistency: reconstruct the PBT from the snapshot leaves, hash all intermediate nodes directly, and check that the root matches the claimed PBT root. Second, consensus anchoring: rehash the same leaves under the MPT schema using the preimages, and check that the result matches the stateRoot of the ANCHOR_BLOCK header. Because the root of trust is the stateRoot obtained from the node's own header chain, a tampered package with fake leaves and a fake pbtRoot that is only internally self-consistent will be caught by the second check. Since the MPT does not hold code, code leaves are anchored separately via code_hash. For each code_hash, the 31-byte fragments of the chunk leaves are concatenated to reconstruct the bytecode, its keccak256 is checked against that code_hash, and the reconstructed code is re-chunked per EIP-8297 and checked byte-for-byte against the code leaves in the artifact. A snapshot that fails either check must be rejected and re-fetched or re-converted.

1j29y03vcmf: EXCHANGE (0xc2) takes a single argument X from the stack and splits it into two operands. N is X >> 4, and M is X & 0x0F. X must be pushed by an immediately preceding PUSH2 instruction, and violating the convention or having N or M equal 0 causes execution to fail with an out-of-gas error. After popping X, it swaps the elements at index N-1 and M-1. The reason for counting from 1 is that, just as SWAP1 and DUP1 operate on the top of the stack, it is natural for EXCHANGE(1, 2) to operate on the top and top-1.
1j2c1ukvlb9: This EIP does not extend the sync protocol, because every table it needs can be rebuilt from recent blocks. Even in the worst case, only TABLE_SIZES[len(TABLE_SIZES)-1] * 5 // 4 - 1 recent blocks, which is 319 blocks with the current parameters, are enough to build the top-level table root. In a fully stateless protocol, merging can be implemented using witnesses of partially merged tables. If evenly spaced entry_index checkpoints are chosen based on the expected entry_count of the merged table, and the witness set includes a Merkle boundary proof of the partially merged table at each checkpoint, the block producer commits the next merge piece and validators verify it using witnesses of the lower-level table pieces. The same approach can be applied to generating execution ZKPs, and there is also the option of proving merges asynchronously.

1j4sa6by52v: The first byte of every key is the zone identifier Z. 0x00 is the account header, 0x01 is a code chunk, 0xFF is storage, and 0x02 to 0xFE are reserved for future categories. A key is assembled from the zone byte, a hash-determined tree position, and a 1-byte sub-index, and the zone byte and tree position together are called the stem. One stem has STEM_SUBTREE_WIDTH = 256 sub-indexes. Key lengths are fixed per zone: ACCOUNT_KEY_LENGTH and CODE_KEY_LENGTH are 34 bytes, and STORAGE_KEY_LENGTH is 66 bytes. Fixing a single length within a zone guarantees prefix-free, and keys in different zones differ from the first byte. 1j4w00sxt5s: The extra charge is applied for every inactive leaf an operation writes. An SSTORE that changes an existing slot's value pays both the slot's share and the account leaf's share that changes along with it via the storageRoot recalculation cascade. An SSTORE that creates a new slot (from 0 to a nonzero value) and an SSTORE that clears a slot (to 0) pay only the account's share. CALL and CALLCODE that transfer value are charged separately for the sending and receiving accounts if each is inactive, and a newly created recipient account is exempt. For simple-transfer transactions and the authority account share of EIP-7702 delegation, the charge is folded into intrinsic gas and evaluated at transaction validation. Nonce increment is charged to that account; CREATE and CREATE2 are charged only to the creator account, and the new contract account, its code, and the slots set by the constructor are all exempt. SELFDESTRUCT is charged for each side whose balance changes, if that side is inactive. Reads such as SLOAD, BALANCE, the EXT* family, and value-less calls are unaffected. The tier is determined by the last_written_block at the time the operation starts. Since writing makes it active, a single leaf is charged at most once per block.

1j5n5toi4n0: The blob base fee adjusts automatically: it rises when usage is above target and falls when it is below. However, when the blob fee becomes a very small share of the total cost a rollup pays, this adjustment stops working. A 10% cut in the blob fee can move the total cost by only 0.0000001%, so the fee keeps falling and ends up stuck at 1 wei, the smallest unit of ether. If demand returns in this state, nearly full blocks have to continue for over an hour before the price recovers its equilibrium. In the meantime users are pushed into first-come bidding competition and the experience gets worse. Swings in resource usage also get in the way of scaling blob space. In addition, nodes perform KZG proof verification, an expensive cryptographic check, for every blob, and at a 1 wei fee blob users barely pay for that computation.
