1jsxehy9dbp: Today, blob data must propagate together with the block within the short window during which the block spreads across the network. The amount that can be processed on this critical path is limited, making it hard to raise blob throughput. Extending the propagation window would worsen the free-option problem, where a builder can watch market conditions during that time and invalidate the block if conditions turn unfavorable. Pre-propagating data through an execution layer blob pool is another option, but since there is no cap on the processing load, different nodes could end up seeing different data, and combined with data availability sampling (DAS) this becomes vulnerable to denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. This proposal solves the problem by requiring a ticket to be purchased in advance to gain propagation eligibility. The set of parties eligible to propagate is restricted to a globally agreed, finite set, and since both honest users and attackers must pay the same network resource cost upfront, the scheme is resistant to DoS. The propagation time can also be chosen flexibly within a fixed time window, reducing congestion and substantially raising overall throughput without extending the block propagation window.

To match cost per cycle with ecRecover, a 12-round call would have an appropriate average of 6.74153 gas (0.5618 gas per round), and 1200 rounds would be 436.1288 gas (0.3634 gas per round). 1jx4mmopvj6: Solidity has checked arithmetic overflow (a result exceeding the representable range) by default since version 0.8.0, and Vyper since the start. However, the EVM itself has no instruction that performs this check, so the compiler inserts a multi-instruction check for every operation. As a result, an addition that should cost 3 gas costs about 79 gas in Solidity, so safety costs 25 times as much. Because the cost is burdensome, developers are tempted to turn off checks with workarounds such as unchecked blocks or unsafe_add, and code that disables checks even where safety is not proven grows more common and harder to audit. There are real attacks that exploited unchecked subtraction. This proposal adds instructions with the check built in directly to the EVM, lowering the cost of a safe addition to 5 gas and removing the reason to bypass the check at all.

The file format is a sequence of fixed-width records, each being address[20] | slotCount[4, big-endian] | slotKey[32] * slotCount. 1kc28qfik2i: Today a single transaction can in theory use the entire block gas limit by itself. Such very large transactions carry three risks. First, one transaction can monopolize the block processing load and become a channel for denial-of-service (DoS) attacks that shake the network. Second, transactions that use a lot of gas usually cause large state changes, which quickly inflates the data nodes must store. Third, block validation takes longer, which hurts user experience and network decentralization. These risks grow as the block gas limit rises. Capping the gas a single transaction can use reduces the single-transaction DoS risk, distributes gas more evenly within a block, and prevents extreme block validation times, which stabilizes synchronization between nodes.

1kdz0mvu94a: In Ethereum, the contract storage instruction SSTORE charges an expensive fee every time a value is written. But in practice, the only thing that ends up recorded on disk is the final value after the transaction ends. Even if a slot is rewritten multiple times within the same transaction, or reset back to its original value, a large fee had to be paid each time, so the actual amount of work and the fee charged did not match. EIP-1283, which tried to fix this, introduced 'net gas metering,' comparing the value before and after the write and charging only for the net change, but because it allowed storage even within the 2300 gas that Solidity gives by default to a simple transfer call, it created a new kind of reentrancy attack risk for existing contracts. This EIP is the final version that merges EIP-1706's safeguard against that risk into EIP-1283, and reorganizes the gas figures into named parameters so they interlock with other gas changes like EIP-1884.

1kh9wa4mhy6: The input is a single big-endian byte string with no header and no length fields. Starting at offset 0, the first PK_LEN bytes are the pubkey, the next SIG_LEN bytes are the signature, and the remaining len(input) - PK_LEN - SIG_LEN bytes are the message. With L = len(input), if L < PK_LEN + SIG_LEN, the precompile MUST return failure (32 zero bytes) without reverting. L == PK_LEN + SIG_LEN is a valid input with an empty message, because FIPS 204 allows an empty message. Putting the message last and dropping the length field is a choice to keep input assembly simple. You write the two fixed-length fields first, append the message, and call with that size, so there is no length word to compute or misplace. It also matches how the witness arrives. In EIP-8141, an ML-DSA witness can arrive as an ARBITRARY signature entry holding pubkey ++ signature, and a VERIFY frame moves it into memory with a single SIGPARAM copy. Appending the message that the signature approves after that makes it the precompile input without repackaging or rescanning the witness bytes.

The old formula targeted a median of 13 seconds, so when miners stamped timestamps as parent_timestamp + 1, the median held but the average rose, and if this kind of mining reached 51%, the average could grow without bound. The new formula targets roughly the average instead, and it can be proven that it is mathematically impossible for the long-run average block time to exceed 24 seconds. Using (block_timestamp - parent_timestamp) // 10 as the input, rather than the raw time difference, preserves the algorithm's coarse granularity, blocking the incentive to tune the time difference to exactly 1 to produce a slightly higher-difficulty block. 1ku4z7qjsir: The entity that writes a root is identified by source_id = keccak256(source_address || salt). source_address can be an externally owned account or a contract, and varying the salt lets one address hold multiple sources. Who may write and how salts are allocated are the app's responsibility. The stored value is entry_hash = keccak256(RECENT_ROOT_ENTRY_DOMAIN || source_id || uint64_be(slot) || root), and the storage location is storage_key = keccak256(RECENT_ROOT_STORAGE_DOMAIN || source_id || uint64_be(i)), where i = slot mod RECENT_ROOT_LENGTH. Each source effectively has a ring buffer entries: bytes32[RECENT_ROOT_LENGTH] of length 8192, and every cell starts at 0. Slots and indexes are 8-byte big-endian, addresses are 20 bytes, and domains, roots, salts, source_ids, hashes, and keys are concatenated as fixed 32-byte lengths. Because the stored value is a hash that contains source_id, slot, and root together, a check cannot be passed with another source's root or with an old root left in the same cell. There is no separate source creation transaction. A source comes into existence on the first write with a new (source_address, salt), and a write that creates a new storage cell usually pays the state growth cost. Total storage grows in proportion to the number of source_ids written, and each source writes at most RECENT_ROOT_LENGTH keys.

1lxwny0s84i: Today the consensus client and the execution client each receive blocks on their own. The consensus client uses gossip and req/resp, and the execution client uses devp2p, so the same networking function is duplicated across two layers. For the consensus client to hand blocks directly to the execution client, it needs to know which block the execution client has up to, and up to which block it has executed and holds state, but the Engine API has no way to ask this. The two values differ when the execution client has received blocks but not executed them. This very difference makes an efficient sync possible, in which blocks are received without execution and the state is caught up quickly by another method. Also, when engine_newPayload returns SYNCING, the consensus client cannot tell whether an ancestor block is missing (in which case it must send the ancestors) or whether there is no pre-state because of a snap sync (in which case sending is pointless and it must wait). Distinguishing these two is what makes the exchange between engine_forkchoiceUpdated and engine_newPayload run deterministically.

1m1i2qjmto8: Today, access control in smart contracts is usually done by registering roles in the contract in advance, or by letting through only addresses that hold a specific NFT. However, these approaches do not suit permissions that are valid only for a short time or screening criteria that change often. With an on-chain registry, the operator must always keep the registry up to date, and an unqualified party can get through while an update is delayed. Also, if eligibility screening requires sensitive information such as identity data, it is undesirable to put that information on a publicly viewable blockchain and query it there. This proposal leaves screening to an off-chain (outside the blockchain) service, issues a short-lived signed token only to accounts that pass, and has the token verified on-chain. Each time a user comes to request permission, the issuer gets a chance to check and update its records, and personal information does not remain on the chain.

1m8mbad105y: Nodes keep seen_attesters and seen_batchers caches per (slot, committee_index, data_root). The principle is a single one: accept only a message that carries at least one vote not seen before. A single attestation already seen, a second batch from the same batcher, and a batch whose members are all already known are silently dropped as IGNORE. As a result, an attacker holding k committee keys can get at most k messages per duty through, and since each message needs a valid attestation, seal, and batcher signature, the bandwidth the attacker consumes is proportional to the attacker's own signing cost. The O(2^k) subset explosion is not propagated. Even if the single attestation of a validator bundled in a batch leaks out first, the batch is not suppressed, thanks to the unseen votes of the remaining members, and no vote is lost regardless of arrival order.

1m9ejds0463: Today an Ethereum transaction verifies the sender in only one way, an elliptic curve signature (ECDSA). The account is bound to a private key, so the key cannot be changed, and there is no path to move to signature schemes that are safe against quantum computers. Bundling several operations at once, or having another account pay the fee, requires separate smart account code and an external intermediary (a relayer), which makes the structure more complex and the risk correspondingly higher. This EIP splits a transaction into multiple frames and runs each frame as a contract call, so that account code decides verification, fee approval, and execution. As a result, the protocol natively supports key rotation, switching to quantum-resistant signatures, batched calls, and alternative fee payment. The original text says this realizes the original vision of account abstraction, in which an account becomes an address that holds code.

1md26f0eiko: SETDELEGATE, added at 0xf6, operates in the following order. It deducts EMPTY_ACCOUNT_COST gas and aborts if the frame is in static mode. It pops salt and target from the stack, computes location = keccak256(DESIGNATOR ++ address ++ salt)[12:], and adds location to EIP-2929's accessed_addresses. If the code at location is neither empty nor starts with 0xEF0100 (that is, it is not a delegation designator), it aborts. If location already exists in the trie, it adds EMPTY_ACCOUNT_COST - BASE_COST to the refund counter. It sets the code to DESIGNATOR ++ target, but if target is 0x0, it clears the code and restores the code hash to the empty hash. If the nonce is 0, it raises it to 1 and pushes location onto the stack. target must be exactly 20 bytes: if shorter it is left-padded with zeros, and if longer the high-order bytes are truncated. Per EIP-7702, the resulting code is exactly 23 bytes.

1ml05ifurpa: CALLF (0xe3) takes a 16-bit big-endian immediate argument target_section_index and costs 5 gas. It does not pop or push values from the operand stack directly, but the input values for the function being called must already be on the stack. If the operand stack size exceeds 1024 minus the target function's max_stack_increase, an exceptional halt occurs, which guarantees that the global stack height limit (1024) is not exceeded after the call. If the return stack is already full with 1024 items, this also causes an exceptional halt. On successful execution, the current section index and the position immediately after the immediate argument are pushed onto the return stack, current_section_index is set to target_section_index, and PC is set to 0, continuing execution in the called section.

1mlyh4v0bbi: Today a frame transaction uses one sequential nonce (a serial number attached so the same transaction is not executed twice) per sender. Because the numbers form a single sequence, if an earlier transaction is delayed, all later transactions from the same sender must wait. This constraint is too heavy for designs in which many users deliberately share one sender address. The main example is privacy protocols. So that on-chain activity is not tied to a specific public address, users send transactions through a single shared sender address. With only one nonce, this address becomes a bottleneck. 1noozgnvddt: The Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) provides only two branch (jump) instructions, JUMP and JUMPI, both of which are dynamic jumps that pop the destination from the stack and compute it during execution. This flexibility makes code analysis complex and requires a JUMPDEST marker instruction to be embedded in the code at every jump destination. In practice, however, a large share of jumps in smart contract code are static branches whose destination is already fixed at compile time. Paying the same verification cost and gas as a dynamic jump in these cases is inefficient. This EIP does not aim to eliminate all dynamic jumps; rather, its goal is to additionally provide compilers with cheaper, easier-to-analyze instructions for branches that resolve statically.

At the block level there are two counters. tx_state_gas = evm_state_gas_used, and tx_execution_gas = max(tx_gas_used_after_refund - tx_state_gas, calldata_floor_gas_cost). The gas_used in the block header is max(block_execution_gas_used, block_state_gas_used), this value must be at most block.gas_limit, and it is also used for gas_used_delta in the base fee update. Unlike the refunds described in EIP-7778, the state gas refill concerns state that was never actually created, so even when applied together with EIP-7778 it is reflected as is in evm_state_gas_used, and only the execution gas side changes to the pre-refund value.

1o1buqw991t: Each entry in signatures is [scheme, signer, msg, signature]. scheme is 0x0 ARBITRARY (100 gas), 0x1 SECP256K1 (2800), or 0x2 P256 (6700), and 0x3 and above are reserved. For SECP256K1 and P256, signer is a 20-byte address, and if it is empty it is taken to be tx.sender. For ARBITRARY, signer must be empty. If msg is empty, the signature is over compute_sig_hash(tx), and if it is 32 bytes, the signature is over that digest. A 32-byte value of all zeros is invalid. A SECP256K1 signature is 65 bytes of v || r || s, where v must be 0 or 1 and s must be low-s. P256 is 128 bytes of r || s || qx || qy, and signer must equal keccak256(qx || qy)[12:]. All signatures verified by the protocol must pass before frame execution, and if any one fails the transaction is invalid. The signature hash is computed as keccak(0x06 || rlp(tx)) after replacing the signature bytes of each signature with an empty msg by its length (an integer), so a signer must know the byte length of every empty-msg signature before signing. The raw bytes of protocol-verified signatures cannot be read from the EVM, to allow future aggregation, and only ARBITRARY signatures can be read with SIGDATACOPY.

1o41iufgew5: Underflow is a property of the code alone. For each subroutine, demand counts how far below the entry depth it reaches, and every way in (call site, jump, fallthrough) is checked to see whether that demand is satisfied. If what the incoming path has stacked up falls short, the shortfall becomes that path's own demand and propagates upward. Demand is a non-decreasing integer bounded by 1024, so this iteration always terminates even in the presence of recursion. Execution starts from an empty stack, so top-level code is valid only if its demand is 0. Overflow, by contrast, generally cannot be statically proven when recursion is present, since stack depth then depends on data. Without recursion it can be proven (the enclosed overflow_validator.py does so), but that would attach a caveat to every safety claim, so this proposal leaves overflow as a runtime check, as it is today. Still, the growth of each subroutine can be computed offline in linear time, so clients can reduce the per-push check they do today to one check per call, with no change to consensus.

1obs1iwmfee: Before this EIP, a transaction signature was formed by hashing only six fields: nonce, gas price, gas limit, recipient address, amount, and data. Nowhere in the signature was there any indication of which chain the transaction was intended for. As a result, a signed transaction sent on Ethereum mainnet could be copied and resubmitted as-is on another chain, such as Ethereum Classic (ETC) or the Morden testnet, and could be processed there as a valid transaction too. This is a replay attack: a transfer a user made on mainnet could be executed identically on another chain without the user's intent. EIP-155 binds a signature to a specific chain by including a chain ID, a number unique to each chain, in the data being signed. The original text explains that this provides a way to send a transaction that works on Ethereum but not on ETC or the Morden testnet, and recommends that ETC and future testnets and consortium chains adopt this approach with their own unique chain IDs.

1ok8nnk5pfl: An atomic batch is a contiguous range from frame i to frame j (j > i), where ATOMIC_BATCH_FLAG is set on frames i through j-1 and unset on j. If one frame in the batch fails, the state is reverted to just before the batch started and the remaining frames are skipped. The logs and state changes of frames that ran earlier are discarded, but the receipt keeps their execution status and execution gas used, empties the logs, and sets state gas to 0. The execution and state gas assigned to skipped frames is refunded at the end of the transaction. Inside a batch APPROVE is not possible, so there is never a need to roll back payer or sender_approved. The receipt payload is [cumulative_gas_used, payer, [frame_receipt, ...]], where frame_receipt is [status, gas_used, logs] and gas_used is [execution, state]. A new status code 0x2 is added to status, meaning a frame skipped because of a batch failure. The receipt has no transaction-level status, so an interface that must show a single status has to derive it itself. The logs bloom and log indices are the logs of the frame receipts concatenated in frame order. Between frames, TSTORE/TLOAD transient storage is discarded, and warm/cold records are shared across frames but are reverted along with a frame if that frame reverts.

1oln1e26rav: The existing CALL-family instructions let the caller directly set the amount of gas passed to the callee. But whenever gas fees changed (for example, the storage gas increase in EIP-1884), contracts that sent calls with a hardcoded gas value repeatedly broke. Even if the caller sent extra gas, the fixed gas limit on the call meant the problem could not be fixed. In addition, the old approach of specifying an output buffer address for the call's result has seen less use since the introduction of RETURNDATACOPY, and it has also caused bugs such as inconsistent handling of return values across ERC-20 implementations. Within EOF format code, the existing CALL family is blocked and replaced with new call instructions that cannot specify gas directly, so that contracts will not break even if gas fees are adjusted in the future.

1osknx6syw9: Ethereum nodes keep transactions that are not yet in a block in a waiting area called the mempool, and exchange them with each other. For small transactions, a node pushes the body directly to a few neighbors, but the remaining nodes, as well as large transactions and type 3 transactions that carry blobs, receive only an announcement that "this transaction exists." Today this announcement contains only the hash, type, and size. The receiving node has nothing to judge by except the order in which announcements arrived, so when it spreads requests across several neighbors, it easily ends up fetching transactions that cannot be included in a block because of gaps in the nonce (the per-account sequence number) of the same account. Even when it tries to fill a gap, it does not know whose transaction with which number is missing, so the only option is to request one more hash at a time. To filter out stale announcements for transactions already on chain, it has to keep the hashes of every transaction on chain in a cache. There is also no way to request only the transactions of a particular sender. As block throughput grows, nodes will increasingly be unable to fetch every transaction, so they need information that lets them pick what to fetch and fill gaps.

1oz7gyelf5d: Blob demand has a property where it does not shrink or grow much even when the fee changes (fee inelasticity). As a result, even a small shift in demand causes large swings in the blob base fee. If blob usage falls short of the target for an extended period, the fee drops to the minimum of 1 wei, and afterward, once demand recovers, nearly full blocks must continue for a long time before the equilibrium price is restored. In the meantime, users experience bidding competition under a first-price auction scheme, where they pay exactly what they bid to get into a block, which degrades usability and causes resource consumption to fluctuate unevenly, becoming an obstacle to throughput scaling. In addition, the appropriate fee range keeps changing depending on the ETH price, circulating supply, and protocol throughput scaling, so a fixed floor may become inappropriate over time. This EIP therefore uses the long-run average fee as a reference point and asymmetrically adjusts the update speed the further the fee falls below the average, so that the fee returns quickly to a desirable equilibrium even as demand changes.

1p0hhtzk6ck: Blob propagation uses the existing mechanisms as is. Once proofs are mandatory, a separate path for receiving the full payload is needed, and the execution_payload gossip topic introduced by EIP-7732 can be used. However, if an overwhelming majority of stake is zk validators that listen only to the header topic, a malicious builder could put the payload only in blobs and not gossip it on the execution_payload topic. In that case zk validators attest, but nodes that need the full payload stall. As a countermeasure, a fallback can be added in which a node that fails to receive the payload from the topic reconstructs it from the first payload_blob_count blobs and supplies it to the topic itself. This makes every node act as a bridge node whenever needed. Also, unlike most type 3 blobs, payload blobs are not propagated before the block is built, so the builder's bandwidth requirements can grow.

Also, the task of converting structured data into a hash is itself tricky, and if each app builds its own method and makes a mistake, it breaks the security properties of the system. 1pkjkharwf0: The commitment is defined as `commitment = hash(nullifier_preimage | validator_key | withdrawal_cred | amount)`, and the nullifier as `nullifier = hash(nullifier_preimage)`. The `nullifier_preimage` is a single random value chosen by the depositor at deposit time, serving both as the commitment's hiding randomness and as the nullifier's source. Without knowing this value, an observer cannot link a published nullifier to a specific commitment. The zkSNARK proves in zero knowledge that an unclaimed commitment exists among the stored roots, and publishes the nullifier. Because the validator credentials and amount are included in the commitment preimage, the proof is inherently bound to those values.

1pm6l73zwsp: Standards Track EIPs cover changes affecting most or all Ethereum implementations and are split into four categories. Core covers improvements requiring a consensus fork and changes requiring core developer discussion; Networking covers network protocol improvements such as devp2p and the Light Ethereum Subprotocol; Interface covers language-level standards such as method names or contract ABIs; and ERC covers application-level standards such as token standards (ERC-20) and name registries (ERC-137). Meta EIPs address processes surrounding Ethereum, apply to areas outside the protocol itself, and users generally cannot ignore them. Informational EIPs merely provide design issues or general guidance, do not propose new features, and do not represent community consensus, so they need not be followed. It is recommended that a single EIP contain only one core proposal, and an EIP is needed only for changes that affect multiple clients or define a standard used by multiple apps.

1pqkhqqwcys: Consensus layer (CL) nodes store recently signed beacon blocks and serve them when other nodes request them. A newly joining node starts from a trusted checkpoint and syncs to the current head, but after that it must still backfill old blocks for the period set by the rules. This period is currently 33,024 epochs, so even if the checkpoint is only a few hours old, the node must download almost five months of blocks. This number is the weak subjectivity period computed for the worst case (MAX_SAFETY_DECAY = 100). Actual checkpoint sync, however, uses SAFETY_DECAY = 10, and under the current mainnet configuration that bound is 3,532 epochs. In effect, nodes keep a much longer history than the real safety policy requires. If a checkpoint is older than the policy allows, a newer checkpoint is needed anyway, so holding older blocks beyond that point does not make anything safer. Shortening the retention period reduces sync bandwidth, disk usage, disk writes, backfill time, and the upload bandwidth of peers.

1pxmd96pu3c: Ethereum stores all account and contract data in a data structure called the Merkle Patricia Tree (MPT), and a transition to a new data structure called the Verkle Tree (VKT) is being prepared. Earlier, EIP-7612 introduced an intermediate mechanism called the Overlay Tree, so that only data newly written by transactions is recorded in the VKT. However, the total state is too large, and simply waiting for transactions to naturally touch the data will not move everything over. So this EIP proposes a procedure that mechanically moves a fixed amount of data from the old tree to the new tree every block. The goal is to finish the conversion within a reasonable time and, once complete, remove the intermediate overlay tree mechanism so that all state access goes directly through the VKT.
1pxrznh5nks: This EIP changes DAS networking but leaves PeerDAS custody assignment and its probabilistic guarantees untouched. Row distribution is an additional recovery path and the existing paths stay almost unchanged, so the added cost is limited to the bitmap signaling and, when data is partially withheld, wasted cell requests of at most half a row per assigned row for each row subnet member. Every reconstruction obligation is conditioned on holding 64 verified cells, so unavailable data cannot be used to trigger reconstruction CPU work. The one exception is that phase 2 full reconstruction is deliberately delayed, which implementations already do in practice, and the delay is a single one rather than a delay at every hop. An attack in which a block producer withholds a single cell from one row and releases 64 columns' worth of cells for the remaining rows, causing recovery work on a block that will end up unavailable, is inherited from PeerDAS. In PeerDAS every supernode duplicates this work, but here phase 1 divides it to about one row per row reconstructor and phase 2 skips completed rows, so total work goes down. A supernode sees the bitmaps of all columns, so it can notice unrecoverable rows and skip the work for that block. Row distribution is only an optimization, so a node MUST NOT change its sampling or availability decision rules, or delay a decision, based on row subnet state, and the column topics and request/response remain the authoritative path. Sending a bitmap per cell can make message complexity grow quadratically, so debouncing, rate limiting, and a cap on the number of GroupIDs tracked per peer are recommended. A peer that does not repeatedly deliver cells it has advertised is handled in peer scoring like a peer that sends late messages. Row subnet assignment is a public function of the node ID, so an attacker could grind node IDs to take over or isolate a particular subnet, but phase 2 reconstruction and the column topics cover that row, so the impact is limited to falling back to the current state.

1q1hsfodekc: In the proof-of-work era, Ethereum scheduled forks by block number. The proof-of-stake consensus layer, however, schedules forks by slot number, and slots are a time-based unit. For the consensus layer and execution layer to fork at the same moment after the Merge, the execution layer has no choice but to schedule forks by timestamp as well. But the fork ID (forkid) that nodes use to identify each other was built assuming only block numbers. The fork ID is a mechanism for quickly learning a peer's chain configuration and disconnecting peers that are misconfigured or configured for a different network. It makes the P2P network more reliable, but if it cannot account for timestamp-based forks, identification does not work properly. So the fork ID calculation is updated to include timestamps.

Looking up registry-like contracts that essentially store a simple mapping, such as ERC-20 or ENS, incurs these same costs every time, making gas fees expensive and hard to predict in advance. Under this structure, a contract must spend far more gas each time than the value it actually intends to expose.

1q4tv5o0fo9: Since the CryptoKitties surge in 2017, Ethereum blocks have remained consistently full and gas price markets have kept climbing. Simply raising the block gas limit increases bandwidth, computation, and disk burden, making it harder for ordinary users to run nodes and eroding decentralization. So eth2 planned a multi-stage path to scale by running multiple chains of similar capacity (shards) in parallel under a single consensus, while also switching that consensus itself to proof-of-stake. Proof-of-stake lowers the barriers to participation and technical requirements, increasing the decentralization of consensus, strengthening security through in-protocol penalties and economic finality, and eliminating energy-intensive mining. Phase 0 is the stage that safely bootstraps this new consensus without touching the current mainnet's consensus rules at all.

Large operators run many validators, and these usually see the same chain state and vote identically. Yet the protocol today allows only one individual message per validator. This is because relaxing the duplicate aggregation rule would let an attacker collect other validators' attestations and form exponentially many subset combinations, flooding the network with spam. Making slots shorter and finality faster requires a large reduction in attestation volume. EIP-7251 reduces the validator count through balance consolidation, but it is optional, so adoption is slow. 1ql0ayrc1my: process_randao takes the hash-chain path if the stored commitment is not 0. It checks that hash_chain_reveal is not 0, that blake3(HASH_CHAIN_RANDAO_DST + reveal) equals the stored commitment, and that randao_reveal is G2_POINT_AT_INFINITY. It then accumulates mix = blake3(existing mix + reveal) and stores the revealed value as the new commitment. If the commitment is 0, it verifies the BLS signature as before and mixes with xor. The hash-chain path uses a hash accumulator instead of xor because of the commitment-copying attack. A commitment carries no identity, so someone can copy another validator's current commitment to create a valid registration, and with a linear xor accumulator they could cancel the victim's contribution by inserting the same value again. A hash has no efficient inverse operation, so inserting the same value again just yields an unrelated new mix, and this attack is blocked at the root. That is why the raw reveal value can be mixed in without per-validator personalization. The assertion that rejects a 0 reveal protects the invariant that 0 means unregistered.

1qn7uzm6830: A BAL is an RLP list that follows the order address → field → block access index → change. For each account it records AccountChanges = [address, storage_changes, storage_reads, balance_changes, nonce_changes, code_changes]. BlockAccessIndex is 0 for pre-execution system calls, 1..n for transactions in block order, and n+1 for post-execution, including withdrawals. Integer fields (StorageKey, StorageValue, Balance, Nonce, BlockAccessIndex) must be encoded as minimal big-endian with no leading zeros, and 0 is encoded as an empty byte string (0x80). Accounts are sorted lexicographically by address, slots and read keys by key ascending, and each change list by index ascending. 1qpv2ljy62b: On Ethereum, gas cost is meant to represent the time it takes to process an operation, converted into money. However, instructions that read data from disk, such as SLOAD for reading storage or instructions that look up another account's balance and code, were priced far below their actual cost. During the 2016 Shanghai DoS attacks, an attacker exploited this gap by sending transactions that touched huge numbers of accounts, slowing down the network. Gas costs were raised afterward, but not enough. Research found that a single maliciously crafted transaction could take 20 to 80 seconds to process, while an average transaction finishes in milliseconds. This proposal raises the cost of these instructions by about 3x, cutting worst case processing time from 7 seconds down to around 27 seconds. At the same time, re-reading something already read once is priced very cheaply, so honestly written contracts are not penalized.

Given this situation, a single instruction was needed. 1r7hxaz1bgf: In the EVM, jump instructions (JUMP, JUMPI) cannot move to an arbitrary location; they can only move to a byte marked with JUMPDEST (0x5b). However, not every 0x5b byte in the code is a genuine JUMPDEST. Instructions like PUSH1 use the byte immediately following them as an immediate argument, a parameter written directly in the code rather than on the stack, and that value can happen to be 0x5b. So currently the entire code must be scanned in advance to identify which bytes are immediate arguments before jump validity can be determined. The source cites three problems with this approach. First, because the code must be preprocessed, the burden grows linearly with code size, creating a denial-of-service (DoS) attack vector. Second, it is difficult to safely introduce new instructions that use immediate arguments. Third, a CODECOPY data region can invalidate a JUMPDEST that follows it. The intent of this check is to prevent unintended code execution, but the proposer's judgment is that in practice almost all jumps go to fixed destinations, so the cost of the check outweighs its benefit.

1rs8e5dpul0: Validator keys today are BLS keys held in an ERC-2335 keystore. This key never changes no matter how many times it signs, so the key itself stays safe even if the file is copied or restored from a backup. But Lean Ethereum switches validator keys to XMSS, a hash-based signature scheme, to prepare for quantum computers. XMSS consumes one one-time signing slot, called a leaf, per signature, and signing two different messages with the same leaf makes forgery possible, effectively destroying the key. This single property makes all three behaviors that were previously taken for granted - the file never changes, copying is harmless, and restoring from any backup is safe - dangerous. Because the existing keystore spec never assumed this kind of consumable key, merely changing the encrypted container is not enough; a new format is needed that also defines where signing state is managed and in what order it is stored.

The execution client no longer fetches blocks itself, so even in a passive state it needs a meaningful query, and none of the existing Engine API methods reports either head directly. Queries outside the Engine API are not consistently offered on the authenticated port and are not precise enough to build a deterministic sync loop on. An alternative that returns every tip of the subtree rooted at the finalized block was set aside because the execution client would have to track all tips. Even with a single head, there is a guarantee that children of the reported head are never answered with SYNCING and that the report changes only in response to engine_newPayload or engine_forkchoiceUpdated, so the consensus client can find the divergence point and redeliver. 1rwzyk4f0rz: The host (usually a stateful EL client) records the account, storage, code, and ancestor header data it uses while executing or building a block. build_stateless_input bundles the ExecutionWitness, ExecutionRequests, the block access list, and chain_id into a StatelessInput. The execution witness is built from the per-block read/write tracker that the EL already uses to build the block access list (BAL), together with pre-state trie data. The host records trie nodes using the same lookups the guest uses when reading, and both sides apply inserts and updates first and deletions afterward in each storage trie. A deletion can collapse a branch, and then the remaining sibling node is needed. Doing deletions last reduces collapses, and because both sides write in the same order, the guest never looks for a sibling node the host did not record. build_execution_witness finally asserts that mpt_root equals the expected post-state root. On serialization, a 2-byte schema ID is prepended to the SSZ bytes. The high byte is the fork (Amsterdam = 0x15) and the low byte is the schema revision, so Amsterdam revision 1 is 0x1501. The guest must accept only the canonical SSZ encoding, and the reference decoder re-encodes the decoded value and rejects the input if the bytes are not exactly the same. This check catches offset gaps and unread trailing bytes, even inside nested containers. Conformance tests must be run with the blockchain_test_engine fixture, not blockchain_test. Because StatelessInput wraps the Engine API NewPayloadRequest, the engine fixture covers more invalid payload variants.

1s0j6i99qu9: When a signer is removed, the majority threshold drops by 1, which can suddenly push another pending proposal over the threshold. That execution could in turn trigger yet another proposal to pass. If conflicting proposals (for example, adding a new signer and removing an existing one) pass at the same time, the evaluation order can significantly change the final list, and since signers can flip their vote every block, it is not even clear which proposal came first. Clique avoids this pitfall by explicitly forbidding cascading effects. Only the account named in the current header's beneficiary can be added to or removed from the list, and any other proposal that reaches a majority as a side effect is executed only when that target is voted on again later and the majority still holds at that point.

1s39c3btcti: EIP-8297 proposes changing Ethereum's state storage structure from the existing hexary Merkle Patricia Trie (MPT) to a Partitioned Binary Tree (PBT). The problem is how to move the enormous state of an already-running mainnet to the new structure without splitting the chain. One path is an online overlay approach that converts gradually, inside consensus, while the chain keeps running, but then every client must match the conversion's progress bit-for-bit block by block, state proofs become complicated by spanning two trees until conversion finishes, and a zkEVM prover would have to prove the conversion process itself. This EIP instead takes an offline approach that finishes the conversion outside consensus. The consensus change shrinks to a single block changing how one header field is computed, and the state root always commits to the full state. In exchange, it pays the disk and compute cost of maintaining both trees during the transition period, and recovers correctness for the conversion, now invisible on-chain, through dual verification and shadow-root observation.

1s4td2k9mac: The consensus layer stores the threshold inside the 0x02 withdrawal credentials without adding a field to BeaconState or Validator. Byte 0 is COMPOUNDING_WITHDRAWAL_PREFIX(0x02), bytes 1 to 2 are the threshold as a little-endian uint16 in units of EFFECTIVE_BALANCE_INCREMENT, bytes 3 to 11 are reserved, and bytes 12 to 31 are the execution address. The constant SWEEP_THRESHOLD_CREDENTIAL_OFFSET is 1 and SWEEP_THRESHOLD_CREDENTIAL_LENGTH is 2. If the threshold equals MAX_EFFECTIVE_BALANCE_ELECTRA, it is stored as 0, and an out-of-range value is read as the default. For example, 0x02e803... is 1,000 ETH. Every place in the sweep and effective balance calculations that used get_max_effective_balance now uses this threshold. The threshold is therefore both the automatic withdrawal threshold and the effective balance cap. The rationale section explains that adding an 8-byte list per validator to BeaconState would grow it by as much as balances, while the credentials already have 11 free bytes and switch_to_compounding_validator already has a path that rewrites the credentials, so the threshold was placed there. Storing the maximum as 0 gives every threshold a single encoding, and a validator can also revert to the original credentials.

1s5wi7s26j4: Row subnets carry only partial messages and do not define a full message form. A node that does not support the Partial Messages Extension must not subscribe to a row subnet (MUST NOT), and mesh peers that do not support the extension may be pruned (MAY). The non-discrimination guidance in EIP-8136 applies to column topics, which have a full-message fallback path, and for nodes without support the column topics and getBlobs remain open as before. Row subnet membership is computed from the node ID alone, so no ENR extension is needed. A node applies get_row_subnet to node IDs it finds through discv5 lookups and similar means to locate peers on the same subnet, and it should secure enough connections to maintain a healthy mesh (SHOULD). This is because subnet members make up only about 1 / ROW_SUBNET_COUNT of all nodes, so they do not appear often enough among random peers. The SSZ containers, bitmap encoding and GroupID derivation are defined in ethereum/consensus-specs following the EIP-8136 approach. The bitmap covers the rows assigned to the subnet in blob_index order, and within a row in cell_index order. Cells received from a row subnet must be verified against the KZG commitment of the corresponding blob before they are forwarded or used (MUST), and a peer that sends an invalid cell is penalized under the same rules as on column subnets. A peer may limit itself to providing only half of the cells of each assigned row (MAY), and this limit applies per row. When a node receives cells through any path, it should send its updated bitmap to peers (SHOULD), and it may debounce this.

1s7b65ucttw: Once EIP-7702 applies, an existing EOA (externally owned account) can delegate itself to a smart account implementation and use features such as batch execution and gas sponsorship. The problem is that the delegated account uses storage tied to its own address. If the user switches wallets and re-delegates to a different implementation, the storage used by the previous wallet stays in place, and if the new implementation uses the same slots, a collision occurs that can lead to unexpected behavior such as account lockup or security vulnerabilities. Until now an EOA worked with only a cryptographic key pair and moved freely between wallets, so moving wallets is already familiar to users. To preserve this freedom after delegation, a common convention is needed so that an account can check in a standard way which storage slots it has used and clean them up before moving.

1s98gwyrlqz: Ethereum consensus data is serialized under a scheme called SSZ (Simple Serialize) and then compressed into a single summary hash through a process called Merkleization. External programs verify proofs against this summary value to confirm that specific data has not been tampered with. For example, a decentralized staking pool's smart contract uses this to check whether a participating validator has been slashed (had its stake forfeited as a penalty). However, whenever a fork (network upgrade) adds or removes a field from the data structure, the Merkleization result changes, breaking existing verification code. Software whose update cycle differs from Ethereum's, such as smart contracts, hardware wallets, and mobile device operating systems, must keep patching their verification logic to match Ethereum's fork schedule. This EIP changes the consensus data structures so that, as long as the feature being verified itself doesn't change, existing proof verifiers keep working across forks. It also separates a list's maximum capacity from its schema, so later EIPs can adjust the limit alone without touching the type or the Merkle proofs.

1sgbph5rfr6: Nodes must be able to process not the average block, but the worst-case block an attacker can construct. EIP-7623, EIP-7976, EIP-7981, and EIP-8131 have bounded the worst-case block size by imposing a gas floor on bytes carried directly in a transaction, such as calldata, access lists, and EIP-7702 delegation tuples. However, the block access list (BAL) introduced by EIP-7928 is a new source of bytes filled in at runtime as opcodes execute, and the existing floors do not price these bytes. The cheapest BAL contribution is a cold SLOAD, which fills 32 bytes for 2,100 gas. An attacker can fill calldata entirely with non-zero bytes to satisfy the floor, then redirect the remaining execution gas to cold SLOADs to inflate the BAL further, allowing a 60M-gas block to reach as much as about 1.55 MiB instead of the targeted 0.89 MiB.
1sgfdekk4x: Adding an item to WAM still requires paying the same cold cost (2100 gas or more) as today, and the 2000-2500 gas savings accrue not to whoever added the item but to whoever accesses the same item afterward, so there is no economic incentive to bloat WAM. Empirically, WAM holds about 170,000 items at roughly 60 bytes each, around 10MB plus SMT internal nodes, which can be kept in memory alongside the existing node cache without needing a storage tier. The worst case is bounded by the block gas limit. A pathological block filled only with unique cold storage accesses adds about 16,000 items, so at W=256 the worst-case WAM is about 4 million items, roughly 250MB, though realistic mainnet workloads come nowhere close to this. On a reorg, since the transition is a deterministic function of the BALs, re-executing the new canonical chain restores WAM, and finality (2 epochs, about 12.8 minutes) bounds reorg depth to a small fraction of the warming window.

1sii5b0uqvw: Users must trust that their key provider will neither disclose the key early (front-running risk) nor late (paying only the envelope fee while execution fails). They must also weakly trust the key providers of encrypted transactions ahead of them in the same block, since those providers can see the key for a later transaction before deciding whether to disclose it, giving them 1 bit of influence over the later transaction's pre-state, and a maliciously designed decryption scheme could make this attack much stronger. If a reorg occurs, the key for an excluded transaction may be disclosed, but because the key message includes the block hash, the verification function invalidates it, preventing payload execution and front-running. Key ID front-running, where someone copies another party's key_id to get included first, can be prevented by a namespacing strategy in which providers only accept key IDs prefixed with the envelope signer's address. Envelope hijacking attacks, where a disclosed key is used to decrypt a transaction and resubmit it in a new envelope to jump ahead, are prevented by the decryption transaction's reference to envelope_signer, and payload substitution attacks are impossible because the encrypted transaction's signature covers the payload. There is also a collusion attack where a key provider and a builder conspire to leak key information in advance, but its impact is assessed as low.

1sintfml5l2: EIP-1153's transient storage is discarded with every transaction, so it suits uses within a single transaction, whereas this EIP targets uses that persist across multiple transactions and blocks but do not need indefinite retention. The two-period rollover was chosen for a lifetime guarantee: an entry is kept for at least one period after being written and disappears after at most two periods. With a single global rollover, data written near the end of a period could be cleared almost immediately, which would be unfriendly to developers. Using two accounts enables constant-time rollover: at each period boundary, only the current account's storageRoot needs to change, the previous account is kept for one more period, and storage older than one period becomes unreachable and can be pruned.
1siqsqmvmt1: Blocks are split into sequencing blocks and execution blocks. A sequencing block is produced at every odd block height; it receives transaction hashes from users, collects the prepayment (gas fee plus optional tip), sorts the hashes in descending order of prepayment, publishes the sort result as a commitment, and stores the hashes in the block. An execution block is produced at every even block height; it verifies that the transaction contents sent by users match the committed hashes and executes them in the predetermined order. The interval between sequencing blocks can be set shorter than that between execution blocks.

1suojfdhmus: On Ethereum, every operation is priced in a fee unit called gas. However, the current gas model has many mismatches between the price and the actual computing resources consumed. The source text gives as an example that even among pure computation operations, there is a large variance in execution time per unit of gas. This means some operations take much longer despite yielding the same gas value. This kind of price distortion causes certain operations to become bottlenecks, making it hard to raise the throughput of the whole network. The core goal of the Glamsterdam fork is improving L1 scalability, and the precondition for that is aligning gas costs with actual resource usage. This EIP gathers together the proposals belonging to that effort, organizing which proposals are under consideration for inclusion and which have been declined, so the community can track progress. The source text notes that this list is a first step and that further adjustments are expected to be needed in later hard forks.

1t2vv5tt0la: Currently, EIP-1559's base fee judges demand solely by the gas a block used and does not consider block production time. Under PoW, block times are irregular, which by itself causes the base fee to fluctuate. Under PoS, missing a single slot stretches the block time to 24 or 36 seconds, which makes the next block appear full and creates a false signal of a demand surge, triggering an unnecessary fee spike while the block space corresponding to the missed slot is permanently lost. This amplifies the effectiveness of denial-of-service (DoS) attacks targeting proposers. More severely, if a fork or outage prevents many proposers from producing blocks for a while, the average block time increases and throughput drops by the same proportion; while PoW recovers quickly through difficulty adjustment, PoS has no such automatic recovery mechanism, so if a third of slots are missed, normalization can take weeks to months.

1t5ng7w7iv5: Today every transaction pays the same 21,000 base gas regardless of what it does. A zero-value transaction to an existing account and a transaction that creates a new account while sending funds pay the same amount. This is so even though the latter touches one more account, writes a new balance, emits a log, and increases the state that the blockchain must keep permanently. A single fixed constant is priced high for the simplest path and low for the path that uses genuinely long-lived resources. This proposal splits that constant into named items such as signature verification, account access, balance write, and new account creation, so that each transaction pays for what it actually does. Pricing the costs in the same units used elsewhere in the gas system also has the advantage that when the price of an individual item changes later, the change is reflected automatically without recalculating a separate constant.

1t67ngbc4v6: The table's max_index is an unsigned 8-bit value, and the number of relative_offset entries that follow is max_index+1, so the table size is at most 256. RJUMPV must have at least one offset, so it occupies at least 4 bytes. If case > max_index, it does not branch and proceeds to the next instruction, which can be used to place a default path right after the instruction. This approach was chosen instead of the alternative of aborting with an exception on a match failure, leaving it to the programmer to decide how to fill empty table slots with zero. RJUMPV 0 relative_offset is an RJUMPI with the condition inverted, so it can replace the two instructions ISZERO RJUMPI. Table entries are at most 256 single-byte units, so reading offsets does not become a DoS attack surface.

1tairs59gxb: Today's Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) assumes that clients always hold recent block hashes directly. However, stateless clients, which will appear in the future, do not store the full state and verify using only the witness data delivered with each block, so this assumption no longer holds. Putting block hashes inside state lets them be delivered in the witness, which solves the problem. Also, directly extending the range the BLOCKHASH opcode can look up (the most recent 256) would change the meaning of existing behavior, but keeping a separate contract storage lets a longer range be offered smoothly while leaving existing behavior untouched. Rollups can also query this contract directly to use a longer hash history, and there is a side benefit that proofs about the most recent 8191 ancestor blocks can be built or verified directly against the current state.

1tm55dp6tqh: Today, putting data into a transaction requires using calldata, which is expensive because the EVM directly reads and processes it. EIP-2028 lowered the gas cost of calldata, but there are cases, such as sidechains, where the EVM never needs to look at the content at all. In a fraud-proof-based sidechain, the block proposer only needs to prove that 'this data exists,' and verification by fraud proof only happens after the fact if the data turns out to be wrong. In other words, the data ends up paying the same cost as calldata even though the EVM has no reason to read it right away. Following the principle of 'not paying for what isn't used,' a separate, cheaper path is needed for recording on-chain data that the EVM does not process.
1tmnb01pjjj: The consensus layer treats root only as an opaque bytes32. What that value commits to is decided by the application, and what it approves must bind the expected (source_id, slot, root) tuple. A successful verify frame proves only that the tuple is currently stored and recent, so application verification must check the defined fields and success status of the completed frame before trusting the frame data. EIP-8141 also allows verification against an explicit 32-byte signature message instead of the standard signature hash, in which case the verification logic must bind the recent root frame and the related frames on its own. For the same (source_id, slot), only the last root in canonical execution order remains, so an application that needs multiple roots in one slot must use an aggregate commitment. This EIP does not guarantee the inclusion of root-writing transactions. An application that must publish on time needs its own publication path, redundant root sources, and an inclusion policy for write transactions. The same (source_address, salt) yields the same source_id on other chains, so proofs, bridge messages, and attestations created off-chain must bind the chain domain outside the tuple. Storage remains permanently under RECENT_ROOT_ADDRESS. Existing sources overwrite at most RECENT_ROOT_LENGTH entries, but new sources add entries, so the EIP notes that if the usual state growth fee proves insufficient, a source registration cost or a first-write surcharge could be proposed later. A single popular root can cause many transactions to be evicted at once through a reorg or simultaneous expiry, but thanks to the dependency index there is no need to re-run the validation prefix of unrelated transactions.

1tsqj1aapao: Ethereum state keeps growing, increasing the burden of running a node. Earlier state expiry attempts required major structural changes such as address space extension (ASE), oil, and multiple per-epoch trees, so complexity grew quickly and progress stalled. This proposal uses a simple approach that expires only the extension-and-suffix tree, the leaf level of the verkle trie. The tree structure itself is left unchanged; only the values and sub-commitments of leaves that have not been used for a long time are deleted, and they can be revived with a simple proof when needed. The goal is to reduce state size without the complex changes that would hurt the user and developer experience.

1tsupw0i2yo: Once an account's code is set to 0xef0101 || pubkey, any ECDSA-signed transaction (type 0x00 through 0x04, or the ECDSA mode of type 0x06) for which that account is the recovered sender is rejected at the validation stage, and any EIP-7702 authorization tuple naming that account as authority is also rejected. The original ECDSA key loses its protocol-level meaning regardless of whether it is still held. The source describes this permanence as a safe design choice: since the new key is the root key, the owner can always replace it via a native key signature tuple, so there is no loss of control, whereas if the conversion could be reversed, a leaked or quantum-broken ECDSA key would leave open a 'dormant key' attack path that could revert the delegation and seize the account. 1twbbh4o75j: is_active_preregistration() compares whether state.latest_execution_payload_bid.slot is less than the stored expiry_slot. It uses the slot of the outstanding parent bid rather than the slot at which the request is applied, because in EIP-7732 a payload's requests are applied one block later. This way the deposit is checked against the registrations that were active at the slot where that payload was built. The comparison is a strict inequality, so a payload at a slot equal to expiry_slot is no longer protected. process_preregistration_expiry() removes expired records during epoch processing, but it is pure garbage collection. Its timing has no effect on whether a registration is enforced or whether a new request is accepted, and an expired record stays until the next cleanup and can be overwritten by a new registration after passing the active capacity check. The absolute expiry slot is computed once at storage time, so later changes to PREREGISTRATION_EXPIRY_SLOTS do not alter existing deadlines. It also lets the execution layer verify the same window without knowing the lifetime parameter, the slot time or SLOTS_PER_EPOCH. If a verification contract proves expiry_slot via EIP-4788 and requires the current EIP-7843 SLOTNUM to be less than it, the deposit is atomically protected or reverted. Expiry does not depend on finality, so it proceeds even while finality is stalled. A registration that expired unused can be re-established by resubmitting the same signed message.

1u58ajfv7dw: Signature permanence: The preregistration signature is fork-independent and never expires cryptographically. Only the onchain record has a window of 262,144 slots (about 36 days at 12-second slots), and anyone holding the signed message can resubmit it after expiry to revive the record. Operators must confirm that the credential they choose is supported in the intended withdrawal flow. Builder deposits: Preregistration applies only to validator deposits, and EIP-8282 builder deposits neither check nor consume it. Preregistering a 0xB0 credential does not register or protect a builder, and sending 0xB0 through the validator deposit path creates a validator that currently cannot withdraw. Race condition: If an attacker deposits before the registration is processed, first-deposit-wins creates the validator and the registration is rejected. If both are in the same payload, the deposit is processed first and the result is the same. So a protocol must verify the registration's existence and expiry atomically with the deposit via EIP-4788, and if it verifies in a separate transaction it must wait until inclusion is finalized. State size: Active records total at most about 46 MB (88 bytes × 524,288), plus up to MAX_PREREGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_PAYLOAD × (SLOTS_PER_EPOCH - 1) = 124 expired records waiting for the next cleanup. At the target rate of 1 per block, filling 2**19 takes about 72.8 days, which exceeds the 36-day expiry window, so in steady state the active count stays near 2**18 (about 23 MB), and saturating it requires a rate above target, which makes the fee rise exponentially. If n requests per block (n > 1) are sustained, excess grows by n - 1 per block, and the fee exceeds 1 ETH after about 17 × ln(10^18) / (n - 1) blocks.

1ulu9imwlxp: Rule 1: if both sides' FORK_HASH match, compare my head against the peer's FORK_NEXT. If a fork the peer announced as not yet passed has already passed on my side, the chains are incompatible and the connection is dropped (1a). If the peer announced no fork, or it has not yet passed on my side either, the nodes connect (1b). Rule 2: if the peer's FORK_HASH is a subset of my past fork history and the peer's FORK_NEXT matches the next fork block number on my side, the nodes connect. This is the case where the peer is syncing. Rule 3: if the peer's FORK_HASH is a superset of my history and can be constructed by filling in future forks I know about, the nodes connect. This is the case where I am syncing. Rule 4: everything else is rejected. There is one asymmetry. Since only the single next fork can be known, not the peer's entire list of future forks, the fact that a syncing peer's software is outdated cannot be known until the peer catches up. The original document explains that this is acceptable since the peer will disconnect first anyway, and it is merely a transient condition during syncing.

1unu8ivzo4s: Ethereum's long-term goal is to verify that a block executed correctly simply and quickly using a validity proof. But the current state tree, the Merkle Patricia Trie (MPT), does not fit this goal. It uses RLP for node encoding and the circuit-unfriendly Keccak hash, has a tree-within-a-tree structure where storage trees are nested inside the account tree, and account code is not even included in the state tree. Proof size is also a problem. Because each node has 16 children, proving a single branch in a tree of size 2^32 requires about 3840 bytes on average, and the source document calculates that a worst-case block reading 1 byte each from different accounts' code at 30 million gas would require about 330MB. Switching to a binary tree with 2 children per node minimizes proof size and also opens the door to switching to a proof-friendly hash function.

1uw6zczoagt: Every storage slot leaf's value becomes STORAGE_LEAF_VALUE_LENGTH (36) bytes. The 32-byte slot_value sits at offset 0, in the same place as in EIP-8297, and a 4-byte big-endian last_written_block follows at offset 32. This applies identically to slots 0..63 stored in the account header stem (sub-index HEADER_STORAGE_OFFSET + storage_key) and to slots 64 and above in the STORAGE_ZONE, and storage keys are unchanged. Since all 256 bits of a slot are meaningful, unlike an account there is no spare byte to repurpose, so the leaf was widened instead. The alternative of a separate metadata leaf was ruled out because it would double the number of slot leaves, require separate keys and branches, and need to be kept in sync with the slot. With both values in one leaf, a single read, write, or proof handles both, and deletion, revert, and migration all happen together automatically.

1uwlvw1wbme: The EVM has the property that execution cannot jump into the middle of an instruction, and this was previously guaranteed by excluding PUSH's immediate from jump destination analysis (jumpdest analysis). This EIP does not change jump analysis at all; instead, if the immediate is 0x5b (JUMPDEST) or in the range 0x60 to 0x7f (PUSH1 through PUSH32), it is treated as an exception at execution time. For example, the byte sequence e6 5b was previously interpreted as INVALID JUMPDEST, which contains a valid jump destination; if jump analysis were changed to exclude the immediate, this destination would disappear and break existing contracts. Since arbitrary data can be included in code, it must be assumed that such byte sequences are already deployed. This design therefore preserves the guarantee that every execution flow that does not execute an undefined opcode behaves identically before and after this change is introduced, and that no jump destination is newly created or removed. Disassemblers should label such cases as INVALID_DUPN and similar.

1uy6w40t9eb: Today the RETURN instruction in the EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) can only return bytes laid out contiguously in memory. But since the introduction of transient storage, many smart contracts use a pattern where data is stored in transient storage to save gas and then returned again in a callback. To return it, the data first has to be read one piece at a time in a loop and copied into memory, which adds the instruction cost of the loop plus memory expansion cost on top. The same inefficiency occurs when returning data that is already in storage. This EIP lets developers choose directly where to return from, eliminating the intermediate step of copying into memory.

1uyju5kqoxc: ExecutionPayloadEnvelope carries payload, execution_requests, parent_beacon_block_root and builder_index, and drops the old beacon_block_root. When a builder creates a bid, the block does not exist yet, so the block root cannot be known. In EIP-7732, the builder could see the bid included in a block and then build the envelope with the root. The block root is instead carried in the chunk message. PayloadChunk consists of payload_chunks_root, index, chunk, chunk_inclusion_proof (Vector[Bytes32, CHUNK_INCLUSION_PROOF_DEPTH]), slot, and beacon_block_root. payload_chunks_root is the same value the bid commits to and identifies the set of chunks. The bid spreads on its own gossip topic ahead of the block, so a recipient that has seen a valid bid committing to that root can verify chunks immediately without waiting for the block. slot and beacon_block_root are unauthenticated hints that sit outside the inclusion proof. slot is used to cheaply filter chunks by slot window and MUST equal the slot of the bid that committed to that root. beacon_block_root is used to find or request the corresponding block and MUST equal the root of the block that contains that bid. Recipients MUST NOT treat the two fields as authenticated values and use them only to decide the lookup path. The only thing that binds a chunk to a bid is payload_chunks_root.

Because the signature field is not included in the canonical hash, it is charged at the worst-case nonzero-byte rate regardless of byte content: authenticator_signature_tokens(sig) = 4 * len(sig.signature), which is used in place of tokens_in in EIP-8141's signature_data_cost and calldata_tokens calculations. 1v2eri5m20p: A system contract called the key provider registry is deployed on the execution layer. Anyone can register as a key provider and receive a unique ID; registration requires specifying a contract with a decryption function and a key verification function that take a key ID and key message as byte strings. A key provider can designate other providers as directly trusted, forming a directed graph, where a path from A to B is defined to mean A trusts B. The beacon chain replicates this registry into state in a manner similar to the deposit processing mechanism. The source code of the registry contract is still TBD. The reason for using a trust graph between providers instead of per-user trust declarations is to reduce transaction size overhead and block-building complexity, and because a small provider need only trust a large provider to be included in the same block, which mitigates monopolization.
1v2ew8ueoj5: Today Ethereum produces one block every 12 seconds. Users wait that long on average to get a transaction confirmed, and the epoch used for finality takes 384 seconds. Raising throughput by enlarging blocks has limits. The source notes that it is hard to grow blocks beyond 10 MiB without major changes to the network. Instead, keeping block size the same and producing blocks twice as often gives the same effect, while bandwidth use is spread evenly instead of arriving in bursts. More frequent blocks mean prices on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) update more often, which reduces liquidity providers' losses (LVR), and rollups tied to L1 block time also get faster.

1v4hvw6zhdw: If input validation passes, ECDSA verification is performed. First compute s1 = s^(-1) (mod n) and recover the random point used when signing as R' = (h * s1) * G + (r * s1) * (qx, qy). If R' is the point at infinity, verification fails. Take the x-coordinate r' of R', and if r' ≡ r (mod n), the signature is valid and the 32-byte value 1 is returned; otherwise empty output is returned. The comparison is done modulo n rather than as simple equality (r' == r) so that the case where the x-coordinate of R' exceeds the curve order n is handled according to the ECDSA standard.

1v52bk36hj1: Deployed contracts spend gas through three channels: reading GAS, the gas argument to a call, and the 2,300 gas stipend, and all three remain in gas units. If the units did not match, a contract passing gasleft() - 5000 would end up leaving only 5 gas instead of 5,000 gas, among other problems. GAS rounds milli_gas_left // 1000 up after flooring, so a contract never sees more gas than it actually has. The gas argument to CALL, CALLCODE, DELEGATECALL, and STATICCALL is in gas units, and the EIP-150 rule is applied to whole = available // 1000, passing message_call_milli_gas = min(gas, max_gas) * 1000. The remainder below 1 gas stays with the calling frame, and when the child returns, the unused milli-gas is returned exactly, without rounding. EIP-2200's SSTORE check compares milli_gas_left against GAS_CALL_STIPEND * 1000, so a frame holding only the stipend still cannot execute SSTORE.
1v5emgz8wt3: This EIP takes effect via a hard fork. An analysis of roughly 168.28 million mainnet transactions from August 22 to November 19, 2026 found that, compared to Glamsterdam, only 0.66% of transactions pay more gas and none pay less. All of those paying more are blob carrier (type 3) and EIP-7702 (type 4) transactions. Blob carriers execute almost nothing, so the 2,048 floor gas per blob hash determines their gas usage, adding about 6,100 gas per transaction, borne almost entirely by L2 batchers. SetCode transactions pick up 8,512 floor gas per authorization, with a single sender accounting for 69% of the added gas. During the analysis period, 26% of blob transactions had a gas limit below the new floor, so wallets and eth_estimateGas must factor in the new floor.

1v6chlm6klu: In 2016, Ethereum experienced a series of denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. Attackers exploited the fact that operations reading state stored on disk, such as account balances or contract code, were priced far too cheaply relative to their actual processing cost. Disk reads take a long time, but since the gas cost was only around 20 to 50, a small amount of money could force nodes to perform a massive amount of read work. This imbalance could not be resolved through software optimization alone, and such attack transactions would also pose a risk under future sharding designs, which would require tens of megabytes of Merkle proofs. This EIP therefore raises the gas cost of state-reading operations to match the actual burden of spam attacks, while also adjusting how gas is forwarded so that existing contracts would not break in the process.

1vb0w4ozbbg: Today Ethereum produces one block every 12 seconds. Users feel those 12 seconds on every transfer, exchange deposit and payment. The source splits the problem into several parts. The loss that liquidity providers on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) suffer to arbitrage is proportional to the square root of the block interval, so cutting 12 seconds to 10 seconds reduces it by about 9%. Shorter slots also bring final confirmation sooner, and more block proposers take part in the same span of time, which makes censoring transactions harder. The need for preconfirmation mechanisms, built up to hide the 12-second delay, also shrinks. The time an L2 waits for several L1 blocks before processing a deposit gets shorter as well. The real bottleneck, though, is not choosing the number. The assumption that a slot is 12 seconds is embedded throughout every consensus client and execution client. This EIP does two things together: it first removes that assumption so that slot time becomes a configuration value, and then it conservatively reduces it to 10 seconds.

1vbt2l5k5o0: Ethereum has a proposal (EIP-8188) to create a consensus-verified record of when an account or storage slot was last written. State-tiering designs that treat long-unused state differently, such as EIP-8295, build on top of this record. However, EIP-8188 is defined in terms of the current state tree, the Merkle Patricia Trie (MPT): it adds a fifth element to the account RLP list and wraps slots in a two-element RLP list. The new state tree, the Partitioned Binary Tree (PBT, EIP-8297), has no RLP. Account fields are filled into fixed byte positions of the BASIC_DATA leaf, and slot leaves hold only a 256-bit value. So EIP-8188's encoding cannot be carried over as is, and a place for last_written_block in the PBT has to be defined separately. This proposal defines that place so tiering can run directly off the tree. However, like EIP-8188, it deals only with metadata, and aside from EIP-8037's state-creation gas adjustment, it does not change gas costs or tiering policy.

1vho7fgq1yi: Blob transactions (type 3) are classified by their max_fee_per_blob_gas value. If it is at or above the current blob base fee, the transaction is JIT: the fee is paid at inclusion time and the data is propagated at block time. If it is 0, the transaction is AOT: no blob fee is paid at inclusion time, but it must be backed by a valid ticket, and the data is propagated ahead of time at the consensus layer. Any value from 1 up to blob_base_fee - 1 is invalid and must be rejected. A single transaction must be entirely JIT or entirely AOT. AOT transactions are signed with max_fee_per_blob_gas == 0, so a builder cannot reclassify one as JIT, because the execution layer rejects as JIT any transaction whose value is below the current fee. Whether AOT reuses type 3 or uses a new transaction type without a blob fee field is a design decision left open for now, and the two approaches are mechanically equivalent.

1viiidfpnfo: Ethereum has special built-in contracts called precompiles that implement frequently used cryptographic operations. Among them, the three alt_bn128 elliptic curve operations (addition, multiplication, and pairing check) are core building blocks for privacy- and scalability-oriented technologies such as zero-knowledge proofs. However, in 2018 Geth switched to Cloudflare's bn256 library, which cut the actual computation cost of these operations to roughly a tenth of what it had been, and the Parity client also became significantly faster through bn library optimizations. Gas costs are supposed to reflect the burden an operation places on the network, but the fee schedule still reflected the slower era, making it far more expensive than it should have been. As a result, protocols such as AZTEC, ZEther, and rollups were constrained in how much they could use on mainnet because of gas costs. This EIP fixes the bottleneck by updating the fee schedule to match reality.

NORMALIZED_DISTANCE = (D - 1) / (WINDOW_SIZE_BLOCKS - 1) is clamped to [0, 1], the smoothstep value 3x² - 2x³ is computed, and then inverted as DISCOUNT_FACTOR = 1 - SMOOTHSTEP_VALUE. At D = 1 the discount rate is maximal, and at D = WINDOW_SIZE_BLOCKS (32 by default) it is 0. The consensus code must implement this with integer arithmetic, and the reference implementation uses 2²⁵ (33,554,432) as a fixed-point scale with round-half-up rounding. Because the curve is gentle, the discount stays near its maximum through roughly the first 12 to 16 blocks and only converges to 0 near the end of the window, so missing the exact block does not make cost jump off a cliff.

1vpm5ez5xxs: In practice, validators are randomly split into 32 committees, so the number of malicious validators per committee is approximated by a binomial distribution. The threshold ϑ for the number of malicious validators within a committee is computed as ϑ = ⌊μ + σ·Φ⁻¹(1-p)⌋ for an allowed failure probability p, where μ = f' and σ² = f'(1 - f/n). Ethereum currently has about 2²⁰ validators, and at p = 10⁻⁶ the ratio is 0.3457, meaning the protocol fails once every 10⁶ slots (138 days). At p = 10⁻⁹, a malicious reorg occurs once every 380 years. As n grows large the ratio converges to f/n, so the conclusion is that ϑ can simply be set to one-third of the committee size.
