1vua05cxzuo: There are currently two ways for a smart contract to determine the current slot number. The first is to compute it from the block timestamp, which requires hardcoding the length of a slot into the contract code. If Ethereum later changes the slot length, all such contracts will then behave incorrectly. The second is to pass the slot number in as calldata and prove it against the beacon block root (using EIP-4788), but the gas cost is high enough that developers end up falling back on the first method anyway. This EIP chooses to hide the slot length from the application. The consensus layer client, which already knows the slot number, computes the value and passes it down, and the contract reads that value with a single opcode. This opens the door to changing the slot length in the future.

If a validator does not see at least one inclusion list, it does not treat the block as subject to validation or fork choice. Transactions in the list must be executable as of the start of slot N, and are valid only if maxFeePerGas is at least 12.5% higher than the current slot.
1vuddek2012: Right now each Ethereum contract can only deploy up to 24KiB (24,576 bytes) of code. This limit is a safeguard created to prevent attacks aimed at halting the network (DoS). Legacy-format contracts must check jump destinations (JUMPDEST) before execution, and many of the algorithms that perform this check can become unpredictably slower as code gets longer, which has made people hesitant to raise the limit. These days, though, contracts are adding features like friendly error reporting, which uses up more space and makes this limit a real obstacle. Developers have resorted to workarounds such as libraries (DELEGATECALL), splitting logic across multiple contracts, and proxies (the diamond pattern). These structures have caused bugs and loss of funds in deployed contracts. In the new contract format EOF, this check is performed only once at deployment time, and its cost is already reflected in the gas fee, so raising the limit poses no known issues.

1wdalsnpnxd: In the current EVM, every jump is a dynamic jump. Since the destination is determined by a stack value, the interpreter must analyze the code before execution to find valid jump destinations, which makes optimization and reducing jump costs difficult. Languages like Solidity mostly generate static jumps in the form of PUSHn..JUMP, but the EVM cannot take advantage of this. EIP-4200 introduced static jump instructions that solved most jump use cases, but did not solve function calls and returns. This EIP eliminates dynamic jumps entirely, instead providing dedicated instructions to call and return from functions, recording the number of inputs and outputs of each function in the specification to make analysis easier, and separating the stack per function so that callers and callees cannot see each other's stacks.

1ye22ayh8kg: In the EVM today, a jump instruction's destination is a value computed at runtime. This forces code-analysis tools to assume that any jump could go to any jump destination (JUMPDEST) in the code, so the number of possible paths grows as the number of jumps times the number of destinations, i.e., quadratically with code size. For tools that run at deployment or execution time (verifiers, native-code compilers), this becomes grounds for denial-of-service attacks, and offline formal analysis or gas estimation can become practically infeasible as the state space grows exponentially or worse. Today, compilers emulate calls and returns with dynamic jumps, and analysis tools then have to reconstruct that structure, creating unwanted work on both sides. This EIP has code that forgoes dynamic control flow prove its safety once, at CREATE time, so that every tool afterward can trust and use that proof.

1yx1jod4t44: There is a loophole in the current consolidation mechanism. Validators with 2048 ETH or more can use the consolidation logic to route exits through the consolidation queue, and because the consolidation queue has consistently been shorter than the exit queue since the consolidation feature was introduced, this has become an attractive way to speed up exits. This method is unfair because it is only available to some validators. Meanwhile, the exit queue has remained over 40 days long for an extended period. A long queue degrades user experience, prevents operators from responding quickly to market or operational events, and also slows down how fast the network can change its stake composition after a problem occurs. 1yxzks8sp8r: Modular exponentiation is the computation of raising a large number to a power and then taking the remainder when divided by another number. Several cryptographic techniques, including digital signatures, verifiable delay functions (VDFs), zero-knowledge proofs (SNARKs), and accumulators, rely on this computation. Ethereum provides a built-in feature (precompile) called ModExp to process this computation quickly, but benchmarks revealed that the fee (gas) charged was excessively high relative to the actual time it takes, because the existing gas formula did not accurately estimate the difficulty of the computation. As a result, using these cryptographic functions on Ethereum was inefficient and expensive. This EIP defines a new gas calculation formula that more accurately reflects the actual computational cost, lowering the fee. This makes practical uses such as stronger security and stronger random number generation (VDFs) realistic.

1z5z2rk26jm: A node can turn on proof-generation mode, proof-checking mode, or both. In generation mode, an active validator acts as a prover, produces execution proofs and publishes them on the execution_proof gossip topic. In checking mode, the node receives the propagated proofs and uses them as a supplementary signal for the validity of the corresponding payload. In this EIP phase, checking nodes also keep re-executing payloads, and verified proofs do not replace re-execution. The design keeps fork choice independent of proofs so that the proof stack can be measured under real network conditions. Proof generation and checking use the execution verification window introduced by EIP-7732. Because execution verification is deferred until the next beacon block, there is more time to produce proofs. There is no reward for proof-generating nodes, so the role is considered altruistic. In addition, independent of the request, generation and checking flow, proof-aware nodes must store proofs for canonical chain blocks up to the latest finalized checkpoint so that syncing peers can backfill. The source says only that a follow-up EIP may propose making proofs mandatory and removing re-execution.

However, without the payload envelope (ExecutionPayloadEnvelope), there is no way to check whether the payload's block hash matches the block_hash in the bid, or whether fields such as execution requests match the execution_requests_root in the bid. 1za2dhrvrek: A Core EIP can only reach Final if there is a client implementation, so the author must either provide the implementation directly or persuade client teams. The best way to get implementers' review is to present at an AllCoreDevs call, requested by commenting a link to the EIP on the AllCoreDevs agenda GitHub issue. This call serves three functions: discussing the EIP's technical merits, gauging other clients' willingness to implement, and coordinating implementation for a network upgrade. 1zaomap8k5k: If the burn were proportional to the rewards actually received, the marginal reward of every duty would shrink by a factor of (1 - b), weakening the incentive to participate correctly. So the burn is based on the reward the validator would have earned by performing perfectly, and it is deducted regardless of whether the validator actually performed. It does, however, reflect network-wide participation. The reward of a flawless attester also shrinks with network participation, and if the burn alone were charged on a full-participation basis, diligent validators would lose out whenever the offline share exceeds 1 - b. During an inactivity leak, when attestation rewards stop entirely, the attestation burn is paused in full. The reason for splitting by duty is the same. Taking one uniform deduction every epoch would keep the spec simple, but it would have to be large enough to cover the rarely occurring proposal and sync committee rewards, and as b grows it would exceed the attestation reward of an ordinary epoch. A validator that attests perfectly would then see its balance fall every epoch while waiting for its proposal turn. Charging per duty means a validator that attests diligently never goes negative merely because it has no proposal or sync committee assignment. The source explains that every base amount is determined only by network-wide aggregates, so no burn depends on the behavior of the validator that pays it, and a diligent validator keeps (1 - b) times the reward it received as net reward at any participation level.

1zea94254zx: Verifying a BLS signature requires a hash-to-curve operation that converts a message into a point on an elliptic curve, but the EVM currently has no dedicated precompile for this operation. Implementing it directly in Solidity costs about as much as a single pairing check, even though the actual computation involved is an order of magnitude smaller. EIP-198 and EIP-1108 lowered the cost of addition, scalar multiplication, and pairing checks on BN256, which also reduced the cost of distributed key generation (DKG) protocols such as ETHDKG, but there was still no way to verify the partial signatures or group signatures produced by a DKG on the EVM. The MapToGroup method from the original BLS paper is non-deterministic, making its computational cost unpredictable on the EVM, and it could be replaced once Fouque and Tibouchi presented a deterministic mapping method and proved it indistinguishable from a random oracle.

1zity1tdxl: The biggest risk is false reassurance. An assertion with a narrow scope of checking leads people to believe a dangerous transaction is safe, so an incomplete assertion should be treated as the same as having none. The protocol does not force the inclusion of an ASSERT frame. A smart account must check in the VERIFY frame that its own ASSERT frame is present, and since ASSERT frames are gathered at the end, it can scan from the back. The target of an assertion must be an immutable contract that cannot be upgraded. Because the execution body runs before the assertion, the state the body can write can be chosen by an attacker. If the result of a call to an oracle, balanceOf, a registry or a proxy, or an after value, is used as the reference value, it can be manipulated, and a called contract can even run TXTRACE, notice that it is inside an ASSERT, and answer differently. The reference value must come from the data of an ASSERT frame fixed at signing time, or from a before value. An assertion constrains only that one transaction. An existing allowance or an off-chain permit is used in other transactions, and a pending withdrawal or a bridge deposit completes elsewhere. Changes by the verification prefix are visible but cannot be reverted, and events show only the fact that code emitted them, so storage and balances are the source of truth. Gas exhaustion is also a problem. Under the current settings a single transaction can emit about 42,600 events, and a malicious dapp can inflate the cost with cheap logs. An assertion must read the count first and check the limit, a framework must pass gas proportional to the expected count, and an assertion's OOG must always be treated as a revert. Sorted tables allow binary search, but events must be scanned in full. The verification prefix is not reverted, so untrusted execution must not be placed there, and a deploy frame must not be used for anything other than installing tx.sender code.

208e7k37ca9: To keep the validator set from centralizing, Ethereum has handed the right to build blocks to specialized firms called builders through an auction. As a result, a small number of sophisticated builders came to dominate block production, and the network's censorship resistance, its ability to stop specific transactions from being left out, got worse. Research followed on letting validators place constraints on builders, and the method is the inclusion list (IL), which forces transactions into a block. However, earlier inclusion list designs and proposals for joint block construction had problems with bribery and coercion attacks, list equivocation, account abstraction, and transaction invalidation. 20cznkttlnp: Data structures in Ethereum's consensus layer are serialized using a format called SSZ (Simple Serialize) and summarized as a Merkle tree. However, as fields are added or removed with each fork, the data structure's version changes, and if the field count exceeds a power of two or a field is removed or replaced, the shape of the Merkle tree itself changes. This breaks every program that was verifying Merkle proofs based on that tree. Fixing a smart contract verifier may require a security committee to upgrade its logic, and embedded devices may need a firmware update. This work is needed even when there is no meaningful change to the fields a given verifier actually cares about. This EIP solves the problem by creating a new container type whose field positions stay fixed even when fields change.

20duwoak54f: Adds five instructions: ENTERPROC, LEAVEPROC, CALLPROC, RETURNPROC, and FRAMEADDRESS. ENTERPROC takes five immediates, dest_section, dest_offset, n_inputs, n_outputs, and n_locals, marks the entry point of a procedure, and lowers FP by n_locals. 20fqt98upd8: Relationships between transactions are measured in two ways. Path similarity is the proportion of path shared by two transactions within the tree, sim_path(xi, xj) = d/D (d is the shared path length, D is the tree's maximum depth). For example, in a tree of depth 3, if x1 and x2 share only the root node (d=1), the similarity is 1/3 ≈ 0.33. Vector space similarity uses cosine similarity computed from each transaction's feature vector, sim_cos(xi, xj) = (xi.xj)/(||xi|| ||xj||). For example, if x1 = [0.7, 0.8] and x2 = [0.9, 0.4], the similarity is 0.91.

20ht1d4fgm8: Ethereum nodes store the entire blockchain history on disk. As of 2024, this historical data totals roughly 500GB, of which about 400GB is block data from the proof-of-work (PoW) era, predating the Paris upgrade that activated proof-of-stake (PoS). If nodes must keep storing this ever-growing historical data, hardware requirements keep rising and the barrier to running a new node keeps growing. Ethereum aims, in the long run, to cap the amount of data a node must store, and this EIP is a first step toward that goal: it prevents execution-layer clients from requesting or responding with pre-Paris block data over the p2p network.

20joyh6kmhv: Every actor and lock change goes through a single entry point, applySignedAccountChanges, as a batch carrying an admin signature, and anyone can relay it. The sequence of the Local channel is local_epoch (upper 32 bits) || local_sequence (lower 32 bits). The Multichain channel (chain_id 0) is a plain monotonic counter used to sync actor state across chains. If the lower half is UNSEQUENCED (2^32-1), the batch is a JIT batch that does not consume the counter and can be reused until the epoch changes. IncrementLocalEpoch cancels all unapplied local signatures from the previous epoch but does not touch live actors or the Multichain channel. Lock blocks every authority change and allows only Unlock and IncrementLocalEpoch. unlock_delay is bounded to the uint16 range (about 18.2 hours at most), which keeps an account from permanently locking its own configuration rotation.

20vqjvonkb9: Right now all Ethereum smart contract execution is public. Because who did what is fully visible, it is not suited to handling sensitive information such as location, identity, or past transaction history. zkSNARKs (zero knowledge succinct non interactive arguments of knowledge), a type of zero knowledge proof, can prove that something is true without revealing its content, which could be a solution to this problem. 20xyxjhukbd: Keeping the raw 256 BALs as-is and checking the union at query time makes membership checks O(256), while materializing the union as a set makes per-block updates expensive. A reference-counted multiset gives O(1) checks and O(|BAL_in| + |BAL_out|) updates, which is favorable on both paths, and recomputation cost on a reorg is identical across all three approaches. For the commitment, a binary SMT is used instead of a Merkle Patricia Trie (MPT). Because keys are determined by the regular structure of SHA256(item), non-inclusion proofs naturally fall out as a zero leaf along a deterministic path and the circuit is uniform, whereas MPT proofs have variable depth and require branch-sibling steps for non-inclusion. The hash function is SHA-256 rather than Keccak-256. In standard R1CS/BN254 arithmetization this costs about 25,000 constraints per hash (5,000-10,000 in lookup-based proving systems), cheaper than Keccak's roughly 150,000. If a ZK-friendly hash precompile such as Poseidon is introduced later, it can be swapped in without changing the structure.

20ypqumvjal: An MEV (Maximal Extractable Value) attack is when the party building a block sees transaction content in advance and manipulates ordering to extract profit. Typical examples are sandwich attacks, which insert a buy and sell around a user's transaction, and frontrunning, which executes a similar transaction ahead of the user's. The source points out that, unlike legitimate arbitrage that supplies liquidity, such attacks are purely exploitative, eroding user trust, raising transaction costs, and causing large monetary losses. Existing alternatives also have limits. Encrypted mempools carry heavy encryption and decryption computation overhead, and private mempools are centralized and require trust. Proposer-builder separation (PBS) still lets builders see transaction content and is becoming increasingly centralized. This proposal takes the approach of eliminating the precondition for the attack itself: seeing transaction content at the ordering stage.

217c9jsp5cr: The EVM (Ethereum Virtual Machine) treats every value as a 256-bit integer. In practice, however, many computations do not need the full 256-bit width, and each one wastes unnecessary execution cycles. Meanwhile, most of the hardware running the EVM is 64-bit, such as x86_64 or arm64, and internally splits 256-bit values into four 64-bit integers for storage. This EIP proposes dedicated instructions that compute only that last 64-bit chunk, to speed up execution. Instead of adding dozens of new opcodes, it introduces a single new prefix byte, C0, with the following byte indicating which 64-bit operation to perform. This way, the limited EVM opcode space is barely touched while still covering 64-bit versions of arithmetic, comparison, bitwise, and branch operations.

However, declaring a storage key in an EIP-2930 access list also requires listing the address that key belongs to, so listing tx.to in the access list means paying ACCESS_LIST_ADDRESS_COST again for an address that is already included by default. 21vnut1qy5q: In today's EVM, pure computation instructions such as addition and multiplication (ADD, MUL, etc.) are significantly underpriced relative to instructions that read and write state (SSTORE, SLOAD, etc.). This is because client optimizations and hardware advances keep making computation faster, while state access performance keeps worsening as Ethereum's state grows, and this trend is expected to continue. So proposals have emerged to reprice computation instructions cheaper and state instructions more expensive, but there is an obstacle. Since gas is an integer unit, pricing computation instructions cheaply causes a rounding error where costs that should truly be less than 1 all round up to 1, and this error reduces the number of operations that fit in a block, hurting scalability. Conversely, pegging the fastest instruction to 1 gas and raising everything else would sharply cut throughput under the current block limit. This proposal scales up the gas unit itself by 1000x to eliminate this rounding error without major changes to internal EVM logic.

Fork choice enforcement: forced inclusion is placed in the fork choice rule, the core of the consensus process, so no one can bypass it. A block that fails the conditions gets no attester votes, so it cannot become part of the canonical chain. Same slot: the list runs in parallel with building the slot N+1 block during slot N, so a transaction submitted in slot N can be enforced right away. This is a clear improvement over forward-looking list designs such as EIP-7547, which had a one-slot delay. Position independence: it does not matter where in the block the list transactions appear, which reduces the incentive to route around the protocol through side channels, and combined with conditional inclusion, it makes an off-protocol market less attractive. No reward: committee members receive no explicit reward. The complexity of adding a fee scheme is judged not to be justified, and because the assumption is that only 1 of N committee members needs to be honest, the design relies on altruistic participation.

22tnimhwsvq: Once the transaction at nonce i is processed, an attacker can recover pk_i from the signature, and a quantum computer running Shor's algorithm can obtain sk_i from pk_i. However, the next valid transaction requires nonce i+1, and that leaf's pk_{i+1} sits behind a keccak256(pk_{i+1}) hash. Finding it requires a Keccak-256 preimage attack. Grover's algorithm only quadratically speeds up brute force, and Keccak-256 retains 128-bit security against preimage attacks, making this computationally infeasible. The security assumption thus shifts from the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem to Keccak-256 preimage resistance. It is also explicitly noted that, while a transaction waits in the mempool, the current public key pk_i is visible in the witness, so an attacker able to run Shor's algorithm within block time could submit a competing transaction with the same nonce. The source states that this requirement far exceeds near-term quantum capability, and that private mempools and L2s with short inclusion delay mitigate it. A depth-20 tree supports roughly 1,048,576 transactions, and as exhaustion nears, funds can be moved to a new account with a new seed, or to a post-quantum scheme. Existing secp256k1 addresses whose public key has already been exposed remain at risk if ECDSA is broken, so preemptive migration is recommended.

23bf3fke1jk: Most Ethereum accounts today are protected by a digital signature scheme called secp256k1 ECDSA. If a sufficiently powerful quantum computer emerges that can actually break this signature, an attacker could take the assets of any account that has not migrated to a quantum-resistant scheme. Accounts whose owners have lost access and cannot migrate themselves remain exposed as well. If freeze and recovery rules are drawn up hastily after such an emergency hits, the implementation burden would be very large. This EIP argues that preparing the rules in advance reduces the implementation work needed in an emergency and gives owners who still hold adequate evidence a way to reclaim their accounts, and on that basis defines a framework for the freeze time and recovery procedure ahead of time.

23cmo91285o: BLS signatures are points on the BLS12-381 curve, so summing multiple signatures still yields a single 96-byte signature, and the whole set is verified with a single pairing equation. The signatures used in quantum-resistant consensus, by contrast, are a stateful XMSS variant; in exchange for relying only on hash function security, they lack any structure for cheaply combining signatures. Under the parameters currently used by the leanVM aggregation engine, a single signature is about 1.17KiB, and N signatures cost roughly N times as much. So aggregation shifts from combining signatures to generating a quantum-resistant succinct argument that "all attached signatures are valid." Measured aggregate proof sizes range from 127 to 344KiB depending on configuration, and the networking target is to propagate a roughly 256KiB proof within 1 second, a size that is nearly independent of the number of aggregated votes.

23ff8d3m510: Each claim i corresponds to a target group element t_i, which is the identity element only if the claim is true. If even one t_j is not the identity, there is exactly one value of r_j in [0, q) that makes the combination the identity, so the probability that an invalid batch passes is 1/q ≈ 2⁻²⁵⁵. This is the degree-1 case of the Schwartz-Zippel lemma, and it holds regardless of how many claims are invalid. Consensus layer batch verifiers that use powers r⁰..rⁿ⁻¹ of a single challenge r have a looser bound of (n - 1)/q, whereas here a single keccak256 per claim maintains a tighter bound. This is a strong Fiat-Shamir transform where not just the proofs but the objects being proven enter the transcript, and it relies on the standard assumption of treating the hash as a random oracle.

But proving EVM execution with ZK-SNARKs has become another important execution benchmark, and by that benchmark hash operations are severely underpriced in gas relative to other operations. Blocks with heavy hash usage take far longer to generate ZK proofs for than an average block. Many layer 2s work around this with stopgaps such as arbitrary limits or centralized sequencer rules, which raise concerns around security and centralization. Costs that can be known without looking at state (base cost, memory expansion, warm/cold access cost) are validated up front, while costs that need state, such as whether an account exists or resolving an EIP-7702 delegation, are validated afterwards. If the up-front validation fails, the target was not accessed and must not be put in the BAL. If it passes, the target stays in the BAL even when a later cost check fails. SSTORE implicitly reads the current value to compute gas, and before that the slot's access_cost and the GAS_CALL_STIPEND sentry (gas_left > GAS_CALL_STIPEND) must both pass. If either fails, the slot is put in neither storage_reads nor storage_changes. Calling a target that carries an EIP-7702 delegation includes both the original target and the delegated address, but if the gas check for the delegated address's own access_cost fails, the delegated address is not included.

24e8xwzq5dx: Many EVM instructions take offset values as input, and these are often 0. For example, the return data parameters of the CALL family of instructions are set to 0 by contracts that use the RETURNDATA family of instructions. Currently, pushing 0 onto the stack requires PUSH1 0, which costs 3 gas at execution and takes 2 bytes of code, so deployment also costs 2 * 200 gas. To save this cost, it is common to use other instructions such as PC, MSIZE, CALLDATASIZE, RETURNDATASIZE, CODESIZE, CALLVALUE and SELFBALANCE as a stand-in for 0, which is risky because these values can vary with context. A mainnet analysis found that about 11.5% of executed PUSH-family instructions pushed 0, and across all existing accounts 340,557,331 bytes were spent on PUSH1 00, costing 68,111,466,200 gas to deploy. Creating a dedicated zero instruction makes code shorter and reduces such workarounds.

24guuvue0ul: Aggregators sit on the path between signatures and finality, so if aggregators stall or selectively drop votes, proposers may fail to include sufficient coverage and finality degrades. The current requirement that there be at least one aggregator formalizes this, and running several redundant aggregators is the main mitigation. The safety of aggregation reduces to the soundness of the leanVM proof system. If a false proof were possible, an attacker could forge consensus participation; the current leanVM instance is reported at about 124 bits classical and 62 bits quantum security, short of the NIST Level 1 target (128 bits classical, 64 bits quantum), and work is underway to close the gap with larger digests and similar measures. Centralization from proving hardware is the biggest concern, but even a captured or colluding set of aggregators must not be able to undermine the widely performed cheap verification. Relying on implicit incentives alone for expensive proving, with no explicit rewards or penalties, is flagged as risky, and whether to publish a minimum hardware spec remains an open question.

It costs about 2100 extra gas for a slot and about 2600 for an address, and this access record is cleared once the transaction ends. On mainnet, this surcharge accounts for 17% of block gas at the median. However, measuring 5,731 blocks showed that 79% of entries that paid the cold fee had already been accessed within the preceding 256 blocks (about 51 minutes). In effect, the same entries are repeatedly being charged a 'first time seen' fee. This EIP keeps a warm access multiset (WAM) as chain state that records entries accessed in the last 256 blocks, treating entries found there as warm from the start of the block, eliminating the duplicate charge. 251z2d7h5ct: Ethereum is currently focused on L1 scaling, and the block gas limit is expected to rise quickly in the near future. But if the gas cost of state creation, such as creating a new account or storage slot, stays fixed, then as the gas limit rises, the data nodes must store grows proportionally, which can degrade client performance. EIP-8037 unifies state creation costs on a per-byte basis and raises them by 3x to 9.5x, but how much users will respond to the higher prices (price elasticity) is unknown. According to the source's analysis, if usage patterns stay the same, state could end up accounting for 78.5% of total gas, and even if state usage is cut in half, it could still settle at 64.7%. If state gas eats into the block limit, it crowds out other resources like computation and blocks scaling. So a mechanism is needed that automatically adjusts price based on state usage and splits state gas out of the regular gas limit.

252ev13uhw5: Every piece of logic that converts block counts into real time changes at the transition. Logic based on block.timestamp is unaffected. Going from 12 seconds to 10, a period of N blocks becomes about 17% shorter and a per-block quantity is consumed about 20% faster. The EIP-4788 and EIP-2935 buffers stay at 8,191 slots, so the lookback window shrinks from about 27.3 hours to about 22.8 hours, and contracts that assumed a full day of history no longer get it. Across the upgrade boundary, 12-second and 10-second intervals are mixed, so two timestamps 2 × 8,191 seconds apart can use the same EIP-4788 buffer slot. About one third of the 8,191 beacon roots present just before the upgrade are overwritten early (the earliest after about 4.6 hours). A lookup reverts rather than returning a wrong root. Timelocks, vesting, governance voting and delay periods, and cooldowns counted in block numbers end early. Per-block interest, rewards, issuance, and rate limits grow per hour, and TWAP windows defined in block counts average over a shorter period. Off-chain tools that compute genesis_time + 12 × slot must switch to a per-interval schedule or to block timestamps. L2 and bridge finality delays, challenge periods, and timeouts measured in L1 block counts become shorter, while those in seconds stay the same. If a client implements retention with real-time timers, timers computed before the transition only keep data longer than needed, which still conforms to the spec.

2548iivkois: EIP-1051 has existing arithmetic opcodes set ovf and sovf flags that are read with the OFV and SOVF opcodes, and EIP-6888 uses carry and overflow flags with the JUMPC and JUMPO conditional jumps. Both approaches need a flag read and a conditional jump after the operation, so they take at least 3 instructions, and they leave implicit state (the flags) between instructions, which complicates static analysis, formal verification and compiler optimization. There is also the problem that if the flag is checked only once across two additions, the earlier overflow silently disappears. This EIP is a self-contained stateless instruction in which each opcode either produces the correct result or reverts, so it has none of these problems, and since it needs no extra instructions the gas savings are maximal.

255d8575kch: The fee works the same way as in EIP-7002 and EIP-7251. get_fee() reads only the stored excess value and computes fake_exponential(MIN_PREREGISTRATION_REQUEST_FEE, excess, PREREGISTRATION_REQUEST_FEE_UPDATE_FRACTION). The minimum fee is 1 wei, the update fraction is 17, and the fee is roughly e**(excess / 17) wei. The end-of-block system call updates excess to max(0, previous_excess + count - TARGET_PREREGISTRATION_REQUESTS_PER_BLOCK), so submissions in block N affect the fee starting from block N + 1. All submissions within the same block pay the same minimum fee. Overpayment is not refunded, so the fee should be queried with empty calldata before submitting. If the excess slot holds EXCESS_INHIBITOR (2**256-1), get_fee() reverts and requests are blocked. The first system call after activation resets this value to 0. If a system call arrives with non-empty calldata, it dequeues requests and then stores EXCESS_INHIBITOR again, disabling the queue. This EIP always makes system calls with empty calldata, so this path is unreachable and is left for a future upgrade that retires or halts the contract. Without this mechanism, even after the protocol stops the system call, the contract would keep accepting fees and requests, which would pile up in a queue that is never drained. The reference implementation of the EIP-8282 builder request contract uses the same approach.

25cdwyoqx5m: The time reference in this EIP is the consensus layer slot, not the block timestamp. During block execution, current_slot is the slot of the beacon block that contains that execution payload, and the execution client must read it from the slotNumber field of EIP-7843. Deriving it backwards by applying a fixed slot length to block.timestamp is prohibited. In public mempool validation, current_slot is the slotNumber of the latest canonical execution header plus 1, and the SLOTNUM value in simulation must be the same. This value is deliberately not incremented when empty slots pass. Instead, the transaction must be revalidated with that payload's slotNumber before it is put into the payload. A reference may only point to a slot strictly earlier than current_slot, and a root written in slot S can be referenced from S + 1. The window size follows from this. A write in slot S updates cell S mod RECENT_ROOT_LENGTH, and the old root sharing that cell is exactly 8192 slots old and therefore already expired. So a write in the current slot cannot break a valid reference, and with RECENT_ROOT_LENGTH = 8192 the referenceable window is RECENT_ROOT_USABLE_WINDOW = 8191, which is the range excluding the current slot. A reference close to expiry becomes invalid if slots are skipped, so the builder revalidates with the exact payload slot.

Using a strategy of calling a new contract each time the TSTORE cost exceeds the cold contract call cost (2600 gas) yields 2600 slots per contract and about 8.8 calls per transaction, so up to about 23,000 slots, 736KB in total, can be allocated. Compared with the current gas schedule, which allows allocating about 9.6MB of memory (30_000_000 / 100 * 32), the total is actually smaller, so this EIP imposes a stronger cap on transient storage resource usage. For reference, the memory that can be allocated in one transaction with SSTORE is 48KB (30_000_000 / 20_000 * 32). This cap is linearly proportional to the gas limit, which is a useful property when the block gas limit rises in the future.

In Plasma, an operator submits blocks summarizing L2 transactions to the base chain, and the timing of these submissions may not align precisely with major events on the main chain, such as a chain ID change. But in delegated staking, such as liquid staking or staking-as-a-service, where the party providing the funds differs from the party creating the key, the operator holding the key can submit a deposit with their own withdrawal address before the funder's deposit. The funder gets no onchain guarantee that their desired withdrawal credentials will be honored. The source states that at least one third of staked ETH goes through such delegation structures. Today each protocol builds, audits, and maintains its own defenses, such as collateral-based pre-deposits or guardian committees. There is no known actual loss, but new entrants are vulnerable by default until they put the same defenses in place.

This is because 0 is used to mark an unregistered validator, and if any link is 0, the chain must be regenerated. An n of 2^16 or more is recommended, generation takes milliseconds, and total storage is about 2MB. A chain cannot be extended in place, so it is exhausted once c_0 is used, but even under aggressive assumptions a validator proposes about 100 times a year, so the recommended length is hundreds of years' worth. If the chain is exhausted or the secret is lost, exiting and re-entering is the only means of recovery.

25werxtl13e: Contract code is split into 31-byte pieces before entering the tree. Each chunk is a 32-byte value, where bytes 1 through 31 are the i-th 31-byte slice of the code and byte 0 is the number of bytes at the start of the chunk that belong to PUSHDATA. For example, if a chunk boundary falls in the middle of a PUSH4's data, the next chunk starts like 2 97 96 PUSH1 128 MSTORE, with the leading 2 marking that the first 2 bytes are data. Chunk placement works as follows: if chunk_id is less than CODE_CHUNKS_IN_HEADER = 16, it goes at the CODE_OFFSET + chunk_id position in the header stem; otherwise it is grouped under CODE_SUBTREE using hash(address + bytes([high])) as the stem, in units of STEM_SUBTREE_WIDTH = 256. Since code now lives in the state tree, code access can also be handled with Merkle proofs.
25wgx8k50bn: The EVM currently has no opcode for reading or writing memory at a relative address. For a compiler to keep temporary data such as local variables in memory, each function must store a 'frame pointer' (the starting position of the current function's memory region) somewhere, then reload and add that value every time it reads or writes a value. This process goes through five opcodes, PUSHn, PUSH1 0, MLOAD, ADD, and MLOAD (or MSTORE), consuming 15 gas and at least 7 bytes of bytecode. Because of this cost, compilers come to prefer placing local variables on the EVM's evaluation stack instead of memory, and since the evaluation stack has a depth limit, this constrains the number of local variables a single function can use.

264gxy3bhd3: The potential for bias is the same as today. The whole chain is fixed before the commitment time, that is, before the proposal slot is known, so the proposer's options are the same as today: reveal, or withhold and give up the block and its reward. If the chain secret is stolen, an attacker can predict that validator's future contributions but cannot choose them. This is strictly less damaging than today's signing key theft, where a stolen key gives the attacker the power to sign as well as predict. Even so, the secret must be stored with the same care as a signing key, and because reaching the end of the chain reveals the seed, the chain must not be derived from the signing key. A reveal included in an orphaned block exposes that validator's future mandatory contributions in advance, but a predictable contribution is no worse than a withheld one, and RANDAO needs only one honest contributor in the mixing window, so there is no practical harm. The basis for this charge is the cost of writing account state at the end of the block, but that write happens only once per account whose balance changed, not once per transfer. So when ether moves back and forth between the same accounts several times within one transaction, the transaction repeatedly pays for state writes that will not actually happen. This gives developers weak financial incentive to deploy on a given network, and public-good contracts must separately secure their own funding to stay maintained. This EIP is not a proposal to change Ethereum L1 itself, but an idea to let L2s experiment with distributing a portion of transaction fees, in proportion to gas usage, to the contracts actually executed. If too much stake exits at once, a malicious validator could withhold a conflicting block, publish it after the stake has exited, execute a double-spend attack, and avoid accountability through slashing. That is why the amount that can exit per epoch is currently fixed, at 16 validators per epoch for a validator set of 1,053,742. This figure comes from a limit of roughly 10% of total stake exiting per month. However, this limit takes no account of past conditions. For example, even if no one has exited in the past 13 days, a large staking operator running 30,000 validators (3% of the total) would still have to wait 1,875 epochs, about 8.33 days, to exit, even though doing so would not violate the overall constraint of allowing up to 5.04% to exit over two weeks. This kind of unnecessary waiting arises during periods of unusually high exit demand, such as institutional liquidations or market events.

However, performing this kind of big-number arithmetic with only the EVM's (Ethereum Virtual Machine) basic instructions is difficult. The original text also notes that addition and subtraction are already efficient enough using algorithms inside the EVM and so do not need a precompile, but argues exponentiation should be provided separately. However, a wallet alone cannot easily confirm whether the response returned by an RPC provider is correct or whether any logs are missing. The conventional approach is to fetch every block header and cross-check it against the log bloom filter, but bloom filters produce many false positives, requiring unnecessary blocks to be filtered out and separate requests per block, resulting in heavy network round trips. As a result, wallets end up trusting a specific provider and are exposed to that provider's privacy policy and potential censorship. This EIP accumulates a commitment of each block's logs into state, allowing the correctness and completeness of a response to be verified using only a proof obtained via eth_getProof.

27jyrnwrg78: The current EVM treats memory as a single contiguous array from address 0 to the highest address accessed, and charges gas accordingly. As a result, writing values to just two far-apart addresses causes the entire space between them to be counted as allocated, inflating cost. This forces compilers to pack memory as tightly as possible to save gas, and flexible memory layouts such as separating the stack from the heap waste gas through excessive reallocation and copying. This EIP proposes dividing memory into fixed-size pages, as operating systems do with virtual memory, and charging only for the pages actually touched.

290atucvmkn: Epoch transition blocks (including genesis) are stateless checkpoints. They must not carry votes, all pending votes are discarded, and tallying restarts from scratch. This lets a client sync from a single checkpoint hash without replaying the voting history before it. On non-epoch blocks, a signer may cast one vote per block, and if the same signer votes on the same target again, only the latest vote is kept. Multiple proposals can be in progress simultaneously, and a proposal takes effect immediately once it reaches SIGNER_LIMIT approvals. Once a proposal passes, all pending votes for that target, for and against, are discarded. Nonsensical proposals, such as proposing to remove an address that is not a signer, are not penalized either, for implementation simplicity. Since a small reorg can make a voting block disappear, the suggested strategy is to configure a proposal on the signer node and have it randomly include one per block. Even if a proposal appears to have passed, it should not be discarded immediately, since it might still be reorged out.

290m74644z4: Blocks from before Ethereum's transition from proof-of-work (PoW) to proof-of-stake (PoS) have no separate compressed structure on chain, so verifying any single past block required chaining and re-checking every block header in order starting from genesis. This approach is inefficient, and there was no lightweight way to confirm pre-Merge data was correct without downloading that data and executing each block directly. This EIP groups the hashes and total difficulties of all pre-Merge blocks into units of 8192 blocks (epochs) and combines them into a single published accumulator root. As a result, users can verify that the entire body of past data is correct simply by comparing a locally computed accumulator root against this value, and can verify whether a specific block is included using a proof of only O(log n) size.

If every address and storage location the block accessed, along with post-execution values, arrives as a list, a node can read the needed data in advance in parallel, execute non-overlapping transactions concurrently, and parallelize the post-execution state root computation. Since then Ethereum state has grown considerably, and reading and writing it has become correspondingly slower. With the price unchanged but the real time higher, state access has become too cheap compared with other opcodes. In addition, EXTCODESIZE and EXTCODECOPY go through the database twice, reading the account information once and then reading the code size or bytecode once more, yet they charged the same as BALANCE or EXTCODEHASH, which read only once. This proposal readjusts these prices based on execution times actually measured per client, and separates the write cost, which had been mixed into composite constants, into named constants.

The source document recommends a sufficient lookahead. Close entries at the end of epoch K and draw using the mix at slot K+N+ε, keeping N at 4 epochs or more and ε small, such as 2 to 4 slots. The time margin for ε is set by MIN_SEED_LOOKAHEAD and is about 6 minutes on mainnet. If you wait 4 epochs or more, the proposer set of epoch N+1 is not known when entries close, and the probability that a missed proposal occurs in that period is effectively 100%, which makes prediction harder.

29zqrycltj9: Ethereum's current state storage structure is a hexary tree called the Merkle Patricia Trie (MPT). A hexary tree has the advantage of shallow depth, meaning fewer hash computations, but in practice disk access has proven to be a bigger bottleneck than hashing. Because of this, clients are moving away from storing every internal node on disk, instead storing only values flatly and recomputing internal nodes as needed. There is also demand for making stateless verification, confirming state via proofs without downloading blocks, easier to use, and binary trees have proofs roughly 4x smaller than hexary trees, which favors this goal. On top of this, the MPT carries a lot of complex machinery, such as RLP encoding and optimizations that embed small nodes into their parent, which creates a high risk of bugs, and the disk space saved by those optimizations is only about 1MB, negligible compared to the roughly 300GB needed for a full sync.
2a00m33dikh: Ethereum charges a fee called gas for every operation, and this cost is meant to reflect the actual computing resources the operation consumes. However, benchmarking the point evaluation precompile introduced in EIP-4844 showed that its current cost of 50,000 gas is priced significantly below its actual resource consumption. When an operation is priced cheaper than its real cost, it becomes a weak link in block processing performance and makes it harder to raise the block gas limit, the cap on how much work can fit in a single block. This EIP proposes doubling the cost of the point evaluation precompile to narrow the gap between price and actual performance, creating room to raise the block gas limit further in the future.

2aaqgieqx5x: Ethereum needs randomness throughout the protocol, for example to select block proposers, and produces that randomness through a mechanism called RANDAO. Each proposer publishes a signature called randao_reveal, and these are mixed together to produce randomness. However, the current randao_reveal is a signature over the current epoch number. Since the epoch number is known to everyone in advance, a proposer with only their own private key can precompute reveals for epochs far in the future. This predictability underlies RANDAO bias attacks, where a proposer skews the randomness in their own favor, and also blocks designs such as single secret leader election (SSLE) that require verifiable randomness. This proposal includes a value in the signed message that is only finalized once the immediately preceding epoch ends, so that even the proposer themselves cannot precompute reveals beyond the current epoch.

2b6hkcu4kd5: The gas costs of hash functions were originally set based on the time they take to run on a typical CPU. But as proving Ethereum blocks with ZK-SNARKs has become important, it has become clear that the same hash operation takes far longer in a ZK-proving environment than on a CPU. Blocks with heavy hash usage take significantly longer than average to generate proofs for, and several layer 2s (L2s) work around this with stopgaps such as arbitrary limits or centralized sequencer rules. These stopgaps raise concerns around security and centralization. In the long run, proving layer 1 blocks themselves with ZK-SNARKs will require narrowing the gap between average and worst-case proving time, and hash operation calls are the single biggest contributor to that gap. While introducing Verkle trees would resolve the KECCAK hashing issue tied to Merkle-Patricia tries, hashing on the order of hundreds of millions of bytes within a single block is still possible using EVM operators alone.

2b9btjfyof7: For GasToken to stop working, no more gas must be extractable from a slot than was put into it. The source derives the condition by pairing each refund with an earlier expenditure on the same slot in the same transaction. If the event that clears a slot whose original value is nonzero to zero is the first one in that transaction, it can be paired with the minimum cost of first reading and modifying that slot, SSTORE_RESET_GAS + ACCESS_LIST_STORAGE_KEY_COST. If it is the second or later, the earlier write that moved the value away from zero deducted SSTORE_CLEARS_SCHEDULE from the refund counter, so the two cancel out. Therefore, if SSTORE_CLEARS_SCHEDULE <= SSTORE_RESET_GAS + ACCESS_LIST_STORAGE_KEY_COST, total gas expenditure per slot is always positive, and this EIP lowers SSTORE_CLEARS_SCHEDULE to exactly that sum. Intuitively, the design leaves no net refund when clearing data that has not yet been read (usually useless), and leaves a net refund when clearing data that has been read (more likely to be useful).

2bbc3sw0yp0: Ethereum has a built-in mechanism called the difficulty bomb. It is code that exponentially raises mining difficulty as blocks accumulate, progressively lengthening block creation time; it is also called the ice age. The effect of this bomb started becoming noticeable again around block 8,600,000 on October 5, 2019. The average block time, which had been 13.1 seconds, rose to about 14.3 seconds by block 8,900,000, and this effect grows exponentially every 100,000 blocks. According to estimates in the original text, block times of 20 seconds are expected by late December 2019, and over 30 seconds from February 2020 onward. Slower blocks bloat the chain and raise the cost of writing to it. This is why the proposal is to delay the bomb once more, to around the time Eth2's finality gadget is expected to launch.

2bdk3f85ypq: Pure reads such as SLOAD, BALANCE, EXTCODESIZE, EXTCODECOPY, EXTCODEHASH, and call instructions that do not change state MUST NOT update last_written_block. There are three reasons. If reads changed the field, every old read would lead to a trie leaf rewrite and a state root recomputation, attaching write-level cost to reads. Also, data in the stable tier would be moved to the mutable tier by reads alone, creating write amplification and contradicting the goal of separating the mutable path. Finally, this field is consensus state reflected in the state root, so if reads changed it, EIP-214's guarantee that state does not change during STATICCALL would be broken. When a call frame reverts, the field is restored to its pre-frame value exactly like balance, nonce, and storage, and updates attached to rolled-back state changes MUST NOT be left behind.

2bhvlbc7de8: The gas limit increase that EIP-7732 makes possible means larger execution payloads. Larger payloads take longer to spread across the network. If a Payload Timeliness Committee (PTC) member does not receive the payload within the attestation deadline, even a valid payload is treated as missing. With the current execution_payload gossip topic, two problems become more pronounced as payloads grow. First, a node that has already received a large message has difficulty cutting off duplicate transmissions arriving by other paths midway, so the same bytes arrive multiple times and consume bandwidth that could carry new data. Second, a node can pass a message on only after receiving all of it, so each hop (one step of forwarding between nodes) adds one full transmission and the delay grows in proportion to message size times hop count. Splitting the message into chunks reduces both problems. At the chunk level no large duplicates can occur, and a node can forward a chunk as soon as it receives it, so hops proceed overlapped instead of queuing one after another.

2bmazbnvxrx: The DAO and the child DAO contracts that split off from it held ether, and returning this money to its original holders required consolidating the balances of specific accounts into one place. However, there was no way within Ethereum's ordinary rules to forcibly move another account's balance. So instead of changing the rules, a special measure was carried out that directly rewrote the blockchain ledger's state once, an irregular state change. Such a measure must be applied identically by every node on the same block, or the chain would fork. A formal record was therefore needed pinning down exactly which account's balance moves, at which block, to which contract, by precise address and block number. EIP-779 is the document that preserved that record within the EIP system.
2bmcxnq6ild: Ethereum is not a single company but a network changed collectively by developers, client teams, and the community scattered around the world. EIP-1 defines this entire process. It requires proposals to be written as documents called EIPs (Ethereum Improvement Proposals) and kept as text files in a version-controlled repository, so that the edit history itself becomes the historical record of the proposal. 2bxsqdgl7xk: Ethereum's long-term goal is to verify blocks with validity proofs, making chain verification as light and fast as possible. That requires proving the state read during EVM execution, and today's Merkle Patricia Trie (MPT) is not suited to this. It uses RLP encoding and the Keccak hash, which is expensive to prove, it has a "tree within a tree" structure in which a separate storage tree hangs under the account tree, and it cannot prove only part of a contract's code. Proof sizes are also large. With an account tree depth of about 12, one branch is 5760 bytes, and in the worst case, if a block's 60 million gas is spent entirely on touching 1 byte each of different accounts' code, about 1.8GB is needed. This is because, if code is not split into chunks, proving even 1 byte requires revealing the entire 64KiB of code. A binary tree with a branching factor of 2 minimizes Merkle proof size, and switching to a proof-friendly hash also improves circuit performance.

2ci9sld8ojy: In Ethereum proof of stake, the number of entries per epoch is limited so that new validators cannot all enter at once. However, this limit (the churn limit) was designed to grow in proportion to the number of validators, so as validators increase, the entry rate also rises and the total amount staked grows exponentially. According to estimates at the time the source was written, if the deposit queue stays full, 50% of the total ETH supply would be staked in May 2024, 75% in September 2024, and 100% in December 2024. Even with 100% staked, consensus rewards alone would still yield about 1.6% a year, and MEV income and liquid staking tokens (LSTs) make it hard to deter additional capital inflow. More validators increase gossip messages and beacon state size, which burdens the consensus layer, and it is also unclear how much additional economic weight further helps security. A fundamental fix to the reward curve takes time, so this EIP is a transitional measure that only caps the entry rate to slow growth and buy the community time to discuss.

This kind of malicious reordering directly harms users, and the competition to capture that profit leads to secondary MEV side effects such as builder centralization. 2dcp0isajvq: Smart contract bytecode carries metadata alongside the execution code, such as the compiler version or a hash of the source files. Currently, the Solidity and Vyper compilers encode this information in a format called CBOR and simply append it after the execution code. Because the bytecode has no structure, it is hard to tell where the execution code ends and the metadata begins. In source code verification, which compares the bytecode deployed on chain against the result of compiling the source, every verification service has to build its own heuristic logic to pick out the metadata. Even once EOF (Ethereum Object Format), which structures bytecode, is introduced, without a dedicated spot for metadata it would have to go into the data section, and then whenever the metadata size changes, the offset values of instructions reading that data would shift, changing the execution code itself and potentially letting code access the metadata. To prevent two contracts compiled from the same source from failing verification merely because of a metadata size difference, a separate section is needed.

2ds7ocwzlyc: The weakness of the offline approach is that consensus never observes the correctness of the conversion. To address this, it is recommended that during the pre-swap period attesters sign and publish, with their validator keys, the shadow root, the PBT root of each block's post-state. The shadow root is delivered through an out-of-consensus telemetry sidecar and is not a block validity condition; omissions or delays are not treated as mismatches and count only toward a coverage metric. Enforcing it as a validity rule would require every validator to compute a PBT root for every block, reviving the on-consensus-path PBT construction that the offline model was meant to avoid. The wire format and aggregation method are deferred to a companion EIP that has not yet been published. Shadow roots must be keyed by block hash rather than height, so that normal root differences on either side of a reorg are not misread as mismatches. The residual risk is a converter bug affecting only the last blocks before a fork, whose PBT roots go live without ever having been validated by consensus. The source text lists two mitigations limited to those final blocks: enforcing shadow roots specifically for them, and relying on cross-client agreement accumulated during the shadow period.

Yet ordinary users and wallet apps have very limited ability to find, collect, review and analyze the EVM code a transaction will actually execute. After signing, there is no means at all to restrict what the transaction actually does. As a result, every time users interact with Ethereum they effectively sign without knowing the contents (blind signing) and are exposed to major risk. 2e9xmjmw79: Ethereum nodes use two methods when propagating a new block. They send the full block to a small number of peers, and announce only the hash to the rest, who can fetch it if needed. Transactions, however, lack this dual mechanism, so a node must send the full transaction as is to every connected peer. With N peers, the same transaction travels N times, when in a perfect world one transmission would suffice. Also, when two nodes newly connect, they need to reconcile their transaction pools, but since there is no way to check what the other side already knows, they had to send their entire pool, which can run from tens to hundreds of MB. The original text points out that transaction propagation was, at the time, the single largest consumer of network resources, and that most of it was wasted on redundant transmission, aiming to first agree on which items to exchange using 32-byte hashes before the expensive exchange, thereby cutting overall operating bandwidth by at least an order of magnitude.
2eakt8z5d73: The gas limit of an Ethereum block is tied to the volume of data the network can handle. When setting the limit, the worst-case block that packs the most bytes for the same gas must be used as the reference. A block filled entirely with ETH transfers is charged 21,000 gas per transfer, so it cannot be made more expensive and serves as a fixed baseline. Right now, however, a block filled entirely with calldata packs about 1.49 times more bytes per gas than that baseline. So even if we want to raise the gas limit, it must be kept low enough that the worst-case calldata block does not exceed the network's bandwidth. Raising the calldata floor cost to 96 brings the density of calldata blocks down to or below the level of transfer blocks, removing calldata as a bottleneck and creating room to raise the gas limit. Ordinary user transactions rarely hit the floor cost, so the impact on them is minimal.

2evlm55b4y6: Let the staking ratio be f = D/S (S is total supply). The current consensus layer yield is y(f) = BE/√(fS) (B is BASE_REWARD_FACTOR, E is the number of epochs per year). The goal is to subtract a term that is 0 at f = 0, grows linearly in f, and exactly cancels the yield at the saturation ratio f_sat. In other words, the net yield is ỹ(f) = y(f) - (f/f_sat)·y(f_sat) for f ≤ f_sat, and 0 above that. Setting this as ỹ(f) = (1 - b(f))·y(f) and solving gives b(f) = (f/f_sat)^(3/2). The exponent is 3/2 rather than 1 because the reward curve itself shrinks as f^(-1/2). The absolute amount to subtract is linear in f, but expressing it as a fraction of a reward that shrinks as f^(-1/2) adds another half power. As a result, total issuance ĩ(f) = f·ỹ(f) is no longer monotonically increasing: it peaks at f* = 2^(-7/3) ≈ 19.8% and falls to 0 at f_sat = 50%. Because b does not depend on B, raising B during the transition period leaves b(f) unchanged.

2f909zjwezn: Ethereum's execution layer transactions have so far been encoded using RLP (Recursive Length Prefix), an older serialization format, and signed by hashing the entire byte sequence with keccak256. EIP-6404 introduced a way to represent these RLP transactions in SSZ (Simple Serialize) format, but the signature itself is still based on RLP, leaving a conversion step in place. This EIP defines a signature scheme for native transactions signed directly in SSZ from the outset, further reducing the need for conversion. According to the source text, this approach reduces hash computation overhead, allows a transaction identifier (tx_hash) commitment to be verified on chain, and opens up the forward compatibility benefits of SSZ ProgressiveContainer, a structure that makes it easy to add fields later.

2fa5tuvbp41: Each signature commits to the payload and to every signature that precedes it. payload_commitment is CA_TX_TYPE || rlp(payload_type) || rlp(payload_body), the first signature signs keccak256(payload_commitment), and the i-th signature signs the hash of that value concatenated with all preceding (sig_type, sig_body) pairs. As a result, swapping out an earlier signature breaks every signature after it, and reordering signatures changes the hash input and causes verification to fail. This guards against key substitution attacks (Fujita et al., IACR ePrint 2024/1728), in which a signature in a multi-signature scheme is swapped or reordered to change the meaning of the authorization. For example, a fee payer includes the sender's signature inside their own signature hash, so they only pay fees for a transaction actually signed by the sender they expected.

It uses Poseidon1 over the Koala-Bear field (and its degree-5 extension), and exposes a `poseidon16` precompile (16 being the permutation width). Since the commitment preimage consists of 31 field elements (8 for the preimage, 13 for the validator key, 9 for the withdrawal credential, 1 for the amount), hashing chains three calls to `poseidon16`. On a MacBook M1 Pro benchmark (N = 500) with a depth-32 tree, proof generation takes 0.032 to 0.041 seconds, verification takes 0.005 to 0.012 seconds, and proof size is about 83 to 189 KB (Rho 1 to 4). Security depends on the soundness of the proof system; if the system is broken, deposits could be intercepted without a valid commitment. Also, `0x03` in its current form is incompatible with EIP-7002, so a separation is proposed where the withdrawal address stays hidden in the commitment while the exit authority address is exposed. The proposal also notes that, beyond deposit privacy, network anonymity (preventing IP exposure) is needed as well, and that the claim timing must be kept variable and unpredictable to avoid timing analysis.

2gfsgquq1do: The EVM has no call and return instructions for use within a single contract. The CALL family are instructions for calling a different contract. So the compiler synthesizes internal calls by pushing the return address onto the stack as ordinary data and, once the routine finishes, jumping to that address with a dynamic JUMP. Every internal function call in every deployed contract is a dynamic jump, and its destination is data. A tool that needs to know where a return goes must walk the code via symbolic execution. A synthesized return at least has compiler labels as candidates, but all of them must be walked, and the step count doubles for every shared routine, producing a path explosion where 20 calls means a million steps. A computed destination does not even have candidates. With explicit calls and returns, a return always goes back to the call site, so it is one step, one answer.

2gftuddc1is: Even rollups that behave equivalently to the EVM currently have to build and maintain a complex separate proof system just to mimic the block validation that Ethereum already performs at L1. This complexity significantly raises the chance of bugs, and prevents projects from removing their security council and reaching Stage 2. It also means that matching Ethereum's functionality requires each rollup to have its own governance, and that governance cannot be forced to follow Ethereum's decisions, so it can diverge arbitrarily. As a result, the best a rollup can do is offer a long exit window, but purposes that rely on timelocked governance, staking, or vesting contracts cannot be fully protected by any finite exit window. This EIP lets rollups reuse Ethereum's state transition verification infrastructure, greatly simplifying rollup infrastructure and upgrade procedures and freeing up resources that can be redirected to user facing features and products.

If the initially offline stake fraction is f, finality returns only when the offline share falls below 1/3. The number of epochs required is N > sqrt(2 · Q · ln(2f/(1-f))) (based on 225 epochs per day). According to the source table, f = 0.50 takes about 4,822 epochs (about 21.4 days), 0.60 takes about 6,072 epochs (about 27.0 days), 2/3 takes about 6,820 epochs (about 30.3 days), and 0.75 takes about 7,754 epochs (about 34.5 days). The leak cuts only the offline stake and leaves the online stake untouched, so the larger the initial offline share, the more the offline side must shrink and the longer it takes for the online side to regain a 2/3 supermajority. The ln(2f/(1-f)) term diverges as f approaches 1.

2sw9ek1y8r: EOF (EVM Object Format) is a new code format for the Ethereum Virtual Machine. EOFv1, within the scope of EIP-7692, removed the ability for contracts to directly read another account's code bytes (code introspection). However, EIP-7702 lets a regular user account record a marker (a delegation designation) in its code slot indicating that execution is delegated to a specific contract. An EOF contract that cannot read code also cannot read this marker. The source cites cases where this becomes a problem. A managed proxy wants to ensure safety by preventing the proxy from being updated to a delegated address. A gas sponsorship service, after granting approval, needs to verify that the delegation written in the transaction data matches the actual delegation, to prevent the delegation from being changed afterward to perform an action different from what was approved. A contract that wants to allow only a small whitelist of delegations in order to reduce risk needs to know not just whether a delegation exists but the actual delegated address. This EIP hands off the job of interpreting the delegation designation to the new EXTCODEADDRESS opcode, allowing the delegated address to be obtained without directly reading the code.

Effective balances still hold that epoch's values, so the proposer burn is charged accurately to the proposer that was actually selected. The attestation burn is charged to every validator that was active in the previous epoch. The base amount is computed by taking the participating balance per flag from get_participating_increments, rounding down for each flag separately, and then summing. Summing first and rounding down once would yield up to 2 Gwei more, and at saturation that difference would come out of the principal of a flawless validator. During an inactivity leak, only the attestation burn is paused. The proposer burn is charged to the 32 proposers of that epoch, and its base amount is the sum of attestation_component and sync_component, computed from current-epoch participation, divided by SLOTS_PER_EPOCH. Sync participation is not accumulated in state, so attestation participation is used as a substitute, and the error stays within 3.57% of the proposer's share. For the sync committee burn, rewards are paid every block, so process_sync_aggregate subtracts participant_reward × b from all 512 committee members regardless of whether they participated. If only participants were charged, abstaining would avoid the burn, and the balance gap between participating and not participating would shrink from 2× participant_reward to (2 - b)×. A get_beacon_proposer_index_at_slot lookup, which does not exist in the current spec, is also newly required.
3cnbos0af7: Code C is split so that code_0 || ... || code_n == C, where every chunk except the last has length CHUNK_SIZE (31 bytes) and the last chunk is at most 31 bytes. Each chunk's FIO_i is the offset at which the first instruction in that chunk begins. It is greater than 0 only when the last instruction of the preceding chunk is a multi-byte instruction like PUSHN that crosses the boundary, and is set to CHUNK_SIZE if the whole chunk is data. The i-th chunk is stored as key BE(i, 4), value BE(FIO_i, 1) || code_i. The FIO lets even a stateless client that does not hold all chunks safely perform jumpdest analysis. Edge cases where the trailing data bytes of the last chunk happen to look like a multi-byte instruction can be safely ignored.

4f5675rcq2: When Ethereum creates a new contract, it checks only that the destination address has nonce 0 (nonce: the number of transactions or contract creations an account has made) and no code (EIP-684). The rule assumes that if the nonce is 0 and there is no code, the storage is also empty. However, before EIP-161 (the Spurious Dragon fork), the nonce was not incremented before the init code ran when a contract was created. So if a constructor wrote values to storage and returned no code, an account with nonce 0, no code and non-empty storage was left behind. This form is the only case in which that assumption breaks. If a new contract is created at such an address, it inherits the old storage as is. One option would be to additionally check that storage is empty on every contract creation, but that would make every contract creation pay a check cost and a disk read forever to protect a few addresses that will not grow in number. This EIP raises the nonce of those accounts to 1 once, removing the problematic account form itself.

4f7ytwhjn8: Ethereum has a mechanism called the difficulty bomb. It is code that automatically raises mining difficulty over time, gradually slowing down block production, also known as the ice age. It is meant to pressure the network toward moving to proof-of-stake, but as development of the transition project, Casper, fell behind, the bomb alone started kicking in first. As a result, average block time has been creeping up little by little. For roughly the next 12 months, proof-of-work mining needs to be able to produce a block every 15 seconds, so the bomb must be delayed. However, delaying the bomb alone would suddenly increase miner revenue, so block rewards are reduced at the same time to offset the delay effect and keep the system in roughly the same state as before. Reducing rewards also lowers the chance of a miner-led chain split ahead of the move to proof-of-stake.

In addition, the Bloom filter (summary data for log search) inside a receipt (the record of a transaction's processing result) is not stored by any client and is recomputed when needed, yet the protocol required it to be transmitted. As a result, for every newly syncing node the serving node had to regenerate and send about 530GB of Bloom filters, and the receiving side only verified and discarded them, a waste that repeated each time. Finally, the total difficulty (TD) value, which has been meaningless since the Merge, still remained in the handshake message.

Thanks to the max(0, ...) clamp, an input shorter than PK_LEN + SIG_LEN pays exactly BASE and is rejected, with no special rule. The base cost makes up most of the total and covers the matrix expansion and the number-theoretic transform (NTT) verification work. The small linear term is the cost of the SHAKE256 hash over the message, which is cheap compared with the lattice operations. 6 gas per word is the same rate the KECCAK256 instruction already charges. SHAKE256 and Keccak-256 absorb with the same Keccak-f[1600] permutation at the same 136-byte rate, so the per-byte cost is the same. The base cost is higher than EIP-8051's 4500 because the matrix is expanded directly from ρ rather than received pre-expanded. Clients MUST deduct the full gas before the verification work. The cost depends only on input length, so it can be computed in advance. Deducting after verification creates a denial-of-service surface where an attacker can make clients do work for free in transactions that end with insufficient gas. The source states that these figures predate reference implementation benchmarks and were set slightly higher than a pairing check of similar workload.

As an exception, CREATE and CREATE2 are treated as returning an empty buffer on success, and only store failure data on failure. It is widely used in math functions such as logarithms, powers and square roots, byte string comparison, data compression and decompression, finding the next set bit in a bitmap, and post-quantum signature verification. However, the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) has no such instruction, so today it must be emulated in Solidity code. Even the fastest known implementation uses about 184 gas and contains several large constants, which increases contract code size. The dynamic bit shift operations this implementation uses are especially expensive in zero-knowledge (ZK) proving environments, so the burden is greater for systems that use ZK proofs. But for transactions that become meaningless if not processed within seconds, such as atomic intent transfers or time-bound fee sponsorship, this approach is overly strict. Because the number enforces ordering, the sender must decide the order in advance, it is hard to queue several transactions at once, and the order in which they land in a block is tied to the nonce order, even though the only real risk to guard against is replay within the short window before the deadline. The block header's transaction root is built as a Merkle Patricia Trie (MPT); since there is no on-chain commitment to tx_hash, inclusion proofs also require the full transaction data. The consensus layer rehashes the same transaction using SSZ, producing hashes incompatible with the execution layer. Edge cases such as legacy transactions lacking a prefix byte and inconsistent chain_id and v/y_parity semantics keep accumulating as technical debt. Also, because the consensus layer treats transactions as opaque data while still needing to validate blobs, the Engine API ends up more complex than necessary. This EIP converts RLP transactions losslessly into SSZ, unifying the transaction representation across both layers while continuing to support processing of existing RLP types.

At a 200M limit, it would grow by about 387 GiB per year and cross the 650 GiB line, where node performance starts to degrade, within a year. Moreover, today the same amount of state costs different amounts depending on how it is created. Contract deployment costs about 200 gas per byte, while a storage slot costs about 313 gas per byte, and even when already existing code is deployed again, clients do not store it twice, yet the cost is the same. This proposal sets a single cost per byte of state, applies the same yardstick to every state-creating operation, and counts state creation cost separately so that the block gas limit can be raised further.

Specifically, sig_hash is the hash_tree_root of an ExecutionSigningData container whose object_root is payload.hash_tree_root() and whose domain_type is DOMAIN_TX_SSZ. By structuring code with EOF, the entire code can be analyzed once before deployment to prove in advance that the stack cannot overflow along any execution path. This removes the need to repeat the check on every execution, and also helps compilers analyze EVM code faster or perform ahead-of-time (AOT) or just-in-time (JIT) compilation.

8jdj3l9fg5: Currently, Ethereum's state is stored in a single hexary Patricia tree, and the proof (witness) needed to access a single account averages 3 kilobytes and can be up to three times larger in the worst case. Dividing a block's 15 million gas by 2500 gas per access allows up to 6000 accesses, during which the proof size could grow to about 18 megabytes. This is too large to safely propagate over the peer-to-peer network within a 12-second slot. A Verkle tree is therefore needed, which can reduce the average proof per account to about 200 bytes. This EIP leaves the Patricia tree in place while adding a new Verkle tree, laying the first step toward eventually replacing the tree entirely.
