In these cases it is desirable for the common fields shared across variants to be provable and verifiable in the same way. However, in the current SSZ (Simple Serialize), when several versions of a container exist at once, the generalized index (gindex), the position number within the Merkle tree, can differ between versions even for the same field. This means that whoever verifies a proof must separately maintain a mapping between fields and gindexes for each version, and update that mapping every time a new version appears. This adds unnecessary complexity for verifiers and accumulates maintenance burden. CompatibleUnion restricts merkleization to only group type options that are mutually compatible, so that no matter which option is chosen, the same field always sits at the same gindex. In addition, thanks to the selector tag, a parser can learn the tree shape of the data early, making deserialization efficient.

Because it uses storage slots like a battery for storing gas, it actually grows the state the network must keep and fills block space inefficiently. Refunds also increase variance in block size. 9uha4ofc6: Sending assets publicly on Ethereum is easy. But there is no common default for transfers that need to hide the sender, the recipient, and the amount. Ordinary financial activity such as payroll, corporate treasury management, and donations becomes problematic when the details are visible to everyone, so it is currently pushed to traditional finance or other blockchains. The source locates the reason the market has not solved this on its own in the scale effects of the pool. The anonymity of a private transfer depends on how many users and how much capital share the same pool, so a small pool has weak privacy no matter how good the product is. Also, if a pool is made upgradeable, whoever holds that authority can threaten user funds, and if it is made immutable instead, it cannot be fixed even when the proof system weakens. This EIP proposes to break this deadlock by providing a protocol-managed pool that changes only through hard forks.

a9wscw9zx3: Today, even as staked ETH grows, the new ETH paid to validators, that is, issuance, keeps increasing. The yield of a single validator falls gently but does not drop below about 1.5%, so there is no point at which the staking incentive switches off. As the staking landscape matures and custodial institutions such as ETFs grow, the risk premium required for staking keeps declining, so the staking ratio can keep rising. The source argues that this creates two problems. First, if most ETH concentrates in a few operators such as exchanges, ETFs, and staking services, large operators become 'too big to fail' and the community has difficulty correcting problems by fork when they arise. Solo stakers, who pay tax on nominal income, see their real return after dilution turn negative first and are pushed out. Second, ETH holders who do not stake keep being diluted, so interest-bearing liquid staking tokens take the place of ETH as collateral and a means of payment. The base asset of the Ethereum economy would then bear the smart contract and governance risk of particular issuers.

anqrzo82gb: Currently, the Ethereum Virtual Machine re-analyzes the entire code every time a contract is executed to determine which locations are valid jump destinations (JUMPDEST). This analysis is overhead repeated every time, and its cost varies by client implementation. Using the EOF container structure introduced by EIP-3540, instead of scattering jump destinations throughout the code as JUMPDEST opcodes, the list can be pre-stored and delivered in a separate section. This moves some of the complexity and processing time from execution time to contract creation (deployment) time, requiring the list's correctness to be validated only once at creation. In addition, this structure also reduces the problem of initcode analysis scope, which previously had no limit other than memory cost, by bounding it to the maximum size of the jumpdests section (0xffff). Legacy code continues to operate unchanged, unaffected by this change.

axxb5t33fv: The source text models and compares censorship cost as the sum of the dummy transaction's gas cost, the ranking fee, and the forgone MEV. In a multidimensional fee market, FOCIL can drive the cost close to zero by filling just the cheapest resource, but under UPIL the censor must pay the censorship target's ranking fee across the entire dummy gas amount. To censor a transaction using 100k gas in a resource with a 60M gas limit, the censor must pay (60-0.1)/0.1 = 599 times the amount the censored party was willing to pay. The censored party does not actually pay the high fee it offered; after censorship ends it only pays that block's marginal ranking fee. Even under the current single base-fee market, FOCIL censorship can be cheap for the first few blocks, but under UPIL the cost can balloon to thousands of times from the very first block. A strategy of filling blocks with slow transactions gathered from private order flow is also ineffective under UPIL because of the ranking fee and opportunity cost.

For the server it is always cheaper. Since the descriptor bits are consumed in the same order as the depth-first traversal, no index arithmetic, helper index computation, or traversal planning is needed. The reason requested nodes and helper nodes are not encoded separately is that whoever built the descriptor already knows which nodes were requested, so the distinction would give neither side new information. If a resource's base fee multiplied by GAS_RESERVE_FACTOR is lower than the base fee of the reference resource (GAS_RESERVE_INDEX), that resource's excess gas can only rise with usage and cannot fall. The constants are GAS_RESERVE_FACTOR = [0, 16, 12] and GAS_RESERVE_INDEX = [0, 0, 1]: blob gas uses a factor of 16 relative to EVM gas's base fee (as in the existing EIP-7918), and calldata uses a factor of 12 relative to blob gas's base fee. Since calldata costs 16 gas per byte and blobs cost 1 gas per byte, this condition prevents calldata's per-byte price from falling below about 1.33x (16/12) of the blob price. This prevents calldata from becoming cheaper than blobs and causing L2s to shift from blobs to calldata, and also prevents the fee update mechanism from dropping into a low-price regime where it stops functioning properly.

Whether the previous slot's payload is part of the canonical chain is decided by a tiebreaker, not by attestation weight. FULL is preferred if the payload has been verified locally and the PTC voted above the threshold on timeliness and data availability, or if a current block that received the proposer boost was built on top of it. The blob availability check is removed from on_block and handled by a new handler, on_execution_payload_envelope, while on_payload_attestation_message aggregates PTC votes. With this structure, proposer unconditional payment, builder reveal safety (a payload revealed on time is included), and builder withhold safety are guaranteed within the stated security margins.

ba083chof2: SWAPN (0xc0) and DUPN (0xc1) take the depth N as an argument from the stack. N must be pushed by an immediately preceding PUSH1 instruction, and failing to follow this calling convention or having N equal 0 causes execution to fail with an out-of-gas error. bl6mb18v7e: Each time Ethereum processes a transaction, it leaves a receipt recording the result. Today the receipt does not record the gas used by that transaction but the sum of all gas used from the first transaction in the block up to this one (cumulativeGasUsed). So to find the gas used by one transaction, you also have to fetch the preceding receipt and subtract the two values. This is a hassle for RPC clients that want to verify things themselves rather than trust the node. In addition, because the receipt content is tied to the results of earlier transactions, receipts can only be built in order, even for transactions that touch entirely different state. This is an obstacle to parallel processing. The log index (logIndex) returned over JSON-RPC has the same problem. It is a number across the whole block, not within the receipt, so it cannot be determined without information about earlier transactions.

bm8lrvfsuk: The key weakness is that the active set only grows in one direction between forks. Once an inactive item is written, it stays active, and there is no mechanism for it to revert to inactive on its own. An attacker could pay the extra charge to revive the inactive set in bulk and inflate the hot working set, but the source material explains that two things limit this: each item requires paying the extra charge, so it is not cheap, and the block gas limit caps the rate; and if a later fork moves CUTOFF_BLOCK forward, state that cooled again in the meantime (including state the attacker revived and then abandoned) gets reclassified as inactive. Also, since this classification is write-based only, a slot that is read every block but never rewritten is still inactive. If a client moves inactive state to slower storage without separately accounting for read frequency, that can become a denial-of-service attack vector. The choice of CUTOFF_BLOCK itself is also a governance question: too close and it over-penalizes ordinary activity, too far and its effect is blunted, so it should be set based on the distribution of write ages at the time of the fork.

bxax6v3l60: EIP-8051 accepts a 20512-byte public key with the matrix materialized and t1 held in the NTT domain, which skips the expansion. This proposal deliberately reverses that trade. The public key travels in the witness alongside the signature, so its size is paid on every verification as transaction bandwidth and data cost, whereas the expansion is paid only once as an operation that can be priced in gas. 20512 bytes is more than fifteen times the 1312-byte compressed ML-DSA-44 key and larger than an entire ML-DSA-87 witness. The judgment is that charging every transaction that cost to save a client work that finishes in microseconds is backwards, and a chain that wants the opposite trade can add a sibling precompile that accepts pre-expanded keys. Message length differs too. EIP-8051 fixes it to a 32-byte pre-hash, but ML-DSA is not a fixed-length-message scheme, and FIPS 204 § 5.4 defines pre-hashing as a separate construction, HashML-DSA, which binds the identifier of the hash function that produced the digest. A bare 32-byte message has no such binding, and a 32-byte-only precompile cannot verify HashML-DSA signatures that grow longer because of the identifier and domain separator. What remains is a third construction, neither pure ML-DSA nor HashML-DSA, for which the caller must supply the security argument. A caller that holds only a digest can still pass the digest and take that responsibility, but this is not forced on callers that can sign the message directly.
bxgvhv77b2: Ethereum summarizes data with a hash structure called a Merkle tree and uses Merkle proofs to confirm that some piece of data is genuine. The existing multiproof format for proving several nodes at once specifies the nodes to be proven as a list of generalized indices, and each index typically takes 2 to 8 bytes, which gets expensive when a different proof is requested dynamically each time. There is also a burden on the server side. Given a list of indices, the server has to separately compute the indices of the helper nodes needed for the proof and plan how to traverse the tree. This EIP's descriptor approach represents the shape of an entire proof at roughly 2 bits per node, and the server simply follows the descriptor bits, walking the tree once depth-first and emitting nodes in order. It is meant as a building block for protocols that dynamically exchange chosen proofs, such as light client protocols or proof-serving APIs.

c1x153g8o7: Until now, Ethereum's regular accounts (EOAs) could only use one signature scheme: ECDSA over the secp256k1 curve. Once a sufficiently powerful quantum computer exists, this scheme allows the private key to be derived back from the public key. In addition, security chips and hardware security modules increasingly support other signature schemes by default, so mandating ECDSA alone complicates the integration layer and increases the number of trusted components. Smart contract wallets or EIP-7702 code delegation can implement other authentication methods, but they incur cost because the EVM must execute code every time a transaction is verified. This EIP moves signature verification into the protocol itself, allowing a single transaction to permanently switch account authentication to ML-DSA-44. It further allows creating accounts where an ECDSA key never existed in the first place, guaranteeing mathematically rather than procedurally that no backdoor key exists.

In Go, the standard library crypto/mldsa from 1.27 is wired into crypto/x509 and TLS, and C# and .NET expose a native ML-DSA type from .NET 10. For C, besides the reference implementation and liboqs there is a portable C90 implementation, and Node.js verifies all three sets through Web Crypto. The test cases use VERIFY_MLDSA44 to show the three results a caller can see. Cases 1 and 2 are tcId 1 and 8 of group 1 in Wycheproof mldsa_44_verify_test.json, which use the same public key and the message "Hello world" and differ only by one bit in the first byte of the signature's c~. Case 1 returns 0x00..01 for a 3743-byte input at 6506 gas, case 2 returns 0x00..00 at the same length and gas, and case 3 returns 0x00..00 without verification for the 21-byte "This is invalid input" at 6500 gas. The call itself succeeds in all three cases, so call success alone cannot distinguish them. Before Last Call, the remaining work is to re-encode the full NIST ACVP and Wycheproof sets for all three parameter sets into this layout and add EVM-specific cases such as the empty message and boundary lengths.

ceelbfmab5: Until now, Ethereum has added a new transaction type every time a new feature appeared, such as blobs or set-code delegation. Although the contents of most of these types are little more than the EIP-1559 shape with a few fields appended, combining features requires a new type for each combination. For example, a user who wants to combine passkey signatures with blob and set-code authorization at once would need yet another top-level type created for them. The signature scheme is also a problem. Today's externally owned accounts (EOAs) are locked into a single secp256k1 ECDSA signature, which will be broken once quantum computers advance far enough. This EIP proposes a common envelope that unifies the fee header and execution content, while attaching features like blobs or set-code as extensions and making the signature scheme a swappable scheme. It also defines a signature scheme that achieves quantum safety by using each key only once, without new cryptography, opening a path for EOAs to move to post-quantum signatures without wrapping execution in a different abstraction.

Also, when higher-level constructs such as functions are implemented on top of the EVM, the input values, output values, and return location all get pushed onto the stack, easily exceeding 16 items, and the compiler needs extra work to arrange things so all these values remain accessible. A failure that ends in REVERT can safely be recorded as final, but a halt caused by, for example, running out of gas can be manipulated by the transaction sender adjusting the gas amount, so it should not be treated as final. The EVM currently exposes only the success flag, the return data, and the remaining gas, so contracts infer the cause through gas arithmetic that compares the GAS instruction's value against a threshold. This inference relies on the assumption that the gas schedule consumes all forwarded gas on an exceptional halt, but every repricing fork has broken these thresholds, and multidimensional gas proposals that charge state creation separately weaken this further. Return data does not help distinguish the cases either, since both a REVERT with no data and an exceptional halt leave empty return data. Because the EVM already knows whether a halt occurred each time a frame ends, exposing that fact directly makes it possible to determine finality without gas arithmetic.

The second byte, 0x79, was chosen to avoid two values it could otherwise collide with: 0x00, the magic of the EOF container format, and 0xF0, the second byte of a contract deployed before London. There is a single version byte because validation rules are expected to change only a few times per decade. Execution starts right after the header, but PC values and destinations are counted from the first MAGIC byte. The version byte is also an extension point for the header, so an EIP that needs to add more to the header can simply define the rules for a new version that includes it.

The rules of this EIP apply only to code executing with ADDRESS being a TCREATE account. This includes that account's initcode and runtime code, and code that the account executes through DELEGATECALL or CALLCODE. It does not include the code of other accounts that the account calls or creates with CREATE, nor this account's code executed by other accounts through DELEGATECALL, CALLCODE, or EIP-7702 delegation. For example, reading one byte at a given position in calldata requires three steps: CALLDATALOAD to read 32 bytes, then PUSH1 248 and SHR to shift out 248 bits. This pattern costs 9 gas per read, and each occurrence adds 3 extra bytes to the deployed bytecode. Contracts that interpret calldata as a byte-oriented instruction stream repeat this read pattern constantly, so the unnecessary cost keeps accumulating. This EIP proposes eliminating that waste by adding MLOAD8 and CALLDATALOAD8, which read a single byte directly in one instruction.

e6hvhom21q: Ethereum's early protocol had a flaw that let 'empty accounts' be added to state at very low cost. An empty account has zero balance, zero transaction count (nonce), and empty code and storage, making it useless, but once created every node still had to keep storing it forever. This caused state size to balloon, increasing the disk burden on full nodes and lengthening the fast sync time for new nodes catching up with the network. This proposal reduces state size by removing these empty accounts from state and preventing new ones from being created. It also means that once all empty accounts are gone, there is no longer a need to distinguish between 'an account being empty' and 'an account not existing,' simplifying the protocol in the long run.

e8pjkq8rzq: The basic network protocol Ethereum nodes use to communicate with each other, DEVp2p, originally applied no compression at all. Block and transaction data compress well, yet exchanging them uncompressed wasted enormous bandwidth across the network, slowing both initial sync, when a node first starts up and downloads the blockchain, and normal operation. In practice, syncing the main network (as of block 4,248,000) with the Geth client via fast sync required 1.01GB upload and 33.59GB download. Enabling compression at the message content level cuts the download for the same sync to 13.46GB, and on the Rinkeby test network the download drops from 2.51GB to 463.65MB. Rather than implementing compression separately in each subprotocol (eth, les, bzz), handling it once at the DEVp2p layer below lets every protocol benefit without modification.

A new helper, compute_blob_data_retention_start_epoch(epoch), returns the epoch containing the point that far back on the piecewise timeline. The retention window start is max(that value, FULU_FORK_EPOCH), and the lower bound of earliest_available_slot in Status v2 and of data_column_serve_range in DataColumnSidecarsByRange v1 and DataColumnSidecarsByRoot v1 uses this value. After the 10-second transition, the number of epochs the window covers grows one epoch at a time up to about 4,916, and the start point never moves backward. So nodes do not need to store more in advance or re-download later. By contrast, the block retention window compute_min_epochs_for_block_requests() (33,024 epochs on mainnet) and other epoch-denominated windows keep their epoch counts, so their real time shrinks gradually from about 146.8 days to about 122.3 days. euej98xnrt: When serializing, bits are filled starting from the most significant bit. Descriptor bit i is stored at bit 7 - i % 8 of byte i // 8, and 0 to 7 zero bits are appended for byte alignment. A valid descriptor must satisfy three conditions: it must have at least one 1-bit, there must be at most 7 0-bits after the last 1-bit, and reading from the start, the point where the count of 1-bits first exceeds the count of 0-bits must be exactly the last 1-bit. Implementations must reject descriptors that violate these. This rule ensures a valid descriptor has exactly one serialization, so there is no possibility of the same proof shape being represented by different bytes. The test cases' invalid examples are 0x00 (no 1-bit), 0x40 (traversal incomplete), 0xff (traversal ended at the first bit yet more 1-bits follow), and 0x25e000 (padding exceeds 7 bits).
eui4k14x5w: Ethereum nodes connect to each other to exchange blocks and data. But it is hard to tell at first whether a peer follows the same network and the same history of upgrades (forks) as you do. EIP-2124 defined a fork ID that summarizes a node's fork history into a single short value, and a way to validate it, but it did not define when or how nodes would exchange that value with each other. As a result, a connection would be kept with an incompatible node for a while, and only after receiving a block and going through expensive validation such as proof-of-work (PoW) checking, EVM execution, and state reconstruction would it become clear that the peer did not match. In the meantime, a useless peer would also occupy a limited peer slot. This EIP has nodes validate each other's fork ID right at the handshake immediately after connecting, so that incompatible nodes are disconnected on the spot. Each node then spends resources only on peers that are useful to it, and across the network as a whole, groups of nodes following different chains separate from each other, letting each spend more resources maintaining its own chain.

f98g4huzkn: Bloom Filter(0x03) is an arbitrary-length byte array used to tell peers which topics' messages a node is interested in. The bloom is built by OR-ing together the per-topic bloom results. The bloom function projects a 4-byte topic onto a 512-bit slice, marking at most 3 bits per topic. RJUMPI relative_offset pops the condition value from the stack; if it is 0, execution continues as is, otherwise it moves by relative_offset. The cost scales with validator count rather than with stake held, and there are currently about 815,000 validators, with aggregation costs set to grow further once quantum-resistant signatures are introduced. fqdqi84b8o: Of the fees paid when sending a transaction on Ethereum, the priority fee is credited to the fee recipient that built the block right after each transaction finishes. As a result, every transaction in a block writes to the same place, the fee recipient's account balance, which makes parallel execution of transactions difficult. It can also happen that a sender only has enough balance after earlier transactions in the same block are processed, which complicates the mempool logic that manages pending transactions. For the fee recipient, accounting is cumbersome because a payment that logically should be one is received as hundreds of small payments. Proposals to log ETH movements also become inaccurate if priority fees are left out, and adding an entry for every transaction makes them expensive. This EIP credits the priority fee once at the end of the block, which solves these problems together.

fqrfy6i0jh: On Ethereum, sending data with a transaction costs gas per byte. This cost was high at 68 gas per non-zero byte, limiting how much data could fit in a block. Layer 2 scaling approaches in particular move storage and computation off-chain, which increases data transmission instead. Proof systems like STARKs or SNARKs compress the fact that computation over many transactions was done correctly into a single proof; fraud proof schemes must transmit Merkle proofs; and some approaches keep the data itself on the main chain as calldata for data availability. When calldata is expensive, all of these approaches become more costly. There was concern that lowering the cost could enlarge blocks, slowing propagation and weakening security, so the authors evaluated this using a mathematical model linking network latency and security along with empirical measurements, and proposed 16 gas based on the results.

g8bt12yu9y: Hashing is one of the biggest performance bottlenecks in consensus layer implementations. As the number of validators grows, the burden of repeatedly hashing each validator's state data via hash_tree_root also grows. hash_tree_root splits all data into 256-bit chunks and hashes them in pairs; the SHA-256 used here goes through a preprocessing step that appends padding to the end of the input to handle variable-length input in general. But because the input to hash_tree_root is always exactly 512 bits, this preprocessing ends up producing a second 512-bit block every time that carries no actual information. On the Holesky testnet, with roughly 1.7 million validators, state root verification alone consumes about 25% of CPU time, so removing this unnecessary block creates room to support more validators on the same hardware.

g9iqbjnj15: Previously, Ethereum set fees through a simple auction in which users bid a gas price directly and miners included the highest bids first. This approach had four problems. First, fees swung by a factor of ten even though the actual marginal cost of including one more transaction barely changed. Second, because block size was fixed, transactions could wait through multiple blocks whenever demand spiked briefly. Third, a first price auction, where you pay exactly what you bid, is highly inefficient, requiring complex fee estimation algorithms that still frequently led to overpayment. Fourth, it is known that a blockchain with no issuance becomes unstable if miners are compensated solely through fees. This proposal lets the protocol raise or lower the base fee gradually based on network congestion, so wallets can set fees automatically and reliably.

gn75fy4097: Relative addressing was chosen to make code relocatable. Code fragments can be inserted into other code, the PUSHn PC ADD JUMPI technique previously used for the same purpose becomes unnecessary, and the PC instruction can even be deprecated. With a 16-bit signed immediate value, the maximum jump distance is 32767, and starting RJUMP at PC=0 reaches up to PC=32770. Considering MAX_CODE_SIZE = 24576 (EIP-170) and MAX_INITCODE_SIZE = 49152 (EIP-3860), this is a sufficient size. An 8-bit version would only reach 125 bytes backward and 127 bytes forward, which is insufficient for jumps between functions, while 16 bits is the same size as a dynamic jump (JUMP PUSH1 n, 3 bytes), so the choice was made to reduce the number of instructions. If a different size is needed later, a new opcode can be added, as was done with PUSH.

h02c3sw927: CPSB is a constant chosen so that annual state growth is 120 GiB (128,849,018,880 bytes) at a reference block gas limit of 150M. With a 12 second slot time there are 2,628,000 blocks per year, and under multidimensional metering the base fee converges to the target (half of the limit), so it is assumed that 50% of block gas can be spent on state gas. The state gas available per year is then 75,000,000 x 2,628,000 = 1.971 x 10^14, and dividing this by the target number of bytes gives about 1530 gas per byte. 150M is a midpoint between the current 60M and the expected 300M, chosen so that costs are neither raised too much at once nor need to be raised substantially again later. In the worst case where a block is filled with state creation alone, state growth is 80 GiB at 100M, 120 GiB at 150M, 160 GiB at 200M, and 240 GiB at 300M. If the gas limit changes substantially and the expected growth rate shifts, CPSB can be derived again in a follow-up EIP.

h2nhjczoou: PAY uses opcode 0xfc. It pops addr (the recipient address) and val (the amount to send, in wei) from the stack in this order and moves val wei from the currently executing address to addr. The other party's code is never executed. The transfer happens only when the current address's balance is at least val. On success it pushes 1 onto the stack, and on failure it pushes 0. In the current specification, insufficient balance is the only case that produces 0. After execution, addr is added to accessed_addresses and becomes warm. There are only two arguments, addr and val, and unlike CALL there is no argument to specify the amount of gas to pass on.
h2o5y9uz0y: Any analysis beyond linear time becomes a denial-of-service vulnerability when run online. Quadratic-cost graph traversal is just as much a problem as factorial-cost path walking. Bytecode verification, AOT compilation at contract-creation time, and JIT compilation at execution time are all tasks that must run online. Even offline, the absence of dynamic jumps and internal calls makes static analysis of many contracts quadratically impractical, exponentially intractable, or mathematically impossible. The source document cites recent papers arguing that interpreting EVM jumps is a core difficulty in static analysis, and notes that even research using neural networks only manages to disassemble most Solidity programs. In other words, there exists an entire body of complex and incomplete academic literature addressing a problem that would be trivial under static control flow.
h33a8uh104: EIP-7928's BAL retains addresses and storage keys already accessed in the BAL even when a call frame reverts. This EIP always measures before an entry is actually written to the BAL, so if measurement raises OutOfGasError, those bytes never enter the BAL either. Conversely, values that are rolled back on revert, such as changes to balance, nonce, code, or storage value, are not rolled back in the measurement counters either, so the result can only be an overcount, never an undercount. This principle, overcounting allowed, undercounting forbidden, is what preserves the safety of the block size ceiling.

Bots see a user's transaction and insert their own transactions before and after it to capture profit. This EIP builds the ordering rule itself into the protocol. Because the order is determined by a randomness value that nobody knows before the slot begins, it becomes difficult to attack by securing an advantageous position in advance. This EIP sets aside two currently unallocated values, 0xEB and 0xEC, and reserves them as extension prefixes signaling that more bytes follow. hm66ekris4: RJUMP (0xe0) is an unconditional jump that sets the PC to PC_post_instruction + relative_offset. RJUMPI (0xe1) pops condition from the stack; if it is 0 it proceeds normally, and if it is nonzero it jumps by relative_offset. RJUMPV (0xe2) has max_index and an offset table as immediate values and jumps to relative_offset[case] corresponding to the case popped from the stack. RJUMPSUB (0xe3) is a subroutine call that pushes PC_post_instruction onto the return stack before jumping, and RJUMPSUBV (0xe4) is its table version. relative_offset is a 16-bit signed (two's complement) big-endian value, and PC_post_instruction means the PC position right after the entire immediate value ends.

hovdlxowie: The EVM uses a quadratic memory model in which cost grows roughly with the square of memory used. It was originally meant to prevent denial-of-service (DoS) attacks, but it now looks outdated. Even at a 30 million gas limit, a single message call can use only about 3MB of memory, and it has to burn all of its gas to do so. Because the quadratic term starts at 724 bytes, using just 64KB, the amount of memory in an early 1980s PC, costs 14,336 gas. Working out the maximum memory a transaction can use requires solving an optimization problem that includes the call stack limit and the 63/64 rule from EIP-150, so it is also hard to reason about. In addition, languages such as Vyper and Solidity cannot use the modern virtual memory layout in which the heap grows upward and the call stack grows downward, which makes their memory models inefficient. This EIP proposes a model like today's hardware: memory is allocated in pages only when needed, and the cost is charged linearly.

i16yng1dg9: A single Ethereum transaction can create multiple layers of execution frames through call instructions like CALL, and the same contract can even be called back into within one transaction. Right now there are only two ways for these frames to exchange information with each other: call input/output and persistent storage. If an untrusted contract sits in between, passing data through input/output is not safe. A classic example is the reentrancy lock. Using persistent storage (SSTORE/SLOAD) is safe but expensive. On top of that, EIP-3529 from the London hard fork capped gas refunds at 20% of the gas used by a transaction, making it hard to get a proper refund for a slot that is written and then cleared shortly after. This EIP solves the inter-frame communication problem cheaply and simply by creating a dedicated transient storage that is discarded entirely once the transaction ends.

Because it has to wait for execution to finish, a bottleneck forms in the consensus process, and this limits the transaction volume the network can handle. This proposal changes the idea. It accepts a block as valid based only on checks such as whether the block structure is correct and whether the sender of each transaction holds enough funds up front to pay the fee, and it confirms the actual execution later. iekon8burd: The tree is a key/value store where keys are byte strings and values are 32 bytes. The first byte of the key is the storage type, the portion before the last byte is the stem, and the last byte is the subindex. The 256 keys sharing the same stem are gathered under the same StemNode. There are four node types. InternalNode has left_hash and right_hash. StemNode has stem, left_hash, and right_hash, and LeafNode has a 32-byte value or is empty. EmptyNode represents an empty subtree. The path does not use all 248 bits; it creates only the minimum InternalNodes needed when another stem shares the same prefix. Unlike the MPT, this approach has no extension nodes along the path, and instead reduces depth this way.

iwsggawtfg: In Ethereum, SSTORE, the opcode a contract uses to store data, charges an expensive fee of up to 20000 gas each time it is used. However, actual client implementations hold changes made during a transaction only in memory and write to disk once, later, in a single batch. Even if the same slot is changed multiple times within the same transaction, the disk write ultimately happens only once, yet the fee is charged in full every time. Because of this, uses such as a reentry lock that is briefly written and cleared only within a transaction, or passing error codes back and forth between a subcall and its caller, ended up excessively expensive. j037n3ljot: There are four reasons for choosing a burn over redrawing the reward curve. First, the only permanent parameter is SATURATION_BALANCE, and its value has a natural reference point: half of the ETH supply. Second, preventing griefing attacks requires rewards and penalties to be paired, and then under any curve a diligent validator always earns a positive yield, leaving a yield floor. A burn removes this floor and lets the market set the equilibrium yield. Third, lowering yield by shrinking all rewards and penalties weakens the per-duty micro incentives and could let MEV crowd them out, whereas a burn leaves the schedule as it is and cuts only the macro yield behind the scenes. Fourth, if the deducted ETH were redirected to other validators or a foundation, total issuance would stay the same and a lobbying target would arise, so destroying it is neutral, like the base fee burn of EIP-1559. 50% is not a target but the point where the issuance incentive switches off completely, and the market settles somewhere below it. When a majority is staked, a rescue coalition would itself be the majority of the economy and there would be no larger group to counter it with a fork, so this is a qualitatively different threshold. There is no basis for distinguishing 60% from 70%, and conversely, setting it at or below today's 33% would make the burn 100% immediately on activation and push stake out. Since issuance peaks at about 20% and then declines, a large operator effectively splits an ever-shrinking pie more widely as it grows, and an operator holding half of the stake finds growth becomes a loss from the point when about 31% of supply is staked. MEV accrues in proportion to stake regardless of the burn, so it acts to raise this threshold.

j444dydvh5: The contract is deployed like an ordinary contract at RECENT_ROOT_ADDRESS (0x8272D9679689Ea2f307140CdF9002D27dC00Ffff), and the protocol does not install it at activation. The deployment transaction is fixed at type 0x0, nonce 0, gas 0x13d620, gasPrice 0xe8d4a51000, and is sent by the synthetic sender 0x14bf16d4c9842bf1EbF396e553477C66EB0a8A82, derived backwards from its signature. A call with a nonzero value reverts, and the two operations, write and verify, are selected by calldata length. A write is exactly 64 bytes, with the first 32 bytes as the salt and the last 32 bytes as the root. The calling msg.sender becomes source_address, and a call that succeeds in slot S stores entry_hash in cell i = S mod RECENT_ROOT_LENGTH. In a static context it fails and storage is unchanged. DELEGATECALL and CALLCODE write the calling account's storage, and EIP-7702 delegated code writes the delegating account's storage, so unless the storage context is RECENT_ROOT_ADDRESS none of them can change the recent root storage. If the same source address and salt write multiple times in one slot, they target the same key, so only the last value in canonical block execution order remains, and only that value can be referenced from S + 1. A successful write has no return value and no logs.
j452poiv71: As of October 3, 2023, more than 830,000 validators participate in the consensus layer. Because the stake of a single validator is capped at 32 ETH, a single entity ends up running thousands of 'duplicate validators' that sit on the same beacon node and differ only in signing key. This 32 ETH cap is technical debt from the early sharding design, which assumed that a committee had to have an honest majority. Committees are now used only for attestation aggregation, so a single honest participant is enough, and the security reason to keep the cap low is gone. Meanwhile, the growing number of validators keeps increasing the number of P2P messages, the number of BLS signatures that must be aggregated every epoch, and the memory usage of the beacon state (BeaconState). The proposal is therefore to keep the 32 ETH minimum balance and raise only the cap, so that the size of the validator set shrinks.

kt8htjhpfl: Transient storage, introduced by EIP-1153, is storage space that is cleared when a transaction ends. In the original design, it was priced the same as warm access to regular storage, to keep the proposal simple and to address denial-of-service (DoS) concerns. However, transient storage does not interact with gas refund accounting, does not touch the actual database, and, unlike memory, does not need to be freshly allocated for each call. This means the current price is fundamentally higher than the real cost. In particular, if the first few slots of transient storage become cheap enough, languages could enable reentrancy protection by default at the language level, which addresses the largest and most damaging class of smart contract vulnerabilities, but the current price makes that too costly. This EIP changes pricing to charge extra gas in proportion to the amount allocated, so that the common case of using fewer than about 95 slots per contract becomes cheaper than today, while DoS using transient storage becomes prohibitively expensive.

l7a69w10vi: As Ethereum prepares EOF (EVM Object Format), a new contract code format, it has established the principle that deployed code should not be inspectable by other code. Because of this principle, EOF contracts cannot be deployed using the existing deployment methods: creation transactions (transactions with an empty recipient address) or the CREATE and CREATE2 instructions. That would leave regular accounts (EOAs) with no way to deploy an EOF contract for the first time. This proposal creates a path where initcode (deployment-preparation code) is carried in the transaction data, and a TXCREATE instruction inside a contract extracts that code and deploys it. Every contract creation method possible in the existing EVM becomes possible under EOF as well, and smart contract wallets gain the same ability as EOAs to deploy arbitrary EOF contracts.

This approach takes about 12 hours for a deposit to be reflected on the beacon chain, and it relies on a safety assumption that an attacker holding more than two thirds of the stake could make honest nodes accept a fake deposit. l9o4xkwjn9: WAM is chain-derived state mapping entries (a 20-byte address Account(addr), or a pair of an address and a 32-byte storage key, Slot(addr, key)) to a u32 counter. If WAM[item] > 0, that entry is warm. Before a block B's transactions execute, +1 is applied to each entry in ADD = items(BAL(B-1)), and -1 is applied to each entry in DEL = items(BAL(B-1-WARMING_WINDOW)), deleting entries that reach 0. ADD is applied before DEL so that an entry present in both does not briefly become 0, and the final WAM does not depend on the order of application. WARMING_WINDOW is 256 blocks (about 51 minutes at 12-second slots). Membership checks are O(1), and per-block updates are O(|BAL|). If the withdrawal credentials differ from the registration, the deposit is silently rejected. Even if the credentials match, the deposit is rejected when is_valid_deposit_signature() is false, and the registration is left in place. If both checks pass, remove_stored_preregistration() deletes the registration and a PendingDeposit is added. A valid new-validator pending deposit and an active registration cannot coexist for the same pubkey. This is the core invariant. A PendingDeposit with an invalid signature can coexist if it entered the queue before the registration, but it is ignored in normal processing, and apply_pending_deposit does not need to change. Builder deposits use a separate request type and process_builder_deposit_request, so this check does not apply to them. The ETH from a rejected deposit stays in the deposit contract, which has no withdrawal function, and is permanently lost. The source describes this as intended design. If mismatched deposits were returned, an attacker could repeat deposit, rejection and recovery at no cost, so the permanent loss is what makes front-running economically self-defeating. The source notes that the risk of an accidental mismatch is low, because pre-registration goes through a separate BLS signing step apart from the deposit data, and the protocol confirms the registration through EIP-4788 before depositing.

lycfatxkrc: Today's EVM has no dedicated instruction for calling a function and returning from it. Compilers imitate calls and returns by combining dynamic jump (JUMP) instructions, which take their destination from the stack. This approach has two problems. First, chaining several jumps together wastes bytecode space and gas. Second, and more importantly, the return address is treated as data, so the control flow of the code is hidden from both people and tools. A tool analyzing the code must mark every possible destination, which can take time proportional to the square of the code size, and following every path in practice can take exponential time or worse. On Ethereum, worse-than-linear complexity becomes a denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability for online static analysis such as bytecode validation and just-in-time compilation. Even offline, automated correctness proofs and formal analysis can become impractically slow or mathematically impossible.

The hard bound on aggregate proof size is 512KiB (the leanSpec container limit), with typical sizes around 185-230KiB, almost independent of the number of votes. About 185KiB for 125 signatures and about 227KiB for 1000, growing only gradually. Proving time, on the other hand, is hardware-bound and sets the lower limit for this role. Aggregating 1000 signatures takes about 11.0 seconds on 2 cores/15GiB, about 3.7 seconds on 8 cores/59GiB, and about 2.6 seconds on 16 cores/118GiB, with core count mattering more than clock speed for meeting the slot budget. m95a3v30uw: For validated code (EIP-8337), every jump and call destination must be a fixed value within the code for safety to be provable in linear time. But dispatch, where one of several destinations is chosen by value, requires repeating N comparisons and jumps or building a comparison tree to pick one of N destinations, unlike legacy code, which could handle a memory jump table with a single computed JUMP. Every contract pays this cost each time it selects a function selector, and interpreters and state machines pay it every time they cycle through an inner loop; compilers also cannot take the path of optimizing a switch statement into a jump table. This EIP returns dispatch to its proper cost while preserving verifiability, by placing the destinations as data in a table inside the code and pushing only that table's location onto the stack for jumping or calling.

First, clients can deterministically separate recently written state from state that has not been written for a long time and place them in different storage tiers. The mutable tier is tuned for write throughput, and the stable tier for compression and read throughput. Second, in the commit path that rehashes and stores the trie paths dirtied by each block, concentrating active state in a narrow key space improves spatial locality, so the per-block write cost scales with the size of the active set rather than the total state size. The effect is the same whether it comes from LSM tree compaction or B-tree copy-on-write page rewrites. Third, on node restart a client can restore its cache by preloading only the recently written entries. None of these is mandatory. The block number is recorded as is because coarser units, such as an update period, can be derived deterministically from a block number, but the reverse is not possible. This allows the metadata to be finalized before the pricing policy is decided, and the encoding does not need to change again if the policy changes later.

muzlmtr7tv: Once the intrinsic gas check passes, state-dependent costs are charged in a pre-execution phase before entering the first EVM frame. First, gas is split into gas_left and state_gas_reservoir according to EIP-8037, and the counters are initialized. Next, EIP-7702 authorizations are processed, the recipient is added to the EIP-7928 block-level access list, and the remaining account creation and access costs are applied. If gas runs short in this phase, the transaction does not become invalid. It is included in the block, the nonce is incremented, and the gas consumed is paid, but all state changes from pre-execution, including delegations, are reverted. By contrast, if gas runs short after entering the first frame, delegations applied during pre-execution are kept as per the EIP-7702 rules, and their state gas also remains consumed. If the initcode of a contract creation transaction reverts or aborts with an exception, the state gas charged at runtime is refunded in the LIFO order of EIP-8037. The portion drawn from gas_left returns to gas_left, and the rest returns to state_gas_reservoir.

mv9iam7xqm: Inclusion of REVEAL transactions follows the same model as inclusion list enforcement in EIP-7805 (FOCIL), enforced through fork choice by the ordinary attestation committee for that slot. During the first REVEAL_DEADLINE (2 seconds) of slot N, every validator observes the mempool and individually records which commitment indices received a valid reveal. At attestation time, each attester checks whether all reveals it observed before the deadline were included in block N, and if even one is missing, it must not attest to that block. This causes the block to lose fork-choice weight and become non-canonical, giving builders an incentive to include every reveal they have seen. If no block is produced in slot N, the commitment does not expire and must be included in a block in a later slot once a valid block appears, with the original REVEAL transaction remaining valid. This guarantees that revealing the payload is safe once block N-1 is finalized.

my1xqodpwe: Ethereum currently uses two separate fee mechanisms, one for execution gas (EIP-1559) and one for blob gas (EIP-4844). As multidimensional markets that price resources such as calldata or state separately are introduced going forward, the current approach would require users to set a separate fee cap for each resource. In that case, even a brief spike in the price of just one resource could exclude a transaction that, overall, was willing to pay enough. This causes a loss where a transaction that the user, the block proposer, and the protocol would all be willing to process gets blocked purely because of design rigidity. Also, users typically do not think in terms of per-resource unit prices, but rather in terms of "how much ETH am I willing to pay for this transaction." This EIP takes advantage of the fact that fee budgets are fundamentally fungible across resources, automatically allocating a single ETH budget across whichever resources incur costs. Since there is no longer a need to keep separate buffers against per-resource price swings, capital can be used more efficiently.

nhmtyum2zq: Every epoch, Ethereum validators cast a target vote on which block to treat as a candidate for finalization. Today this target is the block in the epoch's first slot, and all attestations within the epoch point to the same target. Committees in later slots already know the target when they vote, but the first-slot committee must vote right after the target block is proposed and before the attestation deadline. If the block arrives late, some vote for the new block and some for the previous block. Only the side that matches the checkpoint the chain adopts counts toward justification, the other votes are discarded, and those validators lose their target reward. On the real network, missed target votes cluster in the first slot of each epoch, and roughly 1/SLOTS_PER_EPOCH of the FFG weight is exposed every epoch. The current behavior is not an intended design but a long-standing off-by-one error (consensus-specs issues 2174, 652). As a result, "epoch N finalized" in practice means only the first block of epoch N is finalized, the rest of its blocks can still be reverted, and explorers and tools that show finality per epoch are also inaccurate.

Miners might then rush to dispose of equipment that has become useless, or auction off their entire hash power (computing capacity) in one go. If an attacker can cheaply rent this freed-up hash power even for a short period, the risk of a 51% attack on the network rises. The Capella upgrade opened a path to convert an old BLS key into an execution-layer address, but there has been no way to change it again since. Even at that time there was significant demand to allow further changes, but it was deferred because building a communication channel between the execution layer and the consensus layer was complex. That complexity was later greatly reduced when Electra introduced the general execution request mechanism (EIP-7685). However, for an execution request to be made from a smart contract, the address sending the request must match the address in the validator's withdrawal credentials. A validator whose credentials are bound to an externally owned account (EOA) cannot change its credentials, so it can never use contract-based management. This proposal allows the credentials themselves to be changed, enabling security measures like key rotation and experimentation with new approaches to validator management.

nnvhq3flpg: SETCODEFROM permanently changes account behavior unless the transaction is reverted, so a contract that exposes this instruction must restrict access to a trusted control path. A valid source can change its own code hash, and it can change between the time an adoption is approved and the time it is executed. An adoption that is pre-approved by a signature or a proposal must specify the expected code hash, not just the source address, and the adopting code must compare EXTCODEHASH(source) to that hash, with no external call, immediately before SETCODEFROM. Unlike EIP-6913, this EIP allows delegated execution to change the caller's account code. This preserves existing proxy upgrade patterns, and wallets should treat such modules as code with upgrade authority and restrict delegatecall targets. Delegating via EIP-7702 to an account that can reach SETCODEFROM means trusting all code that account will adopt in the future, and EOAs are now included here. An EOA that adopts ordinary code cannot be reverted. It cannot initiate ECDSA transactions, it cannot re-delegate with 7702, and there is no instruction to return to empty code. Contracts that verify signatures directly with ecRecover (such as permit) will still recover that address, so a companion change such as EIP-8151 is needed, and with 8151 in place, ecRecover authentication for the account's own address fails permanently. Authentication that relies only on uninitialized state can lock the account, so initialization must be completed within the adoption transaction, and initialization that anyone can perform can be front-run. After adoption, ETH arriving by CALL or a token transfer with a receive hook also executes the adopted code. On chains without EIP-8141, the account acts only when it is called, so code without a relay path such as an ERC-4337 entry point is stuck. If the code is called back by a callback before its initialization finishes, the already adopted code runs on top of incomplete storage, so initialization must be finished before adoption.

nruzf0iuhv: This EIP adds an optional trailing element, new_code_hash, to the CodeChange of EIP-7928. Code installed by creation or by EIP-7702 is recorded as before with two elements, [block_access_index, new_code], and code adopted through SETCODEFROM is recorded with three elements, [block_access_index, b"", new_code_hash]. If an account's code hash changed within a transaction and its end-of-transaction value was set by SETCODEFROM, the three-element form must be used, and a BAL recorded any other way is invalid. The bytecode behind new_code_hash must be present in the pre-block state or in the new_code of a code_changes entry with a lower block access index, and no entry may reference an entry with the same or a higher index. From the moment SETCODEFROM_SOURCE_GAS is charged, the source must be included in the BAL regardless of whether it is valid, and if there are no other changes it is included with an empty change list. If the charge fails, it is not included. In the pre-state-access gas validation of EIP-7928, the pre-state validation cost of SETCODEFROM is SETCODEFROM_SOURCE_GAS. The reason for recording a hash instead of the bytecode is that the bytecode already exists. If the BAL could carry code up to the maximum code size for 9300 gas with a warm source, that would be well under 1 gas per byte, which breaks the assumption behind the EIP-7928 bal_items limit. The hash is a separate element because a 32-byte new_code value cannot be distinguished from 32-byte runtime code. Because the entry format reveals the origin and the size is fixed, it can be metered with a byte-floor approach such as EIP-8279.

nzpkpn343i: Ethereum nodes often run an execution layer (EL) client and a consensus layer (CL) client together on one computer. Until now, however, there was no shared standard for which computer to use as the baseline when measuring and judging performance. Without a standard, three problems arise. First, if each client measures performance in a different environment, benchmark results cannot be compared with each other. Second, it is hard to judge how much more node resources a protocol upgrade uses, because performance characteristics depend heavily on hardware. Third, node operators cannot tell which hardware to invest in to meet the network's future requirements. This EIP tries to solve all three problems by writing the recommended specifications for each role in one place. The source states that clients can be run on hardware below the recommended specifications, but benchmarks and decision making are based on these recommended specifications.

Because of this, participants called MEV searchers can see a user's trade in advance and carry out attacks such as front-running, sandwich attacks, back-running, and censorship. The profits from these attacks are large enough that they have had the side effect of concentrating block-production power in the hands of a small number of highly efficient value extractors. This proposal removes most of the attacker's advantage simply by introducing a one-block delay between when a transaction is included in a block and when its content is revealed. There are also proposals to encrypt the mempool itself (EIP-8184, EIP-8105), but such approaches are complex, which could make them hard for a rapidly scaling Ethereum to adopt. This proposal uses only a simple commit-reveal approach, with no new cryptographic techniques, no new consensus participant role, and no delay added to the block production path.

Review is the state in which the author has requested peer review. Last Call is the final review period right before Final, where the author opens a PR specifying a last-call-deadline (usually 14 days out), and if normative changes become necessary it reverts to Review. Final is the final standard; only error corrections and non-normative clarifications are allowed, and the PR moving from Last Call to Final must not include changes other than the status change. If there is no activity for 6 months or more while in Draft, Review, or Last Call, the EIP moves to Stagnant, and it can be revived by the author or an editor. Withdrawn is a state the author has withdrawn from, and it cannot be revived under the same number. Living is a special status designed to keep being updated without ever reaching final confirmation, and EIP-1 itself is the representative example.

BLS relies on the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem, so once a quantum computer capable of running Shor's algorithm (a CRQC) exists, the secret key can be recovered from the public key alone. Since every validator's and builder's public key is already exposed in the beacon state, BLS must be replaced. However, creating post-quantum keys requires the validator's secret key material and new tooling, and staking pools additionally need coordination between node operators and stakeholders. If this work were all bundled into the same fork that switches the signature scheme, how many validators were actually ready would only become apparent at the moment of that fork. So this EIP splits the replacement into two steps and first introduces a fork that only registers keys. The effective balance of active validators with registered keys can be computed from the state, so the transition point can be set against an observed metric, and if a quantum computer appears to be imminent, the keys registered up to that point can serve as a recovery baseline.

ov1uddnzvj: BFT consensus with accountable fault tolerance requires every validator to participate in two rounds before finalization, so for a validator count n and finalization time f, the per-second message overhead must be at least 2n/f. Taking total supply at roughly 2^27 ETH, with a 32 ETH stake unit there can be up to 2^22 validators, and with 2-epoch (768 second) finalization that comes to roughly 5461 messages per second at most. BLS signature aggregation is what makes this manageable: signatures on the same message can be combined through elliptic curve point addition alone, and the marginal cost of one more signature is 1 bit of data and one point addition. BLS is vulnerable to rogue key attacks, which are defended against by using the deposit message signature as a proof of possession. The epoch length of 32 slots is also a safety minimum that, even if randomness is manipulated, guarantees at least one honest proposer per epoch.

p3tc3yjnb6: BLAKE2 was a finalist in the SHA3 competition and is optimized enough to run faster than MD5 on modern 64-bit CPUs. The problem is that the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is designed around 32-byte big-endian arithmetic, so running BLAKE2, which is tuned for 64-bit little-endian operations, as smart contract code makes gas costs disproportionately expensive relative to the actual amount of computation. In particular, verifying Zcash's proof-of-work algorithm Equihash once requires running the hash function 512 times, which makes verifying a Zcash block header with a Solidity implementation of BLAKE2 practically prohibitively expensive. Providing this function as a precompile that the client computes directly in native code enables interoperability such as BTC Relay style SPV clients that verify Zcash blocks on Ethereum, or trustless atomic swaps between the two chains, and can add a privacy dimension to an otherwise highly transparent Ethereum.
p3zhoslqkb: TLOAD (0x5c) and TSTORE (0x5d) are added. Their stack arguments match SLOAD (0x54) and SSTORE (0x55). TLOAD pops one 32-byte word off the stack as an address, reads the corresponding 32-byte word from transient storage, and pushes it onto the stack. TSTORE pops two words, using the top as the address and the next as the value, and stores it. The addressing scheme is the same as SLOAD/SSTORE: a single 32-byte address points to a unique 32-byte word. Early drafts used 0xb3 and 0xb4 to avoid collisions, but once the collisions were gone the current values were adopted. All values are discarded when the transaction ends.

p7v6oofmmo: Each TCREATE execution pays BASE_OPCODE_COST of 100 and the execution gas that normally accompanies CREATE2 (initcode execution, jumpdest analysis, memory expansion, copy costs). It does not pay CREATE2's account creation cost GAS_NEW_ACCOUNT or EIP-8037's code storage state gas (CPSB of 1530 per byte of deployed code). The code hash cost 6 × ceil(L / 32) is paid as in CREATE2 (L is the deployed code length). Account access costs follow EIP-8038: a cold account access costs COLD_ACCOUNT_ACCESS 3000 and a warm access costs WARM_ACCESS 100. An operation that changes a balance pays ACCOUNT_WRITE 9000 per operation, as with other accounts, and there is no refund. This EIP sets the state gas separately. It is charged not for account creation itself but only for state changes that cannot be reverted by the end of the transaction, and it is refilled if the change is reverted within the same transaction. It applies to every operation that changes the balance of a TCREATE target account, including during initialization. When the balance first becomes positive from an original balance of 0, it pays STATE_BYTES_PER_NEW_ACCOUNT × CPSB, and when an account whose original balance was 0 returns to 0, the same amount is refilled. Other balance changes have no state gas adjustment. There is no upfront creation cost because the client knows, at the time TCREATE executes, that this account's code and nonce will not be written to state.

p8kx358sev: At the start of epoch processing, before process_rewards_and_penalties, process_penalty_factors(state) runs and computes one penalty_factor for each slot of the previous epoch. The reference balance get_slot_reference_balance is get_total_active_balance(state) // SLOTS_PER_EPOCH. For each slot it computes offline_balance, then excess = offline_balance - min(offline_balance, state.smoothed_offline_balance), and sets penalty_factor = min(uint64(1) + PENALTY_SLOPE * excess // get_slot_reference_balance(state), MAX_PENALTY_FACTOR). It then updates the moving average. If offline_balance is greater than the average, the difference divided by OFFLINE_BALANCE_SMOOTHING_FACTOR is added, and if it is smaller, the same amount is subtracted in the same way. If the offline balance does not exceed the moving average, the multiplier is exactly 1, and there is no discount region below 1. The moving average only sets the baseline to subtract from, and the slope is normalized by the active balance per slot, so the shape of the curve does not change with network participation.

pbcmciye0e: Today, the beacon chain's randomness (RANDAO) works by having the block proposer contribute a BLS signature over the epoch number. Once the message and public key are fixed, a BLS signature has exactly one valid value. This uniqueness prevents the proposer from grinding, that is, choosing their own contribution at will. However, BLS is not quantum-resistant. A sufficiently strong quantum computer (CRQC) can recover the secret key from the public key, and an attacker could then compute validators' future contributions and the proposer order far ahead. Once prediction is possible, the existing "reveal or withhold" bias attack also becomes stronger. Today an attacker must hold k consecutive slots at the end of an epoch to choose among 2^k candidates, but an attacker who predicts all honest contributions needs only any k slots within the mixing window. Moreover, the hash-based signatures planned for the consensus layer (lean signatures, the XMSS family) use a salt and so lack uniqueness, and using them directly in RANDAO would allow grinding. A hash chain removes the signature itself and cuts this dependency.

pdnyzl7t8x: EIP-8188's RLP integer uses only as many bytes as needed and automatically becomes 5 bytes after block 2^32 - 1, but the PBT uses fixed offsets, so the width has to be decided once up front. 3 bytes (2^24 - 1 = 16,777,215) is already smaller than the current mainnet block height and is insufficient, and 4 bytes is the maximum that BASIC_DATA can spare without touching nonce or balance. Among the candidates for giving up bytes, nonce has a consensus-level cap set by EIP-2681 at 2^64 - 1, and narrowing balance's width would create a new consensus cap. Only code_size could be narrowed, since its protocol limit (64 KiB) is far smaller than the field's width. The storage leaf could have been widened further, but it uses the same 4 bytes so that it is stored the same way as the account. Because this field cannot grow on its own, the width will need to be widened in a separate fork before mainnet reaches block 2^32 (about 1,600 years away at a 12-second slot time, or about 800 years away at a 6-second slot time).

piopnv4kqj: Gas is split into two dimensions: execution gas (execution-gas) and state gas (state-gas). Because a transaction has only one gas limit value, tx.gas, the reservoir model divides it between the two. In the pre-execution phase, evm_gas = tx.gas - intrinsic_gas and execution_gas_budget = TX_MAX_GAS_LIMIT - intrinsic_gas are set, and gas_left = min(execution_gas_budget, evm_gas) and state_gas_reservoir = evm_gas - gas_left are initialized. In other words, gas above the EIP-7825 limit goes into the reservoir. Execution gas is drawn only from gas_left, while state gas is drawn from the reservoir first and, once it runs out, from gas_left, which increases state_gas_from_gas_left. On revert, gas is refilled in the opposite order (LIFO), starting with gas_left. There are four new counters: evm_state_gas_used (total state gas of the transaction), state_gas_from_gas_left (per frame, state gas borrowed from gas_left), state_gas_baseline (the reservoir value at frame entry), and state_gas_committed (used only by the top-level frame, the portion that must not be reverted). The reservoir is passed entirely to child frames, and the 63/64 rule applies only to gas_left. The GAS opcode returns only gas_left, and the SSTORE GAS_CALL_STIPEND check also looks only at gas_left.

pof0egp1jk: Ethereum has a mechanism called the difficulty bomb. It exponentially raises the mining difficulty over time, progressively lengthening the average block time; it is also called the ice age. As this bomb gradually activated, block production was already slowing down. The problem was that development of Casper, the planned transition to proof-of-stake, had been delayed. If the bomb were left as is, it would become difficult to maintain 15-second blocks through proof-of-work mining. So the proposal is to delay the bomb by about a year and a half to keep mining viable. However, delaying the bomb alone would mean a sudden increase in miner rewards. To offset this, the block reward is lowered to 3 ETH, keeping the system in a state similar to before. The reward reduction also lowers the likelihood of a miner-led chain split as the move to proof-of-stake approaches.

pshb64ym2p: PoW Requirement(0x02) carries a single 64-bit IEEE 754 floating-point value. qNAN, sNAN, INF, -INF, and negative numbers are not allowed. A node that receives this message must thereafter not forward messages with PoW lower than the specified value to the sender. PoW is the average number of iterations needed to find the current BestBit (the number of consecutive leading zero bits in the hash), divided by the message size and TTL: PoW = (2**BestBit) / (size * TTL). It is computed by taking the RLP of the envelope excluding env_nonce (short_rlp), appending env_nonce, taking the sha3 hash (pow_hash), and computing 2**leading_zeros(pow_hash) / (size * ttl). size is the size of the fully RLP-encoded envelope. The Rationale explains that it is better to let the network adjust the requirement itself rather than hardcoding a minimum PoW value.

pvqe7garso: When Ethereum reads an address or storage slot for the first time in a transaction, it charges a high price (cold), and from the second read on it charges a low price (warm). This is because the node incurs a real cost when it first pulls the data out of the database. Under the current rule (EIP-2929), if a call fails and is reverted, the access records for what was read inside that call are erased along with it. However, a revert only cancels state changes. It does not evict data that has already been read from the node's cache. If the same transaction reads that data again, it actually finishes cheaply, but the fee is charged as high as if it were the first read. This EIP aims to remove this mismatch between real cost and fee, and to simplify client implementations by detaching access records from the revert mechanism.

q03le9avi0: ASSERT (value 3) is added to the mode values of an EIP-8141 frame transaction. It is the fourth mode, alongside the existing DEFAULT, VERIFY and SENDER. ASSERT frames must come contiguously at the very end of tx.frames, and once an ASSERT appears, all frames after it must also be ASSERT. If this is violated, the transaction itself is invalid. The caller is ENTRY_POINT and the frame runs as a STATICCALL, so it cannot change state. Unlike VERIFY frames, it has no APPROVE exception either, so calling APPROVE inside an ASSERT call tree aborts with an exception due to a STATICCALL violation. An approval scope flag may be set but has no effect, and the atomic batch flag cannot be set on an ASSERT frame or on the frame immediately before it. If an ASSERT frame reverts or aborts with an exception, the entire execution body is unconditionally reverted, and state and approval context are restored to the point immediately after the frame that set the payer. If it fails when no frame has set the payer, the transaction is invalid under EIP-8141 rules. Remaining ASSERT frames are not executed and are left with receipt status 2 and gas 0, and that gas is refunded at the end of the transaction. Even on failure, the transaction is valid and is included in the block. The failed ASSERT frame's receipt has status 0, and the receipts of the reverted execution body frames keep their status and execution gas, but their logs are discarded and state gas is removed. Changes from the validation prefix (gas payment through APPROVE, account creation by a deploy frame) are finalized as is, and the payer pays for all gas used up to the point of failure. The EIP-8141 default code treats ASSERT the same as SENDER or DEFAULT.

q4phyvlg16: Ethereum currently sets gas fees through a first-price auction. When a block is full, users find it hard to estimate how much they need to pay to be included, repeatedly either overpaying by bidding too high or waiting too long and having to resend after bidding too low. This proposal was written at a time when EIP-1559 was being discussed as a fee market improvement, to offer a concrete alternative for comparison with 1559. Computation-heavy failure-handling code becomes cheaper, so handling that previously ran out of gas may now complete, and loops that run until gasleft() falls below some value will iterate more times. Code whose control flow branches on a read gas value may take a different path after the reduction and then run out of gas. A callee receiving only the 2,300 gas stipend can perform more computation, but still cannot write to storage because of the EIP-2200 check. As computation gets cheaper, more transactions fit in a block, increasing the share of block gas spent on state growth, but this proposal itself does not limit state growth; that role belongs to EIP-8037's state gas dimension. r0utbtobka: The beacon chain has a validators list and a balances list, and every time a new deposit comes in, an entry is simply appended to the end of these lists. Even when a validator is fully withdrawn, its index remains empty and is never reused. Because Ethereum is a system where validators keep entering and exiting over a long period, this approach causes both lists to grow without bound. As state size grows, so does the data clients must hold in memory, the burden of computing the state root, and the work of scanning the entire validator set. This EIP aims to eliminate this unbounded growth problem by reusing indices that are fully withdrawn and have passed enough time to be considered safe.

r33j2olzpi: Blob demand can be expressed as Q(b + c), where b is the blob base fee and c is the execution cost per unit of blob gas (execution_cost * base_fee_per_gas / GAS_PER_BLOB). From the fee update mechanism's point of view, c is a fixed value, so when c > 0 there is an inelastic region where lowering b further does not increase demand. The demand curve becomes effectively vertical, and the supply curve is also perfectly inelastic (vertical) in the long run, so the equilibrium blob fee swings sharply even with small changes in demand or execution fees. If execution costs are so high that equilibrium cannot form at the target supply, the blob fee simply falls to the 1 wei boundary. The reserve price solves this by forcing the equilibrium to form on the boundary between the target supply curve and the reserve price curve.

This EIP proposes explicitly selecting one of those constraints and enforcing it flexibly instead. The weak subjectivity constraint cited as an example in the source is 'no more than 50,400 over two weeks,' which corresponds to 5.04% for a validator set of 1 million. As long as this constraint is maintained over every rolling two-week window, there is no need for a rigid per-epoch cap. If there have been no exits at all in the past 13 days, even an immediate exit of 30,000 validators would not violate the two-week constraint, yet under the current rules this would require waiting 1,875 epochs (8.33 days). r691gtigre: Ethereum nodes find each other through the node discovery protocol. However, the existing discovery v4 can only convey a node's public key (on the secp256k1 curve), IP address, and port number, with no way to carry anything else. There is no way to advertise a new transport protocol or the public key material associated with it. Also, when a node changes its connection endpoint and publishes new information, other nodes have no basis for determining which version is more recent. This EIP resolves these constraints by defining a node record format that holds connection-related information as free-form key/value pairs. Records can be distributed not only through future versions of the discovery protocol but also through other channels such as DNS, ENS, and devp2p subprotocols. Because records carry a signature and a sequence number, when a node changes its connection endpoint and publishes a new record, other nodes can tell which record is more recent.

Restricting the field to accounts whose state changed bounds the overhead at 32 bytes per modified account and adds nothing for entries that were only accessed. regyvjvklc: In Ethereum consensus, validators are split into several committees each slot and send votes (attestations). A vote carries both an LMD GHOST vote for fork choice and a Casper FFG vote for finalizing the chain, and currently the committee number (index) that the validator belongs to is also part of what is signed. So even if the vote contents are exactly the same, a different committee produces a different signature, and the votes cannot be merged into one. In a network with 262144 or more active validator indices, checking the two-thirds threshold requires verifying at least 1366 attestations. The pairing operations needed for signature verification grow accordingly, which burdens every client and costs the most in ZK circuits that prove Casper FFG consensus. A block can also hold only about 2 slots' worth of votes, so if few block proposers are online, not all votes may be included on chain.
